docs.title: Irrigated Cropland Mapping with Geospatial Foundation Models
docs.text:
Evaluating geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) for irrigated cropland mapping in North Africa and their transferability to data-scarce regions

Irrigated agriculture covers about a fifth of the world's cropland but produces around 40% of its food and accounts for most freshwater withdrawals. Knowing where and how much land is irrigated is therefore essential for water management and food security, especially in water-stressed regions such as North Africa. Yet most countries lack accurate, regularly updated irrigation maps, and existing global products are coarse or static. Geospatial foundation models, large models pretrained on vast archives of satellite imagery, promise accurate maps from few labels and better transfer to new regions. This research evaluates that promise for irrigated cropland mapping, using Morocco as a case study. It asks how accurately these models separate irrigated from rainfed cropland compared with conventional satellite-based methods, how much adapting them to the task helps, how consistent their maps are from year to year, and how well a model trained in Morocco transfers to a region with little ground truth.

docs.title: D1. Spatial folds instead of a 70/30 split
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.1): stratified 70 / 30 split, validation subset from the training data. (§4.2.4 already asks for spatial cross-validation.)
  • Now: parcels grouped into 20 km blocks, blocks into 5 folds with equal class balance; every parcel tested once by a model that never saw its block.
  • Why: with a random split, 79% of test parcels lie within 250 m of a training parcel (about 2% with 20 km blocks). Random splits overstate accuracy for mapping new areas (Roberts et al. 2017; Ploton et al. 2020).
  • Where: dataset §5, protocol §2.

docs.title: D2. Two agricultural years (per-parcel season)
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.1): the 2024 annual image stack.
  • Now: each parcel gets the 12 months (1 Sep – 31 Aug) of the season in which it was surveyed: 2023/24 or 2024/25. Both seasons in one dataset, months aligned (month 1 = September).
  • Why: the survey ran Dec 2023 – Jan 2025; using only 2024 would mix seasons, and dropping 2024/25 would lose 42% of the rainfed parcels. The agricultural year covers the winter rainfed cycle and the summer, when only irrigated fields stay green.
  • Consequence: region and year are partly confounded (Gharb and Tadla only 2023/24, Souss only 2024/25).
  • Where: dataset §6.2.

docs.title: D3. Validation: PASTIS rotation instead of nested CV
docs.text:
• Before (E01): nested spatial CV, settings by inner CV on the 4 training folds, refit on 4.
  • Now: per round 3 folds train, the next fold chooses the settings (or stops training), 1 fold tests, as in PASTIS (Garnot & Landrieu 2021).
  • Why: one design for classical classifiers and neural networks (L-TAE, fine-tuning), which need a separate validation fold for early stopping. It is the standard design of the PASTIS crop-mapping benchmark.
  • Where: protocol §2; E01 is kept as the sensitivity check.

docs.title: D4. One shared tile store for every input
docs.text:
• Proposal: annual Sentinel-1/2 composites via STAC and xarray.
  • Now: Google Earth Engine builds non-overlapping 128 × 128 px tiles (1.28 km) with 12 monthly composites × 19 bands; the baseline features and the foundation-model chips are all cut from these tiles.
  • Why: STAC processing was too slow for the full set; with one store every input sees identical pixels, compositing and masks, and chips no longer overlap across folds.
  • Where: dataset §6–7.

docs.title: D5. Frozen encoder + classical classifiers
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.2.1): frozen encoder, train a decoder and classification head.
  • Now: the task is per parcel, so the frozen encoder gives one embedding per parcel and the "head" is a classifier (linear probe and three others). Fine-tuning (LoRA, RQ2) follows as planned.
  • Why: tests what the pretrained representation already contains, at equal cost for every model; the linear probe is the standard test of frozen features.

docs.title: D6. Four classifiers instead of one Random Forest
docs.text:
• Proposal: Random Forest baseline.
  • Now: logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting and SVM on every input (RF stays the headline).
  • Why: a classifier that suits hand-built features (RF) may not suit dense embeddings (E01: RF is the weakest classifier on embeddings). Reporting all four keeps the comparison from depending on one choice.
  • Update (12 Nov 2026): from E02 on, three classifiers: logistic regression (linear probe), random forest (standard remote-sensing classifier, the proposal's baseline) and SVM (strongest in E01), plus a trainable MLP head (E03, E04). Gradient boosting is dropped: in E01 it was never the best classifier and always within the confidence interval of SVM. Plan: RQ1 · Experiment plan.

docs.title: D7. Macro-F1 as the headline metric
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.2.4): OA, precision, recall, F1; best model by mean F1 over the five folds, SD as consistency.
  • Now: macro-F1 of all out-of-fold predictions with a 95% block-bootstrap CI as headline; per-fold mean ± SD is reported too, as the proposal asked.
  • Why: with 86% irrigated parcels, overall accuracy and irrigated F1 are high for any model; macro-F1 weights the rainfed class equally. Paired bootstrap differences say whether a gap is real.

docs.title: D8. Two temporal aggregation pipelines
docs.text:
• Proposal: not specified.
  • Now: PCA pipeline (concat 12 months → PCA 128) in E01 / E02; L-TAE pipeline in E04.
  • Why: PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024) found L-TAE better than linear mapping for single-date encoders; testing both shows whether the conclusion depends on how the months are combined.
  • Where: protocol §5.

docs.title: D9. Cloud Score+ instead of QA60
docs.text:
• Now: Sentinel-2 pixels kept when Cloud Score+ cs_cdf ≥ 0.60; scenes with up to 60% cloud admitted.
  • Why: the QA60 band misses thin cloud and shadow; Cloud Score+ is the recommended mask in Earth Engine (Pasquarella et al. 2023).

docs.title: D10. Transfer region under review
docs.text:
• Proposal (§3.2): zero-shot transfer to Tunisia, validated on 54 GMIA-NEXT points (44 irrigated, 10 rainfed).
  • Now: Morocco first. As an alternative, US state datasets with both irrigated and dryland fields (eastern Washington WSDA, Utah WRLU 2017–2025) would allow a spatial and a multi-year test with the same pipeline.
  • Why: 10 rainfed points are too few to measure a rainfed F1; the US data needs a check of its labels (see the progress log, 4–5 Nov 2026).
  • Decided (12 Nov 2026): Utah (WRLU) as the second region. Explicit rainfed class ("Dry Crop"), 13,000–17,000 rainfed crop fields per year, every year 2017–2025 with one method, one UTM zone. Eastern Washington was the fallback: most of its dryland-wheat fields come from the NASS Cropland Data Layer (irrigation not observed).
  • Superseded the same day by D13: Utah is not a transfer target but an independent second study area.

docs.title: D11. Two kinds of head: parcel benchmark and mapping model
docs.text:
• Proposal (§4.2.1, §4.3): frozen encoder with a decoder / head; annual irrigated maps 2021–2025 for Morocco.
  • Problem: the RQ1 pipeline pools the embeddings over the parcel polygon. Annual maps of Morocco (or of a transfer region) have no polygons, and the GeoFM patches (80 m Clay, 160 m the others) are too coarse for parcels of 0.83 ha (median, about 90 m across).
  • Now:
  • RQ1 benchmark (unchanged): frozen encoder → parcel embedding → LogReg (linear probe), RF, HGB, SVM; plus L-TAE + MLP head (E04). Classical heads on frozen embeddings are common practice (Presto; WorldCereal; AlphaEarth irrigated mapping, Yang et al. 2026) and the head matters little in recent comparisons (Mughees et al. 2026).
  • Mapping models (RQ2–RQ4): frozen GeoFM + UPerNet segmentation head trained on the label pixels of the tiles (as in PANGAEA and Prithvi-EO-2.0), then LoRA with the same head (RQ2). Classical baseline: RF on the S1/S2 features of each pixel.
  • Neural baselines from scratch: TempCNN (per-pixel time series; Pelletier et al. 2019) and U-TAE (tiles; Garnot & Landrieu 2021). Both produce 10 m maps. PSE-TAE needs parcel polygons and stays a parcel-level extra (E05).
  • Same scoring: pixel predictions are aggregated per parcel (mean probability) and scored with the same folds, parcels and bootstrap as RQ1, so every number stays comparable.
  • Why: the research must end in wall-to-wall annual maps; a 1D-CNN beat RF for irrigated mapping (Bazzi et al. 2019) and TempCNN-type models transferred better across regions than GeoFM embeddings (Tong & Wang 2025), so a neural baseline is needed next to the classical one.
  • Where: literature notes.

docs.title: D12. AgriFM with its pretrained 4-px patch embedding
docs.text:
• Before: 02d_embed_agrifm.py built the Sentinel-2 encoder with the patch size of the repository's fine-tuning configuration (configs/cropland_mapping.py: 4 time steps × 2 × 2 px, output stride 16 px) and loaded AgriFM.pth through mmengine. No weight was loaded: the checkpoint names carry the prefix encoder., and the pretrained patch embedding (S2_patch_emd, kernel 128 × 10 × 4 × 4 × 4) does not fit a 2 × 2 px patch. mmengine only warns about mismatched names and still reports success, so all AgriFM embeddings produced up to 6 Nov 2026 (local and on the cluster, including E01) came from a randomly initialised encoder.
  • Now: patch size 4 × 4 × 4 (the size of the pretrained patch embedding), output stride 32 px (320 m; 2 × 2 cells per 64-px chip). The weights are mapped by name in the script and every encoder tensor must load; otherwise the script stops. On the cluster 349 of 349 encoder tensors load.
  • Why: the frozen-encoder comparison (D5) must use each encoder as pretrained. In the fine-tuning set-up of the repository the 2 × 2 px patch embedding is trained anew; with a frozen encoder it would stay random. The alternative, resizing the 4 × 4 px kernel to 2 × 2 px, keeps a finer grid but replaces the pretrained first layer by an approximation.
  • Consequence: AgriFM has the coarsest grid of the four models (320 m against 80–160 m), which matters for small parcels; the patch-share weighting is unchanged. Earlier AgriFM results are void and are re-run.
  • Where: models_run/02d_embed_agrifm.py, Foundation models · inputs.

docs.title: D13. Utah as a second independent study area
docs.text:
• Proposal (§3.2, RQ3, RQ4): RQ4 applies the Morocco-trained model zero-shot to a transfer region (Tunisia, 54 GMIA-NEXT points); RQ3 tests temporal consistency within Morocco.
  • Now:
    • Utah is an independent second study area. It is trained and tested on its own data (WRLU labels), with the same pipeline, foundation models, classifiers and evaluation as Morocco; the two regions are reported side by side. There is no Morocco → Utah transfer.
    • Temporal test in Utah: train on WRLU 2024 (2023/24), test on WRLU 2021 (2020/21) on the folds held out in training (same fields in both years, paired comparison). See Utah training data, section 10.
    • Years: WRLU 2024 (training) and 2021 (test). Between them 36% of the crops change but only 0.07% of the fields change class; 2025 repeats 94% of the 2024 crops and is not an independent year; 2019 shows a sudden jump in class changes (1.35%) that may be a revision of the mapping.
  • Why:
    • A Morocco → Utah transfer mixes a change of region, climate, crop calendar (Utah is 2–3 months later), label source and field size; a low score would not say which of these failed. Two independent studies show whether the conclusions on the foundation models hold in a second region.
    • Morocco cannot offer a clean temporal test (the surveyed regions differ between the two years); in Utah the same places are mapped every year.
    • Tunisia has 10 rainfed reference points, too few for a rainfed F1 (D10).
  • Consequence: RQ4 changes from "spatial transferability of the Morocco model" to "do the results hold in a second region"; RQ3 is answered in Utah. To be agreed with the supervisors.
  • Where: Utah training data, ml_dataset_prep/01_prepare_labels_Utah.py.

docs.title: D14. Sentinel-2 only for every input
docs.text:
• Proposal: Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 time series.
  • Before: the baseline used Sentinel-2 + Sentinel-1 features (one orbit), TerraMind received Sentinel-2 + Sentinel-1, the other three GeoFMs Sentinel-2 only.
  • Now: every input of the model comparison uses Sentinel-2 only: the four GeoFMs (TerraMind with MODALITIES = ["S2L2A"]), the feature baseline (S1S2_VARIABLES = "s2") and PSE-TAE (BANDS = "s2"). No model is given an input it was not pretrained on, and no fusion of embeddings with radar features is designed for the optical-only models.
  • Why:
    • Every model sees the same optical data, so a difference comes from the representation and the head, not from one model having radar.
    • Morocco and Utah are treated alike.
    • Sentinel-1 coverage of Utah changed between the years: after Sentinel-1B failed (December 2021) only Sentinel-1A covered the area in 2023/24 (only the descending orbit was usable), while the 2020/21 test year had both satellites. With radar, the 2024 → 2021 temporal test (D13) would partly measure a change in radar coverage.
  • Consequence: the multimodal pretraining of TerraMind is not used in the main comparison. An optional ablation in Morocco (both orbits available) adds Sentinel-1 to TerraMind (terramind-s1s2) and to the baseline (S1S2_VARIABLES = "all", PSE-TAE morocco_s2s1). E01 (done before this decision) used Sentinel-1 in the baseline and in TerraMind and is kept as it is.
  • Where: Foundation models · Configuration, Models pipeline.

docs.title: D15. AgriFM normalised with the statistics of the region's chips
docs.text:
• Before: AgriFM inputs were normalised with the statistics of the repository's fine-tuning example (configs/cropland_mapping.py).
  • Problem: neither the AgriFM paper (Li et al. 2025) nor the repository documents the normalisation of the pretraining data. The config statistics (blue 4,179 ± 4,042) describe raw, partly cloudy time series; the cloud-masked monthly composites of this study have blue 714 ± 344 (Morocco). With the config statistics the visible and NIR bands use only 8–30% of the expected spread and sit about 0.8 SD below zero, so the frozen encoder sees an almost constant input in these bands.
  • Now: per-band mean and standard deviation of the region's own chips (NORM = "data" in 02d_embed_agrifm.py): all valid pixels of 20 evenly spaced chip files, every 4th pixel; computed from imagery only (no labels), saved to agrifm_norm_stats_<tag>.json and reused. For the Utah temporal test the 2023/24 statistics are reused for 2020/21 (NORM_STATS_FILE), so both years are scaled identically.
  • Why: standardising each band to zero mean and unit variance is what a z-score normalisation with the pretraining statistics does on the pretraining data; when those statistics are unknown, the data's own statistics are the closest equivalent.
  • Sensitivity: the config statistics are kept as a second embedding (NORM = "config", agrifm-cfgnorm_*.npz; the Morocco file made on 6 Nov 2026 is this version).
  • Where: Foundation models · AgriFM, models_run/02d_embed_agrifm.py.

docs.title: Foundation models
docs.text: Four geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) are evaluated in this study. It summarises their design and pretraining, specifies how each model is applied to the Moroccan parcels, and lists the primary sources. Other pages refer to this page rather than repeating its content.

docs.title: Selection
docs.text: The four models were selected according to three criteria: (i) pretrained weights are openly available and can be fine-tuned; (ii) the models accept multi-temporal Sentinel-1 and/or Sentinel-2 input; and (iii) together they represent the principal GeoFM families, namely masked-autoencoder Vision Transformers (Prithvi-EO-2.0, Clay), a multimodal generative model (TerraMind) and an agriculture-specific spatio-temporal model (AgriFM).

docs.title: Configuration in this study
docs.text:
All encoders are used frozen, i.e. as fixed feature extractors without gradient updates. Each model receives a 64 × 64 px chip (640 m) centred on the parcel, with the bands and normalisation statistics of its own pretraining. The parcel embedding is the mean of the patch tokens covering the parcel, weighted by the fraction of each patch inside the parcel (Models pipeline §5). The Sentinel-2 feature baseline is listed for comparison. Every input uses Sentinel-2 only (D14).

Input Chips Bands Patch Temporal handling Output per parcel Script S2 baseline parcel features (inner pixels) 12 S2 bands, NDVI, NDWI, EVI parcel median 12 months concatenated 180 features 03 Clay v1.5 p8 10 S2 bands 8 px (80 m) one month per forward pass 12 × 1024 02a Prithvi-EO-2.0 p16 6 S2 bands (HLS set) 16 px (160 m) four months per pass, three passes 12 × 1024 02b TerraMind p16 12 S2 bands 16 px (160 m) one month per forward pass 12 × 768 02c AgriFM p16 10 S2 bands 4 px pretrained patch embedding; output stride 32 px (320 m) full 12-month stack in one pass 1 × 1024 02d

Sentinel-1 is left out of the main comparison (D14): every model then sees the same optical data, and Sentinel-1 coverage of Utah changed between the years. An optional ablation (Morocco only) adds it back where a model was pretrained on it: TerraMind with Sentinel-1 (MODALITIES = ["S2L2A", "S1GRD"] in script 02c, written as terramind-s1s2_agyear_tiles.npz) and the baseline with radar features (S1S2_VARIABLES = "all" in script 03).

docs.title: Clay v1.5
docs.text: Clay encodes each band together with its central wavelength, which allows a single model to process imagery from different sensors. Ten Sentinel-2 bands (B2–B8A, B11, B12) are standardised with the statistics of Clay's metadata.yaml. Additional inputs are the pixel size (10 m), the acquisition date (week of year, sine/cosine encoded; monthly composites are dated mid-month) and the location (latitude and longitude, sine/cosine encoded). The model processes one date per forward pass, so the twelve months are embedded independently. With 8 px patches, a chip yields an 8 × 8 token grid.

docs.title: Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M-TL
docs.text: Prithvi-EO-2.0 is pretrained on HLS time series and encodes acquisition date and location explicitly. The six HLS bands (Blue, Green, Red, Narrow NIR, SWIR 1, SWIR 2; Sentinel-2 B2, B3, B4, B8A, B11, B12) are standardised with the model's pretraining statistics. Following the pretraining configuration, four frames are processed per pass (September–December, January–April, May–August); each frame retains its own tokens, giving one vector per month. The model is loaded through TerraTorch (prithvi_eo_v2_300_tl). Limitation: pretraining used 30 m HLS data, whereas 10 m Sentinel-2 is used here; the resulting 160 m patch is closer to typical parcel size than the 480 m patch at native resolution.

docs.title: TerraMind-1.0-base
docs.text: TerraMind is trained to generate any of nine modalities from any other and therefore learns a joint representation of optical, radar and auxiliary data. Two modalities are supplied: S2L2A (B1–B12) and S1GRD (VV, VH in dB), each standardised with TerraMind's pretraining statistics. The tokens of the two modalities are averaged (merge_method = "mean"). One date is processed per pass, and 16 px patches give a 4 × 4 token grid.

docs.title: AgriFM
docs.text:
AgriFM is designed for crop mapping and models the temporal dimension within the network. The full 12-month stack of ten Sentinel-2 bands is processed in a single pass. Input tokens span four time steps and 4 × 4 px (the pretrained patch embedding); the final feature map has a stride of 32 px (D12). Because time is compressed inside the network, the output is one vector per parcel and season. Only the encoder is used, through the mmengine registries of the cloned repository.

Normalisation (D15). Neither the AgriFM paper nor the repository documents the normalisation of the pretraining data; the only published statistics belong to the repository's fine-tuning example (configs/cropland_mapping.py, blue 4,179 ± 4,042). The cloud-masked composites of this study are on a different scale (Morocco blue 714 ± 344), so with the config statistics the visible and NIR bands would use only 8–30% of the expected spread. AgriFM is therefore normalised per band with the mean and standard deviation of the region's own chips (NORM = "data"; statistics saved to agrifm_norm_stats_<tag>.json), the usual choice when the pretraining statistics are unknown. The config statistics are kept as a sensitivity run (NORM = "config", file agrifm-cfgnorm_*.npz).

docs.title: Weights
docs.text:
All weights are stored in checkpoints/<model>/ (excluded from version control) and are downloaded automatically on the first run of the corresponding embedding script.

docs.title: Why irrigated cropland matters
docs.text:
Irrigated agriculture covers only about 20% of the world's cultivated land, yet it produces around 40% of global food and accounts for about 70% of all freshwater withdrawals (Wu et al., 2023). With population growth, climate change and increasing water scarcity, reliable information on where irrigation takes place, and how it changes from year to year, is essential for water management, agricultural planning and the Sustainable Development Goals on food (SDG 2) and water (SDG 6).

Morocco is a demanding and relevant case. Agriculture provides about 14% of its GDP, 39% of national employment and 74% of rural employment, and the country has developed more than two million hectares of irrigated land across seven large schemes. At the same time it is among the most water-stressed countries in the world: agriculture uses over 80% of the available water, while rainfall has fallen by about 30% over three decades. National programmes (the Green Morocco Plan 2008–2020 and the Green Generation strategy 2020–2030) expanded drip irrigation from 160,000 ha in 2008 to 585,000 ha in 2019 (Guemouria et al., 2023). Tracking whether this expansion meets its goals, and where water use is most intensive, requires precise and up-to-date irrigated cropland maps.

Much of the rest of North Africa lacks the dense, field-verified irrigation data that exists for Morocco. Methods that can be trained where labels are rich and transferred to agro-climatically similar, data-scarce regions would be a significant step for agricultural monitoring across the region.

docs.title: State of the art
docs.text:
Approach Examples Limitation Global irrigation products GMIA (Siebert et al., 2005; ~9 km), GIAM (Thenkabail et al., 2009) far too coarse for fields of a few hectares 30 m global maps LGRIP30 (Teluguntla et al., 2023; 86.5% overall accuracy), GMIE (Wu et al., 2023) static snapshots or decade-maximum extents, no annual series; locally calibrated thresholds Machine learning on Sentinel-1/2 time series current state of the art for field-scale irrigation mapping depends on hand-built spectral and temporal features; degrades when applied to new regions; hard to combine sensors (Yang et al., 2026)

Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) offer a different route. They are large neural networks pretrained with self-supervised learning on vast unlabelled satellite archives. They learn rich spatio-temporal representations directly from the imagery, without hand-built features, can be adapted to a task with few labels, and may transfer across regions and sensors (Tseng et al., 2023; Szwarcman et al., 2024). Adaptation ranges from a frozen encoder with a light classification head, through parameter-efficient fine-tuning such as LoRA, to full fine-tuning.

docs.title: Research gap
docs.text:
1. No annual irrigated cropland maps exist for Morocco or other North African countries. Global products give static extents, not the year-by-year maps needed to monitor irrigation expansion and evaluate policy. This needs a model that is accurate and consistent from one year to the next.
  2. No geospatial foundation model has been evaluated for irrigated cropland mapping, and none in Africa's diverse agro-hydrological landscapes, from semi-arid to sub-humid climates and from flood to drip and pivot irrigation.
  3. It is unknown which foundation model suits the task best, how much fine-tuning adds to a frozen encoder, and whether a model trained in one region still works in a data-scarce region nearby.

docs.title: Objectives and research questions
docs.text:
Main objective: to compare the performance and transferability of geospatial foundation models for irrigated cropland mapping.

Objective Research question 1 · Compare models and adaptation strategies in Morocco RQ1 What classification accuracy does each foundation model achieve for irrigated cropland mapping across Morocco's agricultural regions, and how does it compare with a conventional Sentinel-based classifier? RQ2 To what extent does parameter-efficient fine-tuning improve on a frozen encoder? 2 · Evaluate temporal and spatial transferability of the best model RQ3 How temporally consistent is the best model across years, and does the annual map series for Morocco (2021–2025) reflect the irrigation trends in national statistics? RQ4 When the Morocco-trained model is applied without retraining to another region, how much does accuracy degrade, and do its annual maps stay consistent? 3 · Optional extension: multi-model fusion RQ5 Does fusing the embeddings of several foundation models improve on the best single model?

docs.title: Study area and data
docs.text:
Morocco. Five major agricultural regions that together span the country's diversity (Ouassanouan et al., 2026):

Region Climate Irrigation and crops El Gharb humid surface-water irrigation; rice, vegetables Tadla semi-arid to sub-humid large-scale irrigation; sugar beet, cereals Doukkala Mediterranean mixed irrigated and rainfed systems El Haouz semi-arid groundwater irrigation; olives, citrus Souss arid advanced drip systems; high-value export crops

Second study area. The proposal applied the best Morocco-trained model, without retraining, to Tunisia, validated with the GMIA-NEXT reference points (Kebede et al., 2026), which include only 10 rainfed points. Instead, Utah (USA) is studied as an independent second region with its own field-level labels (Water-Related Land Use, Utah Division of Water Resources), and it also provides the temporal test: models trained on 2024 are tested on 2021 (decision D13, Utah training data).

Data Use Field survey, Ouassanouan et al. (2026): 8,826 georeferenced parcels with crop type, irrigation status and irrigation system (8,781 after cleaning: 7,585 irrigated, 1,196 rainfed) training and validation in Morocco Sentinel-2 multispectral (10 m) and Sentinel-1 SAR (VV, VH) time series model input GMIE, LGRIP30, FAO WaPOR, FAO AQUASTAT comparison of the maps with existing products and national statistics

docs.title: Models compared
docs.text: Four openly available GeoFMs are evaluated: Prithvi-EO-2.0 (NASA, IBM), Clay v1.5 (Clay Foundation), TerraMind (IBM, ESA) and AgriFM (Li et al., 2025). They accept multi-temporal Sentinel-1/2 input and together represent the principal GeoFM families: masked-autoencoder Vision Transformers, a multimodal generative model and an agriculture-specific spatio-temporal model. Architecture, pretraining, configuration and sources are given in Foundation models.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
flowchart LR A["<b>1 · Data preparation</b><br/>Sentinel-1/2 time series<br/>parcel labels · spatial folds"] --> B["<b>2 · Model evaluation</b><br/>frozen encoders · fine-tuning (LoRA)<br/>vs a Sentinel-based baseline"] B --> C["<b>3 · Annual mapping</b><br/>Morocco 2021–2025<br/>temporal consistency"] C --> D["<b>4 · Transferability</b><br/>zero-shot application<br/>to a data-scarce region"] B -.-> E["<i>optional</i><br/>multi-model fusion"]

How each step is carried out: Method.

docs.title: Expected outcomes
docs.text:
1. A comprehensive evaluation of four geospatial foundation models for irrigated cropland mapping in North Africa, against a strong Sentinel-based baseline under spatial validation.
  2. A comparison of frozen-encoder and parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies for this task.
  3. Annual irrigated cropland maps for Morocco at 10 m resolution for 2021–2025, checked against national statistics.
  4. An assessment of the temporal consistency of foundation-model predictions across years.
  5. An assessment of how far the best model transfers to a data-scarce region.
  6. A reusable, ML-ready dataset of irrigated and rainfed parcels with spatial folds.

Full proposal

Background, literature, methods, risks and the work plan in detail: Research proposal (PDF)

docs.title: 2026-11-13 (review before running E02–E05: fixes)
docs.text: An independent code review (no data leakage found; draws identical across scripts; E02 and E03 inputs identical, checked) and a docs check led to these fixes: - Quick checks (QUICK_TEST, QUICK = True) write to experiments/<E>/results_quick/ and write no report; before, a quick run left oof_predictions.csv in the real folder and the real run would have been skipped. - Nested label-efficiency draws: one random order of the blocks per region, round and draw; a fraction takes its first blocks (10% ⊂ 25% ⊂ 50%), accepted if the first 10% hold ≥ 20 rainfed parcels. - Single-seed curve points: 03b and 03c save oof_per_seed.csv; the 100% point of a neural learning curve is the mean over its seeds scored one by one, like the single-seed label-efficiency runs. Training parcels per fraction are reported. - 04: the Holm family is the experiment's own runs only; new paired table differences_vs_earlier_experiments.csv (same input, this experiment's head vs the earlier experiments' heads: E03 vs E02, E04 vs E03 and E02); a borrowed experiment without runs or a missing baseline stops the script; development-mode paths built after the region override. - 05: reports every head (the filter dropped MLP / L-TAE / PSE-TAE); runs without a baseline (E05). - Runners: run_experiment.py and submit_slurm.py drop stray EXPERIMENT_* shell variables and set every run variable explicitly; submit_slurm.py submits a compare job only when the borrowed experiments are finished (or WAIT_FOR). - E04 config: HEAD: ltae (it would have run the MLP head); breakdown step added to E02–E05. - Report: sections for the head-vs-head table, spread over seeds, L-TAE attention per month, permutation importance, training curves and results by zone. - Docs: seeds (42, 1042, 2042), L-TAE time encoding, E04 implementation section, results-page contents (PCA explained variance dropped; crop-group breakdown and compute cost marked as later / by hand), status table.

docs.title: 2026-11-12 (Utah: second study area, years 2024 + 2021)
docs.text:
• D13: Utah is an independent second study area (no Morocco → Utah transfer); RQ3 temporal test in Utah: train on WRLU 2024 (2023/24), test on WRLU 2021 (2020/21) on the held-out folds. D10, Phase 3, the research plan, the introduction and the progress report reworded.
  • Label change between years for all labelled crop fields of WRLU, compared with 2024 (outputs/utah/dataset/01_labels/year_change_vs_2024.csv): crops change 27–41%, class 0.01–0.07% since 2021, 1.35% in 2019 (sudden jump, possibly a revision of the mapping); 2025 repeats 94% of the 2024 crops.
  • 01_prepare_labels_Utah.py: YEARS = [2024, 2021]. Re-run 01, 02 and 03 (plan only): 12,015 fields in 550 cells (2024: 5,000 irrigated + 1,013 rainfed; 2021: 4,987 + 1,015), 183 blocks, 5,436 tiles (2,720 + 2,716). The earlier 2024 + 2025 label rasters were removed (tmp_trash/).
  • Utah training data rewritten with the full design: study design, choice of years, the label-change table, sampling algorithm (cells, strata, block cap, seed), what is labelled in a tile, why a sample, one tile per place and year, temporal test (scores A, B, C), running one year at a time, limitations.

docs.title: 2026-11-12 (Utah training data; one pipeline for two regions; outputs per region)
docs.text:
• Transfer region = Utah (WRLU, Utah Division of Water Resources), see D10 and Utah training data. Data copied to data/Utah_field_data/ (WRLU 2017–2025).
  • One pipeline for both regions.
  • ml_dataset_prep/01_prepare_labels.py renamed 01_prepare_labels_Morocco.py; new 01_prepare_labels_Utah.py. Both write the same file layout and columns.
  • New ml_dataset_prep/regions.py: the settings that differ per region (projection, first month of the agricultural year, block size, map boundaries). Scripts 02–04 and models_run/01_inspect_dataset.py have REGION = "morocco" | "utah" at the top.
  • Admin boundaries now FAO GAUL (data/admin_boundaries/: 2015 level 0 for Morocco, 2024 level 1 for the US states), replacing GADM; the region's features are cached in outputs/<region>/dataset/admin_boundaries.geojson.
  • Field survey moved to data/Morocco_field_survey/.
  • Outputs per region: outputs/morocco/{dataset, study, analysis} (all existing outputs, moved unchanged) and outputs/utah/dataset. Paths updated in ml_dataset_prep/, models_run/, tools/, experiments/make_report.py. The HPC copy still uses the old layout (outputs/dataset, outputs/study); it must be moved the same way before the next sync (only when asked).
  • Morocco unchanged: steps 01–03 (03 without download) re-run into a scratch folder give identical parcels, folds, blocks and tile plan (8,781 parcels, 2,987 tiles).
  • 02_make_spatial_folds.py: the class-similarity curve uses only pairs of the same agricultural year (the same Utah field in two years is not two samples). Folds are not affected.
  • One year at a time (SEASONS setting): 03_build_tiles.py still plans and writes label rasters for every year in the parcel file (parcel numbers and tile index never change), but downloads only the years in SEASONS; 04_make_views.py builds views of the years in SEASONS into their own folder (views_2023-24/), views/ when SEASONS = None (all years, as for Morocco). models_run/01_inspect_dataset.py: new setting VIEWS_NAME. Tested without download (Utah) and on 50 Moroccan parcels of 2024/25 (scratch folder).
  • 02_make_spatial_folds.py now also draws spatial_folds_blocks.png: the blocks coloured by fold, with the fold number in each block and zooms on the N_ZOOMS densest windows of ZOOM_BLOCKS × ZOOM_BLOCKS blocks. The Moroccan figure of the same name was made by hand earlier; a re-run of 02 for Morocco replaces it with this one.
  • Utah dataset (WRLU 2024 → 2023/24, 2025 → 2024/25; water year 1 Oct – 30 Sep):
  • labels: Flood / Sprinkler / Drip / Pivot / Wheel = irrigated, Dry Crop = rainfed; Sub-irrigated dropped; crop groups grain/seeds, hay/turf, field crops. WRLU 2025 split Sprinkler into Sprinkler / Pivot / Wheel; the first run missed Pivot and Wheel (20,000 fewer irrigated fields in 2025) and was corrected.
  • sampling: 550 cells of 1.28 km (400 with rainfed, 150 irrigated only; ≤ 6 per 20 km block), all fields inside → 11,804 fields (9,728 irrigated, 2,076 rainfed, 17.6%).
  • folds: class similarity reaches the random level at 15–20 km → 20 km blocks (193 blocks).
  • tile plan: 5,603 tiles, label rasters written; Sentinel download not yet run.
  • only 14 of 5,850 fields change class between 2024 and 2025 → temporal tests must also hold out space.
  • a run of 01 at 15:33 gave 11,806 fields; runs in condaml give 11,804 every time (one rainfed alfalfa field, UT2024_62293 / UT2025_62293, fewer). The difference probably comes from another GDAL / GEOS version. The current files come from condaml (11,804); 02 and 03 (plan) were re-run from them. Run the pipeline in condaml only.
  • 01_prepare_labels_Utah.py step 4b (EXPORT_ALL_FIELDS): all labelled crop fields before sampling (2024: 107,348 irrigated + 15,276 rainfed; 2025: 108,536 + 15,186) -> all_crop_fields.gpkg with a column sampled, all_fields_summary.csv, all_fields_by_zone.csv and figures (map per year, class balance and size, crops). The sample holds 4.5% of the irrigated and 6.8% of the rainfed fields.

docs.title: 2026-11-12 (results by region and purity; AgriFM input scale examined)
docs.text:
• What: new script models_run/05_breakdown_oof.py splits the out-of-fold predictions of an experiment by zone, agricultural year, 16-px patch purity and parcel area, with Doukkala-only macro-F1 and the false-rainfed rate in the irrigated-only zones (block-bootstrap CIs). Run on E01; results in experiments/E01_frozen_pca_nested/results/breakdown/. Described in Frozen encoders §7.1.
  • Why: a review of the dataset found that the class is confounded with the region (94% of the rainfed parcels in Doukkala) and that 78% of the parcels have a 16-px patch purity below 0.5.
  • Finding (E01): in Doukkala no frozen GeoFM exceeds the baseline; the GeoFM advantage in the hardest fold comes from the 69 rainfed parcels of Souss.
  • AgriFM: the normalisation statistics of configs/cropland_mapping.py do not match the Earth Engine composites (blue: chips 728 ± 344, config 4,179 ± 4,042). The AgriFM paper does not report its normalisation; its pretraining is supervised on GLC_FCS30D land-cover fractions, with 5-day Sentinel-2 series (16 frames per sample).

docs.title: 2026-11-06 (reference summary: GMIA-NEXT)

docs.title: 2026-11-06 (AgriFM weights were not loaded; fixed)
docs.text:
• What: models_run/02d_embed_agrifm.py loads AgriFM.pth by name (prefix encoder. removed, S2_patch_emd → patch_emd.proj) and stops unless every encoder tensor loads; patch size 4 × 4 × 4 px (the pretrained patch embedding), output stride 32 px (STRIDE_PX = 32); a check stops the run if the feature grid does not match the stride. Decision D12.
  • Why: the AgriFM embeddings on the local machine and on the cluster disagreed (cosine similarity ≈ 0.05 against ≈ 1.0 for TerraMind). The cause: no pretrained weight had been loaded (mmengine reported success despite the mismatch), so all earlier AgriFM embeddings, including E01, came from a randomly initialised encoder.
  • Where: AgriFM re-embedded and re-trained on the cluster; old outputs kept as *_random_init on the cluster.

docs.title: 2026-11-06 (content from the results presentation of week 45)
docs.text: Only content that is still valid for the current pipeline was taken over; numbers from the earlier 30-day pipeline were not. - E01 report: new section Additional analyses from the E01 result files — random vs spatial CV (all inputs), grouped permutation importance of the baseline (variables and months) with figure, settings selected per round. - RQ1 page §6.2: principle and fixed settings of each classifier (L2/lbfgs, 500 trees, HGB early stopping off and why, SVM without probability calibration). - Evaluation protocol: why a fold rotation instead of one fixed split; no kappa (Pontius & Millones 2011); block bootstrap (Künsch 1989). - ML-ready dataset §6.2: crop calendar and the reasons for the September–August agricultural year. - References: Valavi 2019, Schratz 2019, Karasiak 2022, Orynbaikyzy 2022, Künsch 1989, Gao 2018, Elwan 2022. - tools/a6_copy_doc_figures.py also copies the two E01 figures.

New experiments/: one folder per experiment with config.yaml (all settings, same names as the scripts), README.md (question, why, what changes, how to run), REPORT.md (answer first; tables and figures generated) and results/. run_experiment.py runs the steps of a config (train_evaluate per input, compare, report), skips finished runs and saves config + git commit + dates in results/run_info.json. make_report.py writes the tables (macro-F1 per input × classifier, differences vs baseline with Holm verdict, per-class metrics with CI, macro-F1 per fold) and two figures into REPORT.md, and refreshes experiments/README.md and docs/05_results.md. When set (or by run_experiment.py), the config's section replaces the settings, unknown names stop the run, results go to experiments/<name>/results/; finished runs are skipped. 03: derived paths moved below the override; no _nested suffix inside an experiment. 04: compares all runs of the experiment, baseline found automatically, EXTRA_RUNS adds runs of other experiments (PCA vs L-TAE); figure title names the experiment.

Without it every models_run script stopped with "views_info.json not found".

docs.title: 2026-11-05 (US parcel data: geodatabases converted to shapefiles; IrrMap code checked)
docs.text:
• Data in IrrMap/US_Parcel_Data (outside this repo). New script there: gdb_to_shp.py (settings at top, resumable in chunks). Output next to each source in <gdb name>_shp/, original CRS, checked against the source (same feature count and total area for every layer).
  • Arizona folder = USGS Verified irrigated agricultural lands 2002-17: 14 state layers (AZ, CA, CO, FL, GA, ID, IL, MS, MT, NM, TX, UT, WA, WY), irrigated only (IRG_STATUS, IRG_SYS, CROP_TYPE, DATA_DATE, DATA_YEAR).
  • Washington = WSDA crop distribution 2025, 222,520 fields; crop names joined from the WSDACrop table. 137,185 fields have Irrigation = "None" -> candidate rainfed/dryland class (to verify: fallow, pasture, CRP).
  • Colorado CRDSS Div 5 (2000-2023) and Utah WRLU (2017-2024) were already shapefiles.
  • Field names shortened to 10 characters (e.g. InitialSurveyDate -> InitSurvey); dates stored as text YYYY-MM-DD.

  • IrrMap code check: random 80/20 split of single-date patches; ~100% of test patch locations also appear in train on other dates (WA 2018: 31,056 of 31,064) -> their scores are not spatially independent. Test set also used for per-epoch evaluation. Minor bugs (missing argparse import, undefined src_path, constant LAND_TYPE band). Reusable for phase 2: the label sources only, not their patches.

  • Usefulness check (both classes needed):

  • Washington WSDA 2025 - most useful. Field crops (cereal, oilseed, vegetable, hay, seed): 53,723 rainfed (Irrigation = None) vs 33,172 irrigated; rainfed mainly in the dry east (Whitman, Spokane, Lincoln, Adams). Use eastern WA only (semi-arid, winter rain, dryland wheat next to irrigated fields = closest US match to Morocco).
  • Utah WRLU 2017-2025 - useful, adds years. 2023: 15,611 "Dry Crop" vs 110,907 irrigated (fallow/pasture removed). Yearly maps -> temporal transfer test.
  • USGS verified irrigated lands 2002-17 (Arizona folder) and Colorado CRDSS Div 5: irrigated only -> no rainfed class; at most extra irrigated examples.
  • Label definitions: Utah metadata defines "Dry Crop" = no irrigation method applied, crop watered by natural processes (rain); "None" there = non-agricultural land. WSDA has no public definition of Irrigation = "None" (WSDA's own "Dryland Crops" layer = crops grown without irrigation water). 34,235 of the 53,723 WA "None" crop fields come from NASS (CDL), not WSDA ground survey -> irrigation probably not observed. Use DataSource = WSDA only: 19,390 rainfed vs 23,705 irrigated.

docs.title: 2026-11-04 (future phase: US data for spatial and temporal transfer — decision deferred)
docs.text: Discussed after reading IrrMap (Mandal et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.08273). Decision: complete Morocco first; come back to this later. - IrrMap itself is not usable as the study area. It labels irrigation method (flood / sprinkler / drip, all else "other"); there is no rainfed class, so irrigated vs rainfed cannot be studied with it. Its labels come from state agency maps (not field survey); inputs are single-season 224 px patches; validation is a random 80/20 split per state, with no validation split and no spatial test; only a U-Net (ResNet-34) is benchmarked, no GeoFMs. -> Keep Morocco as the AOI (field-surveyed labels, data-scarce region, 12-month time series, spatial folds). Cite IrrMap as related work and as a model for the dataset paper (Part 1). - Idea for a second phase: use the original field boundaries and labels behind IrrMap (state datasets), build chips from scratch with the same pipeline (labels -> 20 km block folds -> tile store -> chips -> embeddings -> same classifiers and validation), to test spatial and temporal transferability. - Why it is valuable: state data often covers many years over the same fields -> clean temporal transfer (train earlier years, test later years), which Morocco cannot offer (year and region overlap); a second continent tests whether GeoFMs transfer better than S1/S2 features (Morocco <-> US). - Conditions: (1) the source data must contain non-irrigated / dryland parcels (deal-breaker; e.g. Washington agricultural land-use data includes dryland wheat — to be checked state by state); (2) small scope: 1-2 states, 3-4 years, ~10-20k parcels; (3) only after Morocco is finished. - Pipeline changes needed: new label reader in ml_dataset_prep/01_prepare_labels.py; support other UTM zones in 03_build_tiles.py (now fixed to UTM 29N; western US spans zones 10-13); US season window via START_MONTH; optional fold by year in 02; a new transfer evaluation (train region/year A, test B). models_run/ unchanged. - Risks: administrative (noisier) labels; different crop systems (Morocco <-> US transfer may be poor for all models); ~4-8 extra weeks. - First step when resuming: one-day check of which state sources IrrMap used, whether they include dryland / non-irrigated fields, which years, and whether field boundaries are downloadable. - Fallback if the check fails: keep as future work; use GMIA-NEXT ground-truth points (tools/a1) or Tunisia as the external test.

docs.title: 2026-11-04 (validation design: PASTIS scheme)
docs.text:
• models_run/03_train_evaluate.py: new setting VALIDATION = "pastis" (default). Per round: 3 folds train, the next fold (k + 1) is the validation fold that chooses the hyperparameters, fold k is the test fold; the model is trained on the 3 training folds. Same scheme as PASTIS (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) and 03b_train_psetae.py, so classifiers and the neural-network baseline are trained, tuned and tested identically. VALIDATION = "nested" keeps the earlier design (inner spatial CV on 4 folds, refit on 4) for a sensitivity check; its runs get the suffix _nested, so run names of the default stay the ones 04_compare_models.py expects.

  • Results produced before this change used the nested design.

• New chip design (tile store) replacing 04_download_chips.py (moved to archive/scripts_2026-10-27/):
  • 04_build_tiles.py: fixed non-overlapping 128 x 128 px tiles (1.28 km) in EPSG:32629; only tiles needed by the parcels (1,755 home + 302 outline + 930 context = 2,987 tiles); 12 monthly composites x 19 bands: S2 median (Cloud Score+), S2 clear-observation count, S1 ascending / descending separately as linear-power mean -> dB, S1 scene counts; label (0 ignore / 1 irrigated / 2 rainfed), parcel_idx and edge rasters; scene IDs per tile and month; QA per tile; GeoParquet tile index with fold (87 tiles hold parcels of two folds -> mixed_folds).

Last updated: 6 November 2026

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The dataset is complete: 8,781 field-surveyed parcels with Sentinel-1/2 time series of their agricultural year, five spatial folds and a shared tile store. Embeddings of all four foundation models are computed. The first RQ1 experiment shows that no frozen foundation model beats a well-designed Sentinel-1/2 baseline on average (macro-F1 0.910 for the best pair vs 0.906), while Clay and Prithvi hold up better in the hardest region. The main RQ1 run with the final validation design is ready, and a second way of combining the months (L-TAE) is planned. The experiment setup, documentation and website are in place, so every result can be rerun and traced.

docs.title: Research plan
docs.text: The study is organised in five phases that follow the objectives and research questions of the Introduction, followed by a closing phase of synthesis and dissemination.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: This page summarises the completed experiments in chronological order, each with its principal finding and main figure. Full tables, per-fold results and caveats are given in the individual experiment reports. The list of all experiments, including those still to run, is on the Experiments page.

docs.title: Where each research question stands
docs.text: Phase RQ Question (short) Current answer Evidence 2 RQ1 Do frozen GeoFMs beat a Sentinel-2 classifier? Not in Morocco; slightly in Utah. Best model built only on our labels vs best frozen GeoFM: Morocco 0.911 (PSE-TAE) vs 0.906 (Clay + L-TAE), a tie; Utah 0.764 (S2 + RF) vs 0.791 (Clay + SVM), and Clay is significantly above PSE-TAE (+0.036). Neither the head (E02, E03) nor the temporal aggregation (E04) changes this. No label-efficiency advantage in Morocco; in Utah the GeoFMs need fewer labels. E05 · E04 · E03 · E02 2 RQ2 Does LoRA fine-tuning improve on the frozen encoders? not started – 3, 5 RQ3 Is the best model consistent across years, and do the annual maps follow national statistics? not started – 3, 5 RQ4 How far does accuracy degrade in another region? not started – 4 RQ5 Does fusing several models improve on the best single model? optional, not started –

docs.title: E01 · Frozen GeoFMs + PCA + classical classifiers (nested spatial CV)
docs.text:
Do frozen foundation-model embeddings separate irrigated from rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-1/2 features, with the same parcels, folds and classifiers?

  • Result: best Clay v1.5 + SVM 0.910; best baseline SVM 0.906; 0 of 16 pairs better, 2 worse than the baseline (Holm).
  • Answer: No frozen GeoFM beats the S1/S2 baseline (best Clay + SVM 0.910 vs 0.906, difference within the noise); Clay and Prithvi hold up better in the hardest fold.
  • Full report: E01 report

docs.title: E02 · Frozen GeoFMs + PCA + classical classifiers
docs.text:
Do frozen foundation-model embeddings separate irrigated from rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-2 features, with the same parcels, folds and classifiers? (Sentinel-2 only for every input, D14)

  • Result: Morocco: best Clay v1.5 + SVM 0.901; best baseline SVM 0.900; 0 of 12 pairs better, 2 worse than the baseline (Holm) · Utah 2023/24: best Clay v1.5 + SVM 0.791; best baseline RF 0.764; 4 of 12 pairs better, 2 worse than the baseline (Holm).
  • Answer: Morocco: GeoFMs equal the S2 baseline (about 0.90 with SVM), AgriFM worse. Utah: Clay, Prithvi, TerraMind +0.05 to +0.06 with SVM; the best GeoFM (Clay SVM 0.791) is 0.03 above the baseline best head (RF 0.764).
  • Full report: E02 report

docs.title: E03 · Frozen GeoFMs + PCA + MLP head
docs.text:
Does a trainable neural head get more out of the same PCA input than logistic regression, random forest and SVM?

  • Result: Morocco: best S2 baseline (MLP) + MLP 0.908; best baseline MLP 0.908; 0 of 4 pairs better, 1 worse than the baseline (Holm) · Utah 2023/24: best TerraMind (MLP) + MLP 0.785; best baseline MLP 0.739; 3 of 4 pairs better, 0 worse than the baseline (Holm).
  • Answer: MLP head = SVM for every input, not better. Morocco: S2 + MLP best (0.908), GeoFMs 0.01-0.02 lower. Utah: GeoFMs + MLP beat S2 + MLP by 0.04-0.05, but S2 RF (E02) stays its best head.
  • Full report: E03 report

docs.title: E04 · Frozen GeoFMs + L-TAE temporal aggregation + MLP head
docs.text:
Does a learned temporal aggregation (L-TAE) of the monthly embeddings classify better than concat + PCA, for the GeoFMs and for the monthly Sentinel-2 features? (Sentinel-2 only, D14)

  • Result: Morocco: best Clay v1.5 (L-TAE) + L-TAE 0.906; best baseline L-TAE 0.905; 0 of 3 pairs better, 0 worse than the baseline (Holm) · Utah 2023/24: best Clay v1.5 (L-TAE) + L-TAE 0.784; best baseline L-TAE 0.743; 2 of 3 pairs better, 0 worse than the baseline (Holm).
  • Answer: L-TAE = concat + PCA with the same MLP (within 0.01), not better. Morocco: Clay 0.906 ties S2 0.905. Utah: Clay and Prithvi +0.04 over S2 with the same head; +0.02 over the S2 RF.
  • Full report: E04 report

docs.title: E05 · PSE-TAE trained from scratch on Sentinel-2 pixel sets (neural baseline)
docs.text:
Does a temporal deep model trained only on our labelled parcels match the frozen foundation models?

  • Result: Morocco: best PSE-TAE + PSE-TAE 0.911; 0 of 1 pairs better, 0 worse than the baseline (Holm) · Utah 2023/24: best PSE-TAE + PSE-TAE 0.755; 0 of 1 pairs better, 0 worse than the baseline (Holm).
  • Answer: Morocco: PSE-TAE 0.911 ties the best S2 and GeoFM runs (within 0.01). Utah: PSE-TAE 0.755 = S2 RF, significantly below Clay (-0.03 to -0.04).
  • Full report: E05 report

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page specifies the software environment, the required input data and model weights, the execution order of the scripts and the structure of the repository.

docs.title: 1. Environment
docs.text:
# creates "condaml" (or: conda env update -n condaml -f environment.yml)
conda env create -f environment.yml                 
conda activate condaml

# Clay (--no-deps: avoids an einops conflict with TerraTorch)
pip install --no-deps git+https://github.com/Clay-foundation/model.git  

# AgriFM
pip install mmengine

A GPU (CUDA or Apple Silicon) is recommended for the embedding scripts. Everything else runs on a CPU.

docs.title: 2. Earth Engine
docs.text: Only ml_dataset_prep/03_build_tiles.py uses Earth Engine. Put the service-account key in secrets/ (path set at the top of the script), or run earthengine authenticate once.

docs.title: 3. Input data
docs.text:
File Source Where Field survey (parcels with land use and irrigation method) Ouassanouan et al. (2026), Scientific Data data/field_survey/lulc_fielddata.shp Morocco boundary GADM 4.1 data/admin/gadm41_MAR_0.json

The Sentinel-1/2 imagery is not downloaded by hand. 03_build_tiles.py fetches it from Earth Engine.

docs.title: 4. Model weights
docs.text:
All weights are stored in checkpoints/<model>/ and are downloaded automatically on the first run of each embedding script; later runs reuse them. Folders and sources per model: Foundation models · Weights.

Only the Clay code needs installing by hand (pip install --no-deps git+https://github.com/Clay-foundation/model.git, see Environment above); TerraTorch (Prithvi, TerraMind) and mmengine (AgriFM) come with environment.yml.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Run every script from the project folder. Each script has its settings at the top. A description at the top of each script explains what it does and what it writes.

# Phase 1 · dataset
python ml_dataset_prep/01_prepare_labels.py
python ml_dataset_prep/02_make_spatial_folds.py
python ml_dataset_prep/03_build_tiles.py       
python ml_dataset_prep/04_make_views.py

# Phase 2 · model evaluation
python models_run/01_inspect_dataset.py          # check the data before training
python models_run/02a_embed_clay.py              # 02a–02d: GPU recommended, resumable
python models_run/02b_embed_prithvi.py
python models_run/02c_embed_terramind.py
python models_run/02d_embed_agrifm.py

# Experiments · training, comparison and report from one config file
python experiments/run_experiment.py             # set EXPERIMENT at the top, e.g. "E02_frozen_pca"

For a quick check before a full run, set N_TEST_TILES = 20 in 03_build_tiles.py and QUICK_TEST: true in the experiment's config.yaml. How experiments work, and how to add one: Experiments.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: Every reported result is produced by an experiment: a self-contained folder that records the research question, the complete configuration and the outputs. Each experiment can be re-run from its configuration file and reproduces the reported result.

docs.text:

The experiments of RQ1 follow the RQ1 experiment plan: E02 (PCA + LogReg / RF / SVM), E03 (PCA + MLP), E04 (L-TAE + MLP) and E05 (PSE-TAE from scratch), each in Morocco and Utah. Every experiment E02–E05 also includes the label-efficiency runs (10, 25 and 50% of the training blocks), so its report shows a learning curve next to the main result. docs.text:
An experiment has two halves: what is run lives in experiments/, what is read lives here in the documentation.

experiments/E02_frozen_pca/          (run)
├── config.yaml        ALL settings of the experiment (the only file you edit to change a run)
└── results/           written by the scripts

    ├── morocco/           one folder per region
    │   ├── <run>/             one folder per input (and per label-efficiency fraction and draw: <run>_f010_d1)
    │   ├── comparison/        all inputs on the same parcels, differences vs the baseline, learning curves
    │   └── breakdown/         results by zone, season and purity (E02)
    └── utah/

docs/experiments/E02_frozen_pca/     (read: this website)
├── index.md           setup: question, why, what changes vs the previous experiment, how to run
├── report.md          answer first, then tables and figures (generated) and interpretation (by hand)
└── figures/           figures of the report (written by make_report.py)

experiments/run_experiment.py   runs one experiment from its config: training, comparison, report
experiments/make_report.py      writes tables + figures into report.md, this page, the results page and the menu
experiments/_template/          config.yaml, index.md and report.md to start a new experiment

docs.title: How an experiment runs
docs.text:
flowchart LR CFG["<b>config.yaml</b><br/>inputs · steps · settings"] --> RUN["<b>run_experiment.py</b>"] RUN --> S1["<b>train_evaluate</b><br/>models_run/03 · once per input"] RUN --> S2["<b>ltae</b><br/>models_run/03c · once per input"] S1 --> R["results/<region>/<run>/<br/>out-of-fold predictions"] S2 --> R R --> C["<b>compare</b><br/>models_run/04<br/>same parcels · paired bootstrap"] C --> REP["<b>report</b><br/>make_report.py"] REP --> MD["docs/experiments/<name>/report.md<br/>experiment list · results page<br/>site menu"] EMB[("outputs/morocco/study/02_embeddings<br/>shared by all experiments")] -.-> S1 EMB -.-> S2
  • The scripts in models_run/ are not edited for an experiment. Each has its settings at the top; in experiment mode the values in config.yaml replace them (same names). A misspelt setting stops the run with an error, so a config can never be silently ignored.
  • Embeddings are shared. They depend only on the dataset and the model, so models_run/02a–02d are run once and every experiment reads outputs/morocco/study/02_embeddings/.
  • Runs that are finished are skipped, so an interrupted experiment continues where it stopped. RERUN = True (or deleting results/) repeats it.
  • results/run_info.json keeps the config, the git commit and the dates of every run, so a result can always be traced back to the code that produced it.

docs.title: Two pipelines for the monthly embeddings
docs.text:
The foundation models produce one embedding per month (Clay, Prithvi-EO-2.0, TerraMind) or one per agricultural year (AgriFM). The two pipelines differ only in how the monthly embeddings are aggregated; all preceding and subsequent steps are shared.

flowchart LR E["Monthly embeddings<br/>12 × D per parcel"] --> P1["<b>PCA pipeline</b> (E01, E02)<br/>concat 12 months → standardise → PCA 128"] E --> P2["<b>L-TAE pipeline</b> (E04)<br/>attention over the 12 months (trained)"] P1 --> K["LogReg · RF · HGB · SVM"] P2 --> H["MLP head"] K --> O["out-of-fold predictions<br/>same format"] H --> O O --> CMP["04_compare_models<br/>same parcels, same bootstrap draws"]

Because both pipelines write the same oof_predictions.csv, the comparison and the report need no change. E04 also lists the E02 runs under compare: EXTRA_RUNS, so PCA and L-TAE are compared on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws. Details: evaluation protocol §5.

docs.title: Start a new experiment
docs.text:
1. Copy experiments/_template/config.yaml to experiments/E<NN>_<short_name>/config.yaml (next free number; the name says what varies) and experiments/_template/README.md to docs/experiments/E<NN>_<short_name>/index.md.
  2. Edit config.yaml: title, short title (menu), question, changes_from, inputs, steps and only the settings that differ from the script defaults.
  3. Write the setup page index.md: question, why, what changes (a small table against the experiment it builds on).
  4. Set EXPERIMENT = "E<NN>_<short_name>" in run_experiment.py and run it. Use QUICK_TEST: true first to check that everything runs, then set it back to false and delete results/. The report page and the menu entry are created automatically.
  5. When it has finished: write the Answer, Key findings, Interpretation, Caveats and Next steps in report.md (the tables and figures are already there), set status: done and a one-line answer: in the config, run make_report.py once more, and add an entry to the progress log.

A new pipeline variant (another model or aggregation) gets its own script in models_run/ with settings at the top, the experiment-mode block, and the output format of 03_train_evaluate.py; then add it to SCRIPTS in run_experiment.py.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Do frozen foundation-model embeddings separate irrigated from rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-1/2 features, with the same parcels, folds and classifiers?

docs.title: Why
docs.text: First complete run on the shared 128 px tile store with patch-aligned chips: every input sees the same pixels, the same monthly composites and the same parcels, so any difference comes from the representation.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Inputs S1/S2 baseline (204 parcel features) · Clay v1.5 (chips p8) · Prithvi-EO-2.0 · TerraMind · AgriFM (chips p16) Encoders frozen; one embedding per parcel per month (AgriFM: per year), patch-share-weighted mean over the parcel Temporal aggregation concat 12 months → standardise → PCA 128 (fitted on the training folds only) Classifiers LogReg (linear probe), RF, HGB, SVM; grids in the protocol Validation nested spatial CV: 5 outer folds (20 km blocks); inner spatial CV on the 4 training folds chooses the hyperparameters; refit on 4 folds

docs.title: How to run again
docs.text:
# experiments/run_experiment.py:  EXPERIMENT = "E01_frozen_pca_nested",  RERUN = True
python experiments/run_experiment.py
About 2 h per foundation-model input and 30 min for the baseline on the MacBook (CPU).

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: No foundation model beats the S1/S2 baseline: the best input-classifier pair is Clay + SVM (macro-F1 0.910) against 0.906 for the baseline with the same SVM, a difference well inside the noise. With a linear probe, Clay and TerraMind equal the baseline; with a random forest every GeoFM is lower, and AgriFM is clearly worse. The GeoFMs do better than the baseline in the hardest test fold. Full report: REPORT.md.

docs.title: E01 · Frozen GeoFMs + PCA vs the S1/S2 baseline (nested spatial CV) — report
docs.text: Answer. No frozen foundation model classifies irrigated vs rainfed parcels better than the Sentinel-1/2 baseline. The best pair, Clay + SVM (macro-F1 0.910), is level with the baseline + SVM (0.906; Δ +0.003, 95% confidence interval −0.022 to +0.030). The embeddings carry about the same information as well-designed monthly S1/S2 features, and they hold up better in the hardest region.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• No input differs from the baseline after correcting for multiple tests for Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind, whatever the classifier. The four best results lie within 0.005 of each other (0.905–0.910, all with the SVM).
  • Linear probe: TerraMind 0.896, Clay 0.887 and the baseline 0.887 are level. The frozen embeddings are about as linearly separable as the hand-built features, which is the standard test of what an encoder already knows.
  • Random forest is the weakest classifier on embeddings (0.839–0.878 against 0.892 for the baseline). PCA components spread the information over many dense features, which suits SVM and LogReg better than axis-aligned tree splits.
  • AgriFM is clearly behind (0.839–0.868; significantly worse with RF and SVM). Its input normalisation is still an open point, so this is not yet a fair verdict on the model.
  • The hardest test fold separates the models. In fold 0 (rainfed parcels in Doukkala and Souss), the baseline drops to 0.80 (RF, SVM) while Clay and Prithvi stay higher with every classifier (Prithvi 0.87 and Clay 0.86 with the SVM). Across the five folds Clay and Prithvi vary about as much as or less than the baseline (SD 0.045–0.054 with LogReg/SVM, vs 0.044–0.075 for the baseline).
  • Rainfed is the hard class: rainfed F1 ~0.81–0.84 for the best pairs against irrigated F1 ~0.97.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Question Do frozen foundation-model embeddings separate irrigated from rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-1/2 features, with the same parcels, folds and classifiers? Research question RQ1 Regions Morocco Inputs S2 baseline, Clay v1.5, Prithvi-EO-2.0, TerraMind, AgriFM Temporal aggregation 12 monthly embeddings side by side → standardise → PCA 128 (fitted on the training folds only) Head logistic regression (linear probe), random forest, gradient boosting (HGB), RBF SVM Validation 5 spatial folds (20 km blocks); hyperparameters by inner spatial CV on the 4 training folds, model refit on all 4 (nested spatial CV) Parcels 8,775 / 8,781 (inputs scored on the parcels common to all runs) Uncertainty 95% confidence interval (CI) from a block bootstrap (1,000 draws of whole 20 km blocks), the same draws for every run → paired differences; p-values Holm-adjusted Changed from first experiment on the shared 128 px tile store with patch-aligned chips

docs.title: Macro-F1 of every input and head
docs.text:
Out-of-fold predictions of all 5 spatial folds; bold = best input for that head. Runs marked [E0x] come from an earlier experiment, on the same parcels and bootstrap draws.

How to read this table

What: one score per input (row) and classifier (column), between 0 and 1. Higher is better.

Macro-F1: F1 is computed for each class separately (irrigated, rainfed) and the two are averaged. Rainfed parcels are the minority, so a model that labels everything "irrigated" still gets a high overall accuracy but a low macro-F1. That is why macro-F1 is the main metric.

How: every parcel is predicted once, by the model that did not see its 20 km block in training (out-of-fold). All inputs are scored on the same parcels, so the numbers can be compared directly.

Read it as: about 0.90 = very good; 0.75 = clear errors on the rainfed class; 0.50 = no better than guessing one class.

docs.title: Difference from the S1/S2 baseline (headline heads)
docs.text:
Δ = input minus baseline with the same head (runs with their own model against the baseline's random forest), on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws. Better / worse = the 95% confidence interval (CI) excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05.

How to read this table

What: each row compares one input with the baseline (the Sentinel feature classifier), using the same classifier.

  • Difference in macro-F1 (Δ): the input's score minus the baseline's. +0.013 means 0.013 higher than the baseline; −0.158 means 0.158 lower.
  • 95% confidence interval (CI), e.g. [−0.021, +0.025]: the range in which the true difference probably lies. It comes from resampling whole 20 km blocks 1,000 times (block bootstrap) and recomputing Δ each time.
    • The range includes 0 (one end negative, the other positive): the data cannot tell which input is better.
    • The range is entirely above 0, e.g. [+0.011, +0.049]: the input is better.
    • The range is entirely below 0, e.g. [−0.215, −0.085]: the input is worse.
  • p-value (Holm-corrected): how likely a difference this large would be if the two inputs were really equal. Many pairs are tested at once, so each p-value is raised (Holm correction) to avoid false "wins" by chance. 1.000 = no evidence of a difference.
  • Verdict: "better" or "worse" only if the CI excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05. "Higher/lower, not significant after Holm" = the CI excludes 0, but the evidence does not survive the correction.

Why paired: both inputs are scored on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws, so a difference reflects the inputs, not which parcels happened to be drawn.

docs.title: Per-class metrics (headline heads, 95% confidence interval)
docs.text:
How to read this table

What: the main metric and three others for the headline classifiers, each with its 95% confidence interval in brackets (the range the true value probably lies in).

  • Macro-F1: mean F1 of the two classes (main metric).
  • F1 of the rainfed class: how well the minority class is found. Precision and recall of "rainfed" are combined, so it is usually the lowest number and the most informative one.
  • Balanced accuracy: mean recall of the two classes. 0.5 = guessing.
  • Overall accuracy: share of all parcels labelled correctly. It looks high even for weak models, because most parcels are irrigated, so do not compare inputs on it alone.

Wide CIs (e.g. 0.63–0.88) mean the score changes a lot from block to block, so small differences between rows are not meaningful.

docs.text:
Drop in macro-F1 when a month (or a baseline variable) is shuffled on the test fold: Clay v1.5 · Prithvi-EO-2.0 · S1/S2 baseline · TerraMind

How to read this figure

What: one month (or one variable) at a time is shuffled on the test fold, and the drop in macro-F1 is measured. A large drop = the model relies on that month. Close to 0 = the model does not need it. Bars below 0 are noise.

For foundation models after PCA, importance is usually spread thinly over all months, so it says little about which months the embedding encodes.

docs.title: Random versus spatial cross-validation
docs.text:
The same hyperparameters were re-evaluated with a stratified random 5-fold split that ignores the spatial blocks.

Input Classifier Random CV, mean macro-F1 Spatial CV, mean macro-F1 Spatial CV, worst fold S1/S2 baseline LogReg 0.904 0.895 0.847 S1/S2 baseline RF 0.928 0.893 0.804 S1/S2 baseline HGB 0.946 0.894 0.734 S1/S2 baseline SVM 0.926 0.911 0.830 Clay v1.5 SVM 0.936 0.911 0.844 Prithvi-EO-2.0 SVM 0.916 0.906 0.831 TerraMind SVM 0.933 0.903 0.802 AgriFM SVM 0.913 0.863 0.703

Random cross-validation is 1–5 points more optimistic for every input, and its folds lie within about one point of each other (SD ≤ 0.014), whereas the spatial folds differ by up to 0.24 (SD 0.04–0.10). Random validation thus both overstates accuracy and conceals the dependence of accuracy on the region.

Figure E01.1. Macro-F1 (left) and rainfed F1 (right) per fold for the S1/S2 baseline under random (grey) and spatial (blue) 5-fold cross-validation; bars mark the mean.

docs.title: What the baseline relies on
docs.text:
Grouped permutation importance of the random forest, computed on the test fold of each outer round: all features of one variable (or of one month) are permuted together and the drop in macro-F1 is recorded.

Variable Drop in macro-F1 Month Drop in macro-F1 NDWI 0.262 February 0.141 B12 (SWIR 2) 0.066 July 0.123 NDVI 0.046 August 0.113 EVI 0.026 June 0.091 B11 (SWIR 1) 0.013 October 0.089

Water-sensitive variables (NDWI, SWIR) dominate, and the most informative months are the peak of the rainfed season (February) and the dry summer (June–August), when only irrigated fields remain green. This supports the use of the full agricultural year. For the foundation-model embeddings, permuting a single month changes macro-F1 by at most 0.011 (Clay and Prithvi: February and May; TerraMind: July–September), i.e. the information is spread over the months.

Figure E01.2. Grouped permutation importance of the S1/S2 baseline (random forest) by variable (left) and by month (right); mean ± SD over the five outer folds.

The embeddings require strong regularisation of the linear probe (C = 0.01), whereas the baseline features prefer weaker regularisation. Class weighting and small trees are selected almost everywhere, and the SVM keeps its default setting for every foundation model.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: For RQ1, the frozen foundation models reach the accuracy of a conventional Sentinel-1/2 classifier but do not exceed it on average. This matches PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024), where GeoFMs do not consistently beat supervised baselines. Where they may add value is robustness: in the region the baseline handles worst, Clay and Prithvi do better with every classifier. That points to the next questions: is this fold effect stable under the final validation design (E02), and does a learned temporal aggregation (E04) let the embeddings use the 12 months better than PCA?

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Nested validation design, replaced by the PASTIS rotation in E02; E01 is kept as a sensitivity check.
  • AgriFM normalisation not yet confirmed (open point in PROGRESS.md).
  • Small rainfed class (1,196 parcels, ~240 per fold): per-fold scores for rainfed rest on few parcels, hence the wide intervals.
  • Region and year are partly confounded (Gharb and Tadla only 2023/24; Souss only 2024/25), so the fold differences cannot be attributed to region alone.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Run E02: the main RQ1 result.
  • Resolve the AgriFM normalisation and re-embed if needed.
  • Implement the L-TAE pipeline (E04).

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Do frozen foundation-model embeddings separate irrigated from rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-2 features, with the same parcels, folds and classifiers, under the final validation design? (Q1 of the experiment plan)

docs.title: Why
docs.text: E01 used nested spatial CV. The study now uses the PASTIS rotation for every model (classifiers and, later, neural networks), so they are trained, tuned and tested in exactly the same way (decision D3). E02 is the main result of RQ1; E01 becomes a sensitivity check of the validation design.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Morocco: no frozen GeoFM beats the Sentinel-2 baseline. Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind equal it (macro-F1 ≈ 0.90 with SVM, all differences inside the CI); AgriFM is clearly worse (−0.16 with RF, −0.06 with SVM). Utah (harder, best macro-F1 0.79): with SVM, Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind are significantly better than the baseline (+0.05–0.06), and Clay is also better with the linear probe. With RF there is no gain, and the baseline's RF (0.764) is close to the best GeoFM (Clay + SVM, 0.791). The head changes the ranking as much as the input does. With 10% of the training blocks, the S2 baseline is the best input in Morocco, so the GeoFMs show no label-efficiency advantage. They do generalise better to a zone with few rainfed training parcels (Souss: rainfed recall 0.61–0.71 vs 0.22), but E03 shows that this is an effect of the classical heads: with an MLP, the S2 features reach 0.84. Full tables, figures and interpretation are in the report.

docs.title: E02 · Frozen GeoFMs + PCA + classical classifiers — report
docs.text: Answer. Only in Utah, and only with some heads. In Morocco, Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind match the Sentinel-2 baseline (macro-F1 ≈ 0.90 with SVM), and AgriFM is clearly worse. In Utah, Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind beat the baseline by 0.05–0.06 with SVM, and Clay also beats it with the linear probe. The best GeoFM (Clay + SVM, 0.791) is 0.03 above the baseline's best head (RF, 0.764).

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• Morocco: no gain. Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind are within ±0.02 of the S2 baseline with LogReg and SVM, and every CI includes 0. With RF they are 0.00–0.04 lower. AgriFM is the only clearly different input: −0.16 with RF and −0.06 with SVM (significant after Holm).
  • Utah: a small gain that depends on the head. With SVM, Clay (+0.063), Prithvi (+0.055) and TerraMind (+0.049) are significantly better than the S2 baseline, and Clay is also better with LogReg (+0.031). With RF there is no gain, and Prithvi is worse (−0.049). Utah is harder than Morocco for every input (best macro-F1 0.79 vs 0.90).
  • The head matters as much as the input. RF is the weakest head on embeddings (AgriFM in Morocco: 0.71 with RF, 0.84 with SVM), but the best head on the hand-crafted S2 features in Utah. SVM is the best head for every GeoFM in both regions.
  • Label efficiency: no advantage for the GeoFMs in Morocco. At 10% of the training blocks (≈ 590 parcels per round), the S2 baseline is the best input with every head (SVM 0.82 vs 0.75–0.77). The GeoFMs catch up at 25%. In Utah at 10%, the best GeoFM (Prithvi + SVM, 0.71) is level with the baseline's RF (0.70).
  • With these heads, the GeoFMs do better in an under-represented zone. In Morocco's Souss zone (69 rainfed parcels, test fold 0), SVM finds 61–71% of the rainfed parcels with Clay, Prithvi or TerraMind, but only 22% with the S2 features. This explains the baseline's drop in fold 0. Inside Doukkala, where most rainfed training parcels are, the baseline is as good as or better than every GeoFM. Corrected by E03: with an MLP head, the S2 features find 84% of Souss's rainfed parcels, so this gap comes from the classical heads, not from the inputs.

  • Difference in macro-F1 (Δ): the input's score minus the baseline's. +0.013 means 0.013 higher than the baseline; −0.158 means 0.158 lower.
  • 95% confidence interval (CI), e.g. [−0.021, +0.025]: the range in which the true difference probably lies. It comes from resampling whole 20 km blocks 1,000 times (block bootstrap) and recomputing Δ each time.

    • The range is entirely above 0, e.g. [+0.011, +0.049]: the input is better.
    • The range is entirely below 0, e.g. [−0.215, −0.085]: the input is worse.

What: one score per input (row) and classifier (column), between 0 and 1. Higher is better.

How: every parcel is predicted once, by the model that did not see its 20 km block in training (out-of-fold). All inputs are scored on the same parcels, so the numbers can be compared directly.

Read it as: about 0.90 = very good; 0.75 = clear errors on the rainfed class; 0.50 = no better than guessing one class.
