docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
RQ1 with frozen embeddings, PCA and a classical head. When both are classified the same way, frozen GeoFM embeddings do not separate irrigated from rainfed parcels better than a well-built Sentinel-2 feature set. Where they are better (Utah, with SVM or the linear probe), the gain is 0.03–0.06 macro-F1. If each input gets its best head, the gain shrinks to 0.03, and that comparison is not tested. E01 (nested CV, S1/S2 baseline) found the same, so the conclusion does not depend on the validation design or on Sentinel-1.

Why the head changes the ranking. After PCA, an embedding is 128 dense, rotated components, and no single component means "July NDVI". Margin-based heads (SVM, logistic regression) use such features well. A random forest splits on one feature at a time, which suits the S2 features: each variable (NDVI in August, SWIR in December) carries meaning on its own. E02 compares inputs only through these three heads, so E03 (MLP head) and E04 (L-TAE, which keeps the months apart) are needed before calling a GeoFM weaker or stronger.

Where the GeoFMs help. With these heads, their clearest advantage is outside the training distribution. In Morocco, the GeoFMs recognise rainfed parcels in Souss, a zone with few rainfed training parcels, much better than the S2 features do. E03 shows that this is a head effect: with an MLP, the S2 features find 84% of them, more than any GeoFM. In Utah, the GeoFMs gain in Bear River, the zone with most rainfed parcels (+0.04–0.09 with SVM and LogReg). In the small zones (Sevier River, Uintah, West Colorado River), every input misses most rainfed parcels, and the S2 features miss fewer than the GeoFMs. Whether this robustness to new zones holds up across regions is tested in RQ4 (transfer to another region).

AgriFM. AgriFM is the weakest input in both regions and with every head, even with the region's chip statistics (D15). It is the only model that returns one embedding for the whole year: the video encoder pools the time axis, so the classifier never sees the seasonal shape that separates irrigated from rainfed fields. Its RF score is the lowest of the experiment. For the same reason, there is no permutation importance by month for it.

What the S2 baseline uses. In Utah, the random forest relies on NDVI, EVI and SWIR (B11, B12) in July–September, the irrigated summer, and in December–January. For Clay in Morocco, importance is spread thinly over all months (≤ 0.015 each). This is expected for PCA components, and it says little about which months the embedding encodes.

Label efficiency. Fewer labels do not favour the GeoFMs here. With 10% of the training blocks, the hand-crafted features are the most reliable input in Morocco, and the spread between draws is large for every input (SD up to 0.09). At that size, which blocks are drawn matters more than the input. From 25% on, the curves of S2, Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind overlap. With frozen embeddings and classical heads at parcel level, the foundation models show no label-efficiency advantage.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Classical heads are deterministic and run once per draw; the spread over seeds is measured from E03 on.
  • The hyperparameter grids are small (2–8 settings per head) and the same for every input. A larger grid could favour some inputs.
  • Differences are tested per head. "Each input with its best head" is reported here but not tested.
  • Utah covers one season (2023/24); Morocco's two seasons are mixed within the folds.
  • The Holm correction covers this experiment's own runs only.
  • The S2 baseline is built from the same 128 px tiles (inner pixels of each parcel), so both inputs use the same imagery.
  • Per-zone results for small zones (< 50 rainfed parcels) are indicative only.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• E03: an MLP head on the same PCA input. Does a trained head close the gap between heads?
  • E04: L-TAE on the 12 monthly embeddings, without PCA. Does keeping the months apart help the GeoFMs? AgriFM is excluded because it has one time step.
  • E05: PSE-TAE trained from scratch on the S2 pixels, the neural baseline the GeoFMs have to beat.
  • RQ4: test robustness to new zones and regions directly (the Souss gap of this experiment disappears with an MLP head, see E03).

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Does a trainable neural head get more out of the same PCA input than logistic regression, random forest and SVM?

docs.title: Why
docs.text: GeoFM benchmarks evaluate frozen encoders with a trained neural head. E03 gives every input the same small MLP on exactly the E02 input, so a difference between E02 and E03 comes from the head alone. E03 is also the reference for E04: E03 → E04 changes only how the months are combined (PCA → L-TAE), with the same MLP head.

docs.title: What changes
docs.text:
E02 E03 Input 12 months concatenated → PCA 128 (baseline: 180 features) same Head LogReg, RF, SVM (grid on the validation fold) MLP 128 → 256 → 128 → 2, ReLU, batch normalisation, dropout 0.2 Training – AdamW 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 128, class-weighted cross-entropy, ≤ 100 epochs, early stopping on validation macro-F1 (patience 15) Seeds 1 3 (mean ± SD)

Inputs (all Sentinel-2 only): S2 baseline, Clay, Prithvi, TerraMind, AgriFM. Regions: Morocco and Utah 2023/24.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Each parcel enters the MLP as one row of numbers, exactly the E02 input:

Input Per parcel (file) Steps (fitted on the training folds of each round) Into the MLP S2 baseline 15 variables × 12 months = 180 (parcel_features_inner.csv) fill remaining gaps with the training median → standardise 180 Clay v1.5 12 months × 1,024 = 12,288 (clay_agyear_tiles[_2023-24].npz) fill months without a clear pixel with the training median → concatenate → standardise → PCA 128 Prithvi-EO-2.0 12 × 1,024 = 12,288 same 128 TerraMind 12 × 768 = 9,216 same 128 AgriFM 1 × 1,024 (one vector per year) same 128
  • Parcels: Morocco 8,775–8,781 and Utah 6,011–6,013 (the parcels common to all runs are scored).
  • Labels: irrigated (class 1) or rainfed (class 2).
  • No leakage: median, standardisation and PCA are computed on the 3 training folds only, then applied to the validation and test fold.

docs.title: Model
docs.text: flowchart LR X["input<br/>128 numbers<br/>(baseline: 180)"] --> H1["Linear → 256<br/>BatchNorm · ReLU<br/>Dropout 0.2"] H1 --> H2["Linear → 128<br/>BatchNorm · ReLU<br/>Dropout 0.2"] H2 --> O["Linear → 2<br/>softmax: P(irrigated), P(rainfed)"] Setting Value What it does Hidden layers 256 and 128 units (MLP: [256, 128]) learn non-linear combinations of the inputs Activation ReLU makes the network non-linear Batch normalisation after each hidden layer keeps training stable Dropout 0.2 (DROPOUT) switches off 20% of the units at random during training, against overfitting Output 2 units + softmax probability of each class; rainfed if P(rainfed) ≥ 0.5 Trainable weights ≈ 67,000 (baseline input: ≈ 80,000) small compared with the ~1,200–5,000 training parcels × many epochs

docs.title: Training
docs.text: Setting Value (config ltae: section, script models_run/03c_train_ltae.py, HEAD: mlp) Optimiser AdamW, learning rate 0.001 (LEARNING_RATE), weight decay 0.0001 (WEIGHT_DECAY) Loss cross-entropy with class weights (rainfed errors count more, as rainfed is the minority class) Batch size 128 parcels (BATCH_SIZE) Epochs at most 100 (EPOCHS) Early stopping macro-F1 on the validation fold after every epoch; stop after 15 epochs without improvement (PATIENCE), keep the best epoch Seeds 3 per round: 42, 1042, 2042 (N_SEEDS); the out-of-fold prediction of a parcel is the mean probability of the 3 seeds Tuning none: the settings are fixed in advance, the validation fold only decides when to stop Validation PASTIS rotation: 3 folds train, the next fold validates, 1 fold tests; 5 rounds, so every parcel is predicted once Hardware GPU (one Slurm job per run)

docs.title: Label efficiency (part of this experiment)
docs.text:
Every input is also trained on 10, 25 and 50% of the training blocks, so the report shows a learning curve next to the main result (Q5 of the experiment plan).

Setting Value Fractions 10, 25, 50% of the training blocks of each round; 100% = the main run Sampling whole blocks: rainfed and irrigated-only blocks each put in a random order (per region, round and draw), and a fraction takes the first blocks of each list, so the draws are nested (10% ⊂ 25% ⊂ 50%); the order is accepted only if its first 10% hold ≥ 20 rainfed parcels. No fraction below 10%. Draws 3 per fraction; draw k is the same in E02–E05 and for every input (paired) Seeds 1 seed per draw (the main run keeps its 3 seeds) Validation and test folds unchanged Runs 5 inputs × 3 fractions × 3 draws = 45 per region, for the MLP head Result macro-F1 and rainfed F1 against the training fraction, one line per input, Morocco and Utah

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
# on the Mac (all regions, main and label-efficiency runs, compare, report):
#   experiments/run_experiment.py:  EXPERIMENT = "E03_frozen_pca_mlp"
python experiments/run_experiment.py
# on the cluster: one Slurm job per run, then one compare job per region (EXPERIMENT and DRY_RUN in the script)
python experiments/submit_slurm.py
  • Order: after E02 (compares with its runs: EXTRA_RUNS: "E02_frozen_pca/*").
  • Hardware: GPU (CPU works). QUICK = True checks the whole chain in a few minutes first.
  • Results: experiments/E03_frozen_pca_mlp/results/<region>/; the report page is written by the report step on the Mac.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The MLP head is as good as E02's SVM for every input (all differences within ±0.01, none significant) and clearly better than LogReg and RF for most GeoFMs. A trained head therefore removes the weak-head problem, but it does not change the ranking of the inputs. Morocco: the S2 baseline with an MLP is the best result so far (0.908). Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind are 0.01–0.02 lower (not significant), and AgriFM is worse. Utah: Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind with an MLP beat the S2 baseline with an MLP by 0.04–0.05 (significant; +0.08–0.09 in Bear River). The S2 baseline's best head is still E02's random forest (0.764), so the best GeoFM (Clay + SVM, 0.791) leads by about 0.03. E03 also corrects E02: with an MLP, the S2 features find most of the rainfed parcels in Souss (84%), so the GeoFMs' advantage there was a head effect. Full tables, figures and interpretation are in the report.

docs.title: E03 · Frozen GeoFMs + PCA + MLP head — report
docs.text: Answer. A trained MLP head is as good as the best classical head (SVM) for every input, but not better. It removes the weak-head problem (RF, LogReg) without changing the conclusion of E02. In Morocco, the S2 baseline with an MLP is the best single result so far (0.908), and the GeoFMs are 0.01–0.02 below it. In Utah, the GeoFMs with an MLP beat the S2 baseline with an MLP by 0.04–0.05, but not the baseline's random forest from E02.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• MLP ≈ SVM for every input, in both regions. Against E02's SVM, the MLP is within ±0.01 for all 10 input–region pairs, and none of these differences is significant. It is clearly better than LogReg and RF for most GeoFMs, by up to +0.14 (AgriFM vs RF, Morocco).
  • Morocco: the S2 baseline is still on top. S2 + MLP scores 0.908. Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind score 0.892–0.898 (−0.010 to −0.016, not significant after Holm), and AgriFM is worse (−0.051).
  • Utah: the GeoFMs beat the S2 baseline with the same head. Clay (+0.042), Prithvi (+0.041) and TerraMind (+0.046) are significantly better than S2 + MLP. In the focus zone, Bear River, the gap is +0.08–0.09. But S2 + MLP (0.739) is below S2 + RF from E02 (0.764), so against the baseline's best head the GeoFMs gain only about 0.02.
  • E02's Souss finding came from the head, not the input. With an MLP, the S2 features find 84% of the rainfed parcels in Souss (E02 SVM: 22%), more than any GeoFM (64–74%). The S2 baseline's weak fold 0 in E02 was a weakness of the classical heads.
  • Label efficiency differs by region. In Morocco at 10% of the training blocks, S2 + MLP is the best input (0.827 vs 0.71–0.80) and the most stable (SD 0.019). In Utah, every GeoFM except AgriFM is above S2 + MLP at every fraction. With 25% of the blocks, Clay and Prithvi (0.735) already equal S2 + MLP with all blocks (0.733).
  • Seeds are stable. Single-seed macro-F1 varies by at most ±0.008, which is less than the differences between inputs in Utah. Averaging the 3 seeds adds about +0.005 over a single seed.

docs.title: Macro-F1 of every input and head
docs.text:
Out-of-fold predictions of all 5 spatial folds; bold = best input for that head. Runs marked [E0x] come from an earlier experiment, on the same parcels and bootstrap draws.

How to read this table

What: one score per input (row) and classifier (column), between 0 and 1. Higher is better.

Macro-F1: F1 is computed for each class separately (irrigated, rainfed) and the two are averaged. Rainfed parcels are the minority, so a model that labels everything "irrigated" still gets a high overall accuracy but a low macro-F1. That is why macro-F1 is the main metric.

How: every parcel is predicted once, by the model that did not see its 20 km block in training (out-of-fold). All inputs are scored on the same parcels, so the numbers can be compared directly.

Read it as: about 0.90 = very good; 0.75 = clear errors on the rainfed class; 0.50 = no better than guessing one class.

docs.title: Difference from the S2 baseline (headline heads)
docs.text:
Δ = input minus baseline with the same head (runs with their own model against the baseline's random forest), on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws. Better / worse = the 95% confidence interval (CI) excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05.

How to read this table

What: each row compares one input with the baseline (the Sentinel feature classifier), using the same classifier.

  • Difference in macro-F1 (Δ): the input's score minus the baseline's. +0.013 means 0.013 higher than the baseline; −0.158 means 0.158 lower.
  • 95% confidence interval (CI), e.g. [−0.021, +0.025]: the range in which the true difference probably lies. It comes from resampling whole 20 km blocks 1,000 times (block bootstrap) and recomputing Δ each time.
    • The range includes 0 (one end negative, the other positive): the data cannot tell which input is better.
    • The range is entirely above 0, e.g. [+0.011, +0.049]: the input is better.
    • The range is entirely below 0, e.g. [−0.215, −0.085]: the input is worse.
  • p-value (Holm-corrected): how likely a difference this large would be if the two inputs were really equal. Many pairs are tested at once, so each p-value is raised (Holm correction) to avoid false "wins" by chance. 1.000 = no evidence of a difference.
  • Verdict: "better" or "worse" only if the CI excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05. "Higher/lower, not significant after Holm" = the CI excludes 0, but the evidence does not survive the correction.

Why paired: both inputs are scored on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws, so a difference reflects the inputs, not which parcels happened to be drawn.

docs.text:

docs.title: Difference from the S2 baseline (headline heads)
docs.text:
Δ = input minus baseline with the same head (runs with their own model against the baseline's random forest), on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws. Better / worse = the 95% confidence interval (CI) excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05.

How to read this table

What: each row compares one input with the baseline (the Sentinel feature classifier), using the same classifier.

  • Difference in macro-F1 (Δ): the input's score minus the baseline's. +0.013 means 0.013 higher than the baseline; −0.158 means 0.158 lower.
  • 95% confidence interval (CI), e.g. [−0.021, +0.025]: the range in which the true difference probably lies. It comes from resampling whole 20 km blocks 1,000 times (block bootstrap) and recomputing Δ each time.
    • The range includes 0 (one end negative, the other positive): the data cannot tell which input is better.
    • The range is entirely above 0, e.g. [+0.011, +0.049]: the input is better.
    • The range is entirely below 0, e.g. [−0.215, −0.085]: the input is worse.
  • p-value (Holm-corrected): how likely a difference this large would be if the two inputs were really equal. Many pairs are tested at once, so each p-value is raised (Holm correction) to avoid false "wins" by chance. 1.000 = no evidence of a difference.
  • Verdict: "better" or "worse" only if the CI excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05. "Higher/lower, not significant after Holm" = the CI excludes 0, but the evidence does not survive the correction.

Why paired: both inputs are scored on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws, so a difference reflects the inputs, not which parcels happened to be drawn.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The head question is settled for the PCA input. E02 left open whether the GeoFMs only looked weak because of the classical heads. With a trained MLP, every input reaches about the level of its SVM result and no further. So E02's SVM column was already close to what this input can give. What remains is a real difference between inputs, not between heads, and it is small: none in Morocco, 0.02–0.05 in Utah depending on the comparison.

Morocco and Utah disagree, and the reason is probably the data. In Morocco, the rainfed parcels are concentrated in Doukkala and have a clear seasonal signal (winter cereals without a summer crop), which hand-crafted indices (NDVI, EVI, SWIR per month) capture well. A flexible head on these features is hard to beat. In Utah, rainfed and irrigated parcels share crop types and are spread over many zones. There, the GeoFM embeddings separate the classes better inside the main zone (Bear River +0.08–0.09), so they seem to carry field-level information the indices miss. Utah is also where the GeoFMs help with few labels: 25% of the blocks with Clay or Prithvi match all blocks with S2 + MLP.

The S2 baseline needs the right head. The S2 features gain most from flexible heads in Morocco (MLP +0.039 vs LogReg), but in Utah their best head is still the random forest (0.764 vs 0.739 for the MLP). In Utah the MLP on S2 features predicts "rainfed" too often: highest balanced accuracy (0.797) and rainfed recall (0.86 in Bear River), but lower precision and overall accuracy (0.823). The fairest single comparison is therefore each input with its best head: Morocco S2 0.908 vs best GeoFM 0.901 (Clay SVM, E02); Utah S2 0.764 vs best GeoFM 0.791 (Clay SVM, E02).

Correction to E02. E02 suggested that the GeoFMs transfer better to Souss, a zone with few rainfed training parcels. E03 shows that this was an effect of the classical heads on the S2 features. With an MLP, the S2 baseline finds 84% of Souss's rainfed parcels, more than any GeoFM. The E02 report now points to this.

AgriFM gains the most from a trained head (+0.14 over RF in Morocco), which confirms that its single pooled embedding needs a non-linear head. It stays the weakest input in Morocco, and in Utah it equals the S2 baseline with the same head.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The MLP has fixed settings (no grid search), while E02's heads chose from a small grid on the validation fold. A tuned MLP might do slightly better, but the MLP already equals SVM, so a large change is unlikely.
  • The main MLP result averages 3 seeds (≈ +0.005 over a single seed); the E02 heads run once. The label-efficiency table uses single seeds throughout, so its 100% column (mean of the seeds scored one by one) is slightly below the main table.
  • The Holm correction covers this experiment's own runs only: the 4 differences from the baseline, and the 15 MLP vs E02 comparisons, each family on its own.
  • Confusion matrices and permutation importance are not produced for the neural heads. The per-zone tables are in results/<region>/breakdown/.
  • Per-zone results for zones with fewer than 50 rainfed parcels are indicative only.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• E04: L-TAE on the 12 monthly embeddings, without concatenation and PCA, with the same MLP after attention. E03 → E04 isolates the effect of temporal attention. AgriFM is excluded because it has one time step.
  • E05: PSE-TAE trained from scratch on the S2 pixels, the neural baseline. Utah is the region to watch: does a temporal model on raw pixels close the gap to the GeoFMs there?
  • Reporting: for the RQ1 summary, compare each input with its best head (Morocco S2 0.908 vs Clay 0.901; Utah Clay 0.791 vs S2 0.764) and test that comparison explicitly.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Does a learned temporal aggregation of the 12 monthly embeddings (L-TAE) classify irrigated vs rainfed parcels better than concatenating the months and reducing them with PCA?

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind give one embedding per month. E01/E02 put the 12 months side by side and reduce them with PCA (a fixed, unsupervised step). PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024) combines the monthly encodings of single-date models with a trained L-TAE and found it better than a linear mapping. E04 tests whether that holds for irrigated vs rainfed mapping. The same L-TAE is trained on the monthly Sentinel-2 features, so the baseline gets the same temporal model (protocol §5).

docs.title: What changes
docs.text:
E03 (PCA + MLP) E04 (L-TAE + MLP) Monthly embeddings → parcel vector concat 12 months → standardise → PCA 128 L-TAE attention over the 12 months (trained) Head MLP 256-128 L-TAE output → MLP 256-128 (trained together) Trained on 3 training folds; early stopping on the validation fold same Inputs (Sentinel-2 only) S2 baseline, Clay, Prithvi, TerraMind, AgriFM S2 baseline, Clay, Prithvi, TerraMind (AgriFM has no months) Seeds 3 3

E04 is also compared with the classical classifiers of E02.

The comparison step also reads the E03 and E02 runs (EXTRA_RUNS), so PCA and L-TAE are compared on the same parcels with the same bootstrap draws. Regions: Morocco and Utah 2023/24.

docs.title: Implementation (models_run/03c_train_ltae.py, HEAD: ltae)
docs.text:
1. Reads the same embedding files as 03_train_evaluate.py (<model>_agyear_tiles[_2023-24].npz, 12 steps × D) or the monthly Sentinel-2 features (15 variables × 12 months; gaps filled by interpolation in time, as in script 03).
  2. Standardises each channel with the training parcels' observed months; months without a clear pixel are masked in the attention, not filled.
  3. L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020) with the paper's default size (16 heads with one learned master query each, d_k 8, d_model 256, sinusoidal encoding of the mid-month day, output MLP 256-128), then a linear layer with 2 outputs; class-weighted cross-entropy, AdamW.
  4. PASTIS rotation: train on 3 folds, early stopping on the validation fold (macro-F1, patience 15), test on the test fold; 3 seeds per round, the out-of-fold probability is their mean.
  5. Writes oof_predictions.csv, metrics_per_fold.csv, metrics_with_ci.csv, metrics_per_seed.csv, training_history.csv, attention_by_month.csv and run_config.json in the format of script 03 (model = "ltae"), so 04_compare_models.py and make_report.py treat it like any other run.

docs.title: Label efficiency (part of this experiment)
docs.text:
Every input is also trained on 10, 25 and 50% of the training blocks, so the report shows a learning curve next to the main result (Q5 of the experiment plan).

Setting Value Fractions 10, 25, 50% of the training blocks of each round; 100% = the main run Sampling whole blocks: rainfed and irrigated-only blocks each put in a random order (per region, round and draw), and a fraction takes the first blocks of each list, so the draws are nested (10% ⊂ 25% ⊂ 50%); the order is accepted only if its first 10% hold ≥ 20 rainfed parcels. No fraction below 10%. Draws 3 per fraction; draw k is the same in E02–E05 and for every input (paired) Seeds 1 seed per draw (the main run keeps its 3 seeds) Validation and test folds unchanged Runs 4 inputs × 3 fractions × 3 draws = 36 per region, for L-TAE + MLP Result macro-F1 and rainfed F1 against the training fraction, one line per input, Morocco and Utah

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: L-TAE attention over the 12 monthly embeddings gives the same result as concat + PCA with the same MLP head (E03): all differences are within ±0.01 except TerraMind in Utah (−0.015, not significant). It is also level with E02's SVM. The temporal aggregation therefore does not change the conclusion. Morocco: Clay + L-TAE (0.906) ties with S2 + L-TAE (0.905), and no GeoFM differs significantly from the baseline. Utah: Clay (+0.041) and Prithvi (+0.039) beat S2 + L-TAE, and the gap is +0.05–0.07 in Bear River. Against the S2 baseline's best head (E02 RF, 0.764), Clay + L-TAE (0.784) leads by 0.02. The attention weights are spread over the year and nearly the same for both classes. In Utah, Clay and Prithvi weight July–September most. Full tables, figures and interpretation are in the report.

docs.title: E04 · Frozen GeoFMs + L-TAE temporal aggregation + MLP head — report
docs.text: Answer. No. Learned temporal attention (L-TAE) over the 12 monthly embeddings classifies as well as concat + PCA with the same MLP head, but not better: every input is within ±0.01 of its E03 result. The ranking of the inputs stays the same. In Morocco, Clay (0.906) ties with the S2 baseline (0.905). In Utah, Clay and Prithvi beat the S2 baseline with the same head by about 0.04.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• L-TAE ≈ PCA + MLP. Against E03's MLP on the same input, the differences are −0.003 to +0.008, none significant. The one exception is TerraMind in Utah (−0.015, not significant after Holm). L-TAE is also level with E02's SVM for every input (within ±0.007).
  • Morocco: the GeoFMs equal the S2 baseline. Clay + L-TAE (0.906) and S2 + L-TAE (0.905) are the two best L-TAE results. Prithvi and TerraMind are 0.007–0.009 lower, and every CI includes 0. The same holds inside Doukkala.
  • Utah: Clay and Prithvi are better than the S2 baseline with the same head. Clay +0.041 and Prithvi +0.039 (significant); TerraMind +0.027 (CI just touches 0). In Bear River the gap is +0.05–0.07. Against the S2 baseline's best head, E02's random forest (0.764), Clay + L-TAE (0.784) leads by 0.02.
  • Souss confirms the E03 correction. With L-TAE, the S2 features find 84% of Souss's rainfed parcels, as many as Clay (84%) and close to Prithvi (87%). The S2 features have no weakness there once the head is non-linear.
  • Label efficiency, same picture as E03. In Morocco at 10% of the training blocks, S2 (0.819) and Clay (0.811) are level, with Prithvi and TerraMind lower. In Utah, all inputs are similar at 10% (0.65–0.68), and the GeoFMs pull ahead from 25% (Clay and Prithvi 0.73 vs S2 0.70).
  • Attention is spread over the year. Month weights range from 0.04 to 0.14 (uniform = 0.083), and irrigated and rainfed parcels get almost the same weights. In Utah, Clay and Prithvi put most weight on July–September, the irrigated summer.

docs.title: Macro-F1 of every input and head
docs.text:
Out-of-fold predictions of all 5 spatial folds; bold = best input for that head. Runs marked [E0x] come from an earlier experiment, on the same parcels and bootstrap draws.

How to read this table

What: one score per input (row) and classifier (column), between 0 and 1. Higher is better.

Macro-F1: F1 is computed for each class separately (irrigated, rainfed) and the two are averaged. Rainfed parcels are the minority, so a model that labels everything "irrigated" still gets a high overall accuracy but a low macro-F1. That is why macro-F1 is the main metric.

How: every parcel is predicted once, by the model that did not see its 20 km block in training (out-of-fold). All inputs are scored on the same parcels, so the numbers can be compared directly.

Read it as: about 0.90 = very good; 0.75 = clear errors on the rainfed class; 0.50 = no better than guessing one class.

docs.title: Difference from the S2 baseline (headline heads)
docs.text:
Δ = input minus baseline with the same head (runs with their own model against the baseline's random forest), on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws. Better / worse = the 95% confidence interval (CI) excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05.

How to read this table

What: each row compares one input with the baseline (the Sentinel feature classifier), using the same classifier.

  • Difference in macro-F1 (Δ): the input's score minus the baseline's. +0.013 means 0.013 higher than the baseline; −0.158 means 0.158 lower.
  • 95% confidence interval (CI), e.g. [−0.021, +0.025]: the range in which the true difference probably lies. It comes from resampling whole 20 km blocks 1,000 times (block bootstrap) and recomputing Δ each time.
    • The range includes 0 (one end negative, the other positive): the data cannot tell which input is better.
    • The range is entirely above 0, e.g. [+0.011, +0.049]: the input is better.
    • The range is entirely below 0, e.g. [−0.215, −0.085]: the input is worse.
  • p-value (Holm-corrected): how likely a difference this large would be if the two inputs were really equal. Many pairs are tested at once, so each p-value is raised (Holm correction) to avoid false "wins" by chance. 1.000 = no evidence of a difference.
  • Verdict: "better" or "worse" only if the CI excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05. "Higher/lower, not significant after Holm" = the CI excludes 0, but the evidence does not survive the correction.

Why paired: both inputs are scored on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws, so a difference reflects the inputs, not which parcels happened to be drawn.

docs.title: Per-class metrics (headline heads, 95% confidence interval)
docs.text:
How to read this table

What: the main metric and three others for the headline classifiers, each with its 95% confidence interval in brackets (the range the true value probably lies in).

  • Macro-F1: mean F1 of the two classes (main metric).
  • F1 of the rainfed class: how well the minority class is found. Precision and recall of "rainfed" are combined, so it is usually the lowest number and the most informative one.
  • Balanced accuracy: mean recall of the two classes. 0.5 = guessing.
  • Overall accuracy: share of all parcels labelled correctly. It looks high even for weak models, because most parcels are irrigated, so do not compare inputs on it alone.

Wide CIs (e.g. 0.63–0.88) mean the score changes a lot from block to block, so small differences between rows are not meaningful.

docs.title: Difference from the S2 baseline (headline heads)
docs.text:
Δ = input minus baseline with the same head (runs with their own model against the baseline's random forest), on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws. Better / worse = the 95% confidence interval (CI) excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05.

How to read this table

What: each row compares one input with the baseline (the Sentinel feature classifier), using the same classifier.

  • Difference in macro-F1 (Δ): the input's score minus the baseline's. +0.013 means 0.013 higher than the baseline; −0.158 means 0.158 lower.
  • 95% confidence interval (CI), e.g. [−0.021, +0.025]: the range in which the true difference probably lies. It comes from resampling whole 20 km blocks 1,000 times (block bootstrap) and recomputing Δ each time.
    • The range includes 0 (one end negative, the other positive): the data cannot tell which input is better.
    • The range is entirely above 0, e.g. [+0.011, +0.049]: the input is better.
    • The range is entirely below 0, e.g. [−0.215, −0.085]: the input is worse.
  • p-value (Holm-corrected): how likely a difference this large would be if the two inputs were really equal. Many pairs are tested at once, so each p-value is raised (Holm correction) to avoid false "wins" by chance. 1.000 = no evidence of a difference.
  • Verdict: "better" or "worse" only if the CI excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05. "Higher/lower, not significant after Holm" = the CI excludes 0, but the evidence does not survive the correction.

Why paired: both inputs are scored on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws, so a difference reflects the inputs, not which parcels happened to be drawn.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The temporal aggregation does not matter here. Concatenating the 12 months and reducing them by PCA keeps the information the classifier needs. Learning which months to attend to (L-TAE, the temporal module of PANGAEA's multi-temporal evaluation) gives the same result. Two reasons are likely. First, at parcel level, 12 monthly embeddings are a short sequence: concat + PCA can still represent the whole seasonal profile, so there is little for attention to add. Second, the L-TAE has to learn its attention from a few thousand parcels, while PCA needs no labels. The L-TAE's larger spread between seeds in Utah (SD up to 0.013, vs ≤ 0.005 for the MLP) fits this: it has more to learn from the same data.

RQ1 after E02–E04. Once the head is non-linear (SVM, MLP or L-TAE + MLP), neither the head nor the temporal aggregation changes the conclusion. Each region's result is stable across all three experiments:

Best S2 baseline Best GeoFM Difference Morocco 0.908 (MLP, E03) 0.906 (Clay, L-TAE, E04) none Utah 0.764 (RF, E02) 0.791 (Clay, SVM, E02) ≈ +0.03; +0.04 with the same head

The frozen GeoFM embeddings do not beat a well-built Sentinel-2 feature set in Morocco. In Utah they give a small but consistent gain, which is largest inside the main rainfed zone (Bear River, +0.05 to +0.09 in E02–E04). Clay is the best GeoFM in both regions with every non-linear head. Prithvi is close behind, and TerraMind gains least from the L-TAE.

What the attention shows. The attention weights are close to uniform and nearly the same for both classes, so the L-TAE does not single out one decisive month. In Utah, Clay and Prithvi weight July–September most, the months when irrigated fields stay green and rainfed ones have dried out. In E02, the same months mattered most for the S2 random forest. In Morocco, the weights are spread over the winter and spring growing season and the early summer, with no clear peak. This fits the result that a simple concatenation already works well.

AgriFM is not part of E04. It returns one embedding per year, so there is no sequence to attend to. Its best result remains E03's MLP (Morocco 0.857, Utah 0.747).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The L-TAE settings follow PANGAEA and the original L-TAE (16 heads, d_k 8, d_model 256) and are not tuned. The validation fold only stops training.
  • Attention weights show where the model looks, not why. They come from the first seed and are averaged over heads and test folds.
  • The main L-TAE result averages 3 seeds; the label-efficiency points are single seeds.
  • The Holm correction covers this experiment's own runs: 3 differences from the baseline, and 16 L-TAE vs E02/E03 comparisons.
  • Per-zone results for zones with fewer than 50 rainfed parcels are indicative only.

docs.text:

  • RQ1 summary: after E05, write the RQ1 answer from each input's best configuration, and test the "best vs best" differences explicitly.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Does a temporal deep model trained only on our labelled parcels, with no pretraining, match the frozen foundation models?

docs.title: Why
docs.text: A foundation model is only useful if it beats what a model trained from scratch on the same labels achieves. PSE-TAE (Garnot et al. 2020) was built for parcel classification from satellite time series: it samples pixels inside each parcel and learns the temporal pattern with attention. It is the neural baseline of RQ1, next to the classical Sentinel-2 feature baseline.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Setting Value Input pixel sets: inner pixels of the parcel (edge pixels within 10 m left out; parcels with < 4 inner pixels keep all), 10 Sentinel-2 bands × 12 months (D14) Model PSE-TAE: 64 pixels sampled per parcel; mean of 5 random draws at prediction Training Adam 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4, batch 128, ≤ 100 epochs, early stopping on validation macro-F1 (patience 15) Validation PASTIS rotation: 3 folds train, next fold validation, 1 fold test Seeds 3 (mean ± SD; out-of-fold prediction = mean probability) Runs morocco_s2 (views/), utah_s2 (views_2023-24/); morocco_s2s1 only for the Sentinel-1 ablation (A5)

docs.title: Label efficiency (part of this experiment)
docs.text:
Every input is also trained on 10, 25 and 50% of the training blocks, so the report shows a learning curve next to the main result (Q5 of the experiment plan).

Setting Value Fractions 10, 25, 50% of the training blocks of each round; 100% = the main run Sampling whole blocks: rainfed and irrigated-only blocks each put in a random order (per region, round and draw), and a fraction takes the first blocks of each list, so the draws are nested (10% ⊂ 25% ⊂ 50%); the order is accepted only if its first 10% hold ≥ 20 rainfed parcels. No fraction below 10%. Draws 3 per fraction; draw k is the same in E02–E05 and for every input (paired) Seeds 1 seed per draw (the main run keeps its 3 seeds) Validation and test folds unchanged Runs 1 input (pixel sets) × 3 fractions × 3 draws = 9 per region, for PSE-TAE Result macro-F1 and rainfed F1 against the training fraction, one line per input, Morocco and Utah

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
# on the Mac (all regions, main and label-efficiency runs, compare, report):
#   experiments/run_experiment.py:  EXPERIMENT = "E05_psetae_scratch"
python experiments/run_experiment.py
# on the cluster: one Slurm job per run, then one compare job per region (EXPERIMENT and DRY_RUN in the script)
python experiments/submit_slurm.py
  • Order: after E02 (compares with its baseline and GeoFM runs).

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: Morocco: PSE-TAE trained from scratch on Sentinel-2 pixel sets reaches macro-F1 0.911, the highest number of RQ1. It ties with the best runs of E02–E04 (S2 + MLP 0.908, Clay + L-TAE 0.906; all differences within ±0.01, CIs include 0). Utah: PSE-TAE (0.755) equals the S2 random forest (0.764, difference not significant), but it is significantly below Clay (−0.036 vs Clay + SVM, −0.028 vs Clay + L-TAE). Utah is therefore the only region where a frozen GeoFM beats every model trained only on our labels. PSE-TAE has the highest rainfed recall of all models (e.g. Souss 0.90), at the cost of precision in Utah. Full tables, the best-vs-best comparison and the interpretation are in the report.

docs.title: E05 · PSE-TAE trained from scratch on Sentinel-2 pixel sets (neural baseline) — report
docs.text: Answer. In Morocco, yes. PSE-TAE trained from scratch on Sentinel-2 pixels scores 0.911, the highest macro-F1 of all RQ1 experiments, but it ties with the best S2 and GeoFM runs (all differences within ±0.01). In Utah, no. PSE-TAE (0.755) equals the S2 random forest, but it is significantly below Clay (−0.028 to −0.036). Utah is the only region where a frozen GeoFM beats every model built only on our labels.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• Morocco: PSE-TAE 0.911, a tie at the top. It is +0.003 above S2 + MLP (E03), +0.004 above Clay + L-TAE (E04) and +0.009 above Clay + SVM (E02), and every CI includes 0. Only against the S2 random forest is it clearly higher (+0.038, p = 0.07 in the experiment's own test).
  • Utah: PSE-TAE equals the S2 baseline, and the GeoFMs stay ahead. PSE-TAE (0.755) vs S2 + RF 0.764: −0.009, not significant. Against the best GeoFMs on the same parcels: Clay + SVM −0.036 [−0.056, −0.015], Clay + L-TAE −0.028 [−0.048, −0.009]. Both are significant, also after a Holm correction over the five comparisons.
  • PSE-TAE finds the most rainfed parcels. It has the highest balanced accuracy in both regions (Morocco 0.942, Utah 0.810). In Souss, it finds 90% of the rainfed parcels (best of all models), and in Utah's Sevier River 49% (others ≤ 37%). In Utah this comes at the cost of precision: in Bear River, rainfed recall is 0.84 but precision 0.58.
  • Label efficiency: no advantage from pixels. At 10% of the training blocks, PSE-TAE reaches 0.812 in Morocco, level with the best inputs of E03/E04 (0.81–0.83). In Utah it reaches 0.664, below Clay and Prithvi with an MLP (0.69–0.70).
  • Seeds: SD 0.010 (Morocco) and 0.008 (Utah), similar to the other neural heads.

docs.text:
Out-of-fold predictions of all 5 spatial folds; bold = best input for that head. Runs marked [E0x] come from an earlier experiment, on the same parcels and bootstrap draws.

How to read this table

What: one score per input (row) and classifier (column), between 0 and 1. Higher is better.

Macro-F1: F1 is computed for each class separately (irrigated, rainfed) and the two are averaged. Rainfed parcels are the minority, so a model that labels everything "irrigated" still gets a high overall accuracy but a low macro-F1. That is why macro-F1 is the main metric.

How: every parcel is predicted once, by the model that did not see its 20 km block in training (out-of-fold). All inputs are scored on the same parcels, so the numbers can be compared directly.

Read it as: about 0.90 = very good; 0.75 = clear errors on the rainfed class; 0.50 = no better than guessing one class.

docs.title: Difference from the S2 baseline (headline heads)
docs.text:
Δ = input minus baseline with the same head (runs with their own model against the baseline's random forest), on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws. Better / worse = the 95% confidence interval (CI) excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05.

How to read this table

What: each row compares one input with the baseline (the Sentinel feature classifier), using the same classifier.

  • Difference in macro-F1 (Δ): the input's score minus the baseline's. +0.013 means 0.013 higher than the baseline; −0.158 means 0.158 lower.
  • 95% confidence interval (CI), e.g. [−0.021, +0.025]: the range in which the true difference probably lies. It comes from resampling whole 20 km blocks 1,000 times (block bootstrap) and recomputing Δ each time.
    • The range includes 0 (one end negative, the other positive): the data cannot tell which input is better.
    • The range is entirely above 0, e.g. [+0.011, +0.049]: the input is better.
    • The range is entirely below 0, e.g. [−0.215, −0.085]: the input is worse.
  • p-value (Holm-corrected): how likely a difference this large would be if the two inputs were really equal. Many pairs are tested at once, so each p-value is raised (Holm correction) to avoid false "wins" by chance. 1.000 = no evidence of a difference.
  • Verdict: "better" or "worse" only if the CI excludes 0 and the Holm-corrected p-value < 0.05. "Higher/lower, not significant after Holm" = the CI excludes 0, but the evidence does not survive the correction.

Why paired: both inputs are scored on the same parcels and the same bootstrap draws, so a difference reflects the inputs, not which parcels happened to be drawn.

Input Classifier Difference in macro-F1 (Δ) 95% confidence interval (CI) p-value (Holm-corrected) Verdict PSE-TAE PSE-TAE (pixel-set encoder + temporal attention) (vs baseline RF) +0.038 [-0.004, +0.082] 0.074 no clear difference

docs.title: Per-class metrics (headline heads, 95% confidence interval)
docs.text:
How to read this table

What: the main metric and three others for the headline classifiers, each with its 95% confidence interval in brackets (the range the true value probably lies in).

  • Macro-F1: mean F1 of the two classes (main metric).
  • F1 of the rainfed class: how well the minority class is found. Precision and recall of "rainfed" are combined, so it is usually the lowest number and the most informative one.
  • Balanced accuracy: mean recall of the two classes. 0.5 = guessing.
  • Overall accuracy: share of all parcels labelled correctly. It looks high even for weak models, because most parcels are irrigated, so do not compare inputs on it alone.

Wide CIs (e.g. 0.63–0.88) mean the score changes a lot from block to block, so small differences between rows are not meaningful.

How to read this table

What: how the score changes when the model is trained with fewer labelled parcels.

How to read this table

What: how the score changes when the model is trained with fewer labelled parcels.

  • Columns: share of the training blocks used (10%, 25%, 50%; 100% = the main result). The row training parcels per round gives the actual number of parcels. Validation and test folds are always complete, so every column is tested on the same parcels.
  • 0.807 ± 0.091: the mean over 3 different random draws of blocks ± their standard deviation. A large ± means the result depends on which blocks were drawn.
  • Read it as: an input that stays high at 10% needs fewer labels (it is "label-efficient"). If its curve rises steeply, it needs many labels.

Why whole blocks: dropping single parcels would leave neighbours of every parcel in training. Dropping whole 20 km blocks simulates having field data from fewer places.

How to read this table

What: the score inside the one zone where both classes are common (the focus zone), not over the whole region.

Why: across a whole region, a model can score well just by learning where parcels are (one zone is almost all irrigated, another has the rainfed parcels). Inside one zone, location does not help, so this shows whether the input separates irrigated from rainfed fields themselves.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
PSE-TAE vs the best of E02–E04. The tables above test PSE-TAE only against the S2 random forest, the baseline classifier of the comparison script. For RQ1, the relevant question is how it compares with the best model of each earlier experiment. The paired differences below are computed in the same way: out-of-fold predictions on the parcels common to all runs, and 1,000 block-bootstrap draws of whole 20 km blocks.

Region PSE-TAE minus … Difference in macro-F1 (Δ) 95% confidence interval (CI) p-value Morocco S2 + MLP (E03) +0.003 [−0.006, +0.011] 0.56 Morocco S2 + SVM (E02) +0.011 [−0.011, +0.044] 0.44 Morocco Clay + L-TAE (E04) +0.004 [−0.007, +0.015] 0.43 Morocco Clay + SVM (E02) +0.009 [−0.010, +0.026] 0.34 Utah S2 + RF (E02) −0.009 [−0.028, +0.012] 0.39 Utah S2 + L-TAE (E04) +0.012 [−0.002, +0.026] 0.09 Utah Clay + SVM (E02) −0.036 [−0.056, −0.015] < 0.001 Utah Clay + L-TAE (E04) −0.028 [−0.048, −0.009] 0.008 Utah Prithvi + SVM (E02) −0.027 [−0.051, −0.003] 0.028 (0.08 after Holm)

Morocco: everything good ends at about 0.90–0.91. A temporal model trained from scratch on 64 pixels per parcel, a flexible head on 180 hand-crafted S2 features, and the frozen GeoFMs with SVM, MLP or L-TAE all reach the same level. The task in Morocco is limited by the labels and the region rather than by the model. The rainfed parcels are concentrated in Doukkala, and their seasonal signal (winter crop, no summer crop) is clear in plain Sentinel-2 reflectance. Pretraining has nothing left to add.

Utah: the only place where pretraining helps. PSE-TAE does as well as the S2 random forest, so a stronger supervised model on raw pixels does not close the gap. Clay is still 0.03–0.04 ahead, with CIs that exclude 0. In Utah, rainfed and irrigated fields share crops, are spread over many zones and have less training data (≈ 6,000 parcels). There, the GeoFM embeddings seem to carry information about the field and its surroundings that 400–1,700 training parcels per round cannot teach a model from scratch. The label-efficiency curves point the same way: at 10% of the training blocks, Clay and Prithvi with an MLP are 0.03 above PSE-TAE.

What PSE-TAE does differently. It looks at individual pixels (a random set of 64 per parcel), not at the parcel mean or an 80–160 m patch. It is the most sensitive model for the rainfed class: highest balanced accuracy in both regions, best rainfed recall in Souss (0.90) and Sevier River (0.49). In Utah it overpredicts rainfed (Bear River: precision 0.58), which lowers its macro-F1. A threshold other than 0.5, or the class weights, could trade some of this recall for precision. That is not tuned here, to keep every model on the same rule.

RQ1 after E02–E05.

Best model built only on our labels Best frozen GeoFM Difference Morocco 0.911 (PSE-TAE, E05) 0.906 (Clay + L-TAE, E04) none (+0.004, CI includes 0) Utah 0.764 (S2 + RF, E02) 0.791 (Clay + SVM, E02) GeoFM ahead by ≈ 0.03 (vs PSE-TAE: +0.036, significant)

Frozen GeoFM embeddings are not better than well-built supervised models in a region with clear class signals and a concentrated rainfed area (Morocco). They are better, by a small but significant margin, in a region with mixed crops and spread-out rainfed fields (Utah). Clay is the best GeoFM in both regions.

Training behaviour: would other settings change the result? The figure shows the training loss and the validation macro-F1 of every epoch, for all 5 rounds × 3 seeds of the main runs (from each run's training_history.csv).

Training loss (top) and validation macro-F1 (bottom) per epoch; colour = round (test fold), line style = seed, dot = best epoch (kept by early stopping). Median over the 15 trainings Morocco Utah Training loss: epoch 1 → best epoch → last epoch 0.32 → 0.09 → 0.06 0.51 → 0.29 → 0.18 Best epoch / last epoch (limit 100) 7 / 22 8 / 23 Typical change per epoch: loss / validation F1 0.009 / 0.014 0.020 / 0.018
  • The training loss falls smoothly in every round and seed, so the learning rate is not too high. A too-high rate would make the loss itself jump or stall.
  • Validation F1 stops improving after about 7–8 epochs while the loss keeps falling (by another third). This is overfitting to the training blocks, and early stopping already keeps the best epoch. More epochs cannot help: no run came close to the limit of 100.
  • The epoch-to-epoch zigzag in validation F1 is evaluation noise: small validation folds and the random draw of 64 pixels per parcel. It does not come from unstable training.
  • The test fold matters more than the epoch. Each round stays in its own band (Morocco: fold 1 ≈ 0.95, fold 4 ≈ 0.80–0.85; Utah: fold 4 ≈ 0.78, fold 0 ≈ 0.68) for every seed. Some 20 km blocks are harder, whatever the training.
  • In Utah, generalisation is the limit, not optimisation: the loss is still 0.29 when validation F1 peaks.

A lower learning rate or more epochs would therefore not change the result. More regularisation targets the overfitting after epoch 8, and a different class weight or decision threshold targets the rainfed over-prediction in Utah. Each would probably gain about 0.01–0.02, less than the 0.03–0.04 gap to Clay. Testing them is a sensitivity check of the baseline, not part of E05.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The best-vs-best table is an extra check for this report, computed with the same block-bootstrap method but outside the comparison script. It uses its own bootstrap draws, and Holm applies only where stated. The experiment's own Holm family has one comparison per region (PSE-TAE vs the S2 random forest).
  • PSE-TAE uses the settings of the original paper (64 pixels, PSE and TAE dimensions), Sentinel-2 bands only (D14), and no tuning. The validation fold only stops training.
  • It sees pixels inside the parcel (no edge pixels), while the GeoFMs see 80–160 m patches that can include neighbouring land. The models therefore do not see exactly the same area.
  • The main result averages 3 seeds; the label-efficiency points are single seeds.
  • results/psetae_agyear_s2s1/ is an older Sentinel-1/2 run from before D14 and is not part of this experiment.

docs.title: Morocco training data
docs.text:
This page describes the construction of the machine-learning-ready dataset for Morocco: labelled parcels, spatial train / validation / test folds, a common store of monthly Sentinel-1/2 imagery with label rasters, and derived views for the different model families.

Contents

  1. Overview
  2. Design principles
  3. Source data
  4. Script 01 — labels
  5. Script 02 — spatial folds
  6. Script 03 — tile store
  7. Script 04 — model views
  8. Output layout and file formats
  9. How to use the dataset
  10. Running, settings and run time
  11. Known limitations
  12. References

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD subgraph IN["Inputs"] FS["Field survey<br/>~10,000 parcels<br/>Dec 2023 – Jan 2025"] WC["ESA WorldCover 2021<br/>(cropland check)"] GEE["Google Earth Engine<br/>Sentinel-2 L2A · Cloud Score+<br/>Sentinel-1 GRD"] end FS --> S01["<b>01_prepare_labels_Morocco.py</b><br/>clean geometry · label · cropland only<br/>agricultural year"] WC --> S01 S01 -->|"parcels_labelled.geojson<br/>8,781 parcels"| S02["<b>02_make_spatial_folds.py</b><br/>20 km blocks → 5 balanced folds"] S02 -->|"parcels_folds.geojson<br/>+ block_id, fold"| SPLIT[["Split by agricultural year<br/>(ag_season from survey date)"]] SPLIT -->|"2023/24 · 6,887 parcels<br/>imagery Sep 2023 – Aug 2024"| S03["<b>03_build_tiles.py</b><br/>run per agricultural year:<br/>128 × 128 px tiles · 12 months × 19 bands<br/>label / parcel-ID / edge rasters"] SPLIT -->|"2024/25 · 1,894 parcels<br/>imagery Sep 2024 – Aug 2025"| S03 GEE --> S03 S03 -->|"tiles/ · parcels.csv · tiles.parquet"| S04["<b>04_make_views.py</b><br/>cut every model input from the same pixels"] S04 --> VA["A · parcel feature tables<br/>(RF / boosting)"] S04 --> VB["B · pixel sets<br/>(PSE-TAE)"] S04 --> VC["C · patch-aligned chips<br/>chips_p8 · chips_p16<br/>(foundation models)"] S03 --> VD["D · full tiles<br/>(segmentation, U-TAE)"] Step Script What comes out 1 01_prepare_labels_Morocco.py 8,781 labelled cropland parcels (7,585 irrigated, 1,196 rainfed) 2 02_make_spatial_folds.py a fold (0–4) per parcel, from 91 spatial blocks of 20 km 3 03_build_tiles.py the tile store: monthly images + label rasters + QA 4 04_make_views.py model inputs A–C (D = the tiles themselves)

Steps 1–2 complete within minutes. Step 3 requires several hours and resumes from the last completed tile when restarted. Step 4 runs locally.

docs.title: 2. Design principles
docs.text:
Principle How it is achieved One set of pixels for every model All imagery is downloaded once into one tile store. Every model input is cut from it locally, so differences between models cannot come from different compositing, masks or download windows. No duplicated downloads Fixed, non-overlapping 1.28 km tiles in one projection. Neighbouring parcels share tiles instead of each getting its own overlapping chip. Imagery matched to the label date Each parcel gets the 12 months of the agricultural year (1 Sep – 31 Aug) in which it was surveyed. The same place in another year is a different tile. Honest validation Folds are made of whole 20 km blocks, so a test parcel never has its next-door neighbour in training (section 5). Uncertain pixels kept, not dropped Label 0 = ignore (unlabelled or overlapping parcels), plus a separate edge flag for mixed boundary pixels. Users decide how to treat them. Documented quality Clear-observation counts per pixel and month, scene IDs per tile and month, QA per tile, overlap list, patch-purity scores. Patch-aware chips Chips for patch-based models are shifted so the parcel centroid sits at the centre of one model patch (section 7).

The layout follows existing ML-ready crop datasets. PASTIS (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) and Sen4AgriNet (Sykas et al. 2022) use fixed tiles with dense label and parcel-ID rasters. Fields of The World (Kerner et al. 2025) keeps an "unlabelled" ignore class. The ClarkCGA / Prithvi crop chips report QA counts per chip.

docs.title: 3.1 The field survey
docs.text:
Ouassanouan, Y., Elfarkh, J., Grich, S., Liblab, A., & Chehbouni, A. (2026). Crop and irrigation types ground-truth dataset for Moroccan agricultural regions. Scientific Data, 13, 746. doi:10.1038/s41597-026-06993-y · paper summary

About 10,000 geolocated parcels were surveyed with the QField mobile app between December 2023 and January 2025, in the five main agricultural regions of Morocco. Each record has the land use, crop (45 types), irrigation method (six systems, from flood irrigation to pivots) and a geo-referenced photograph. The authors checked the records against 2024 NDVI time series.

Region Irrigation and crops Survey seasons used here El Gharb surface-water irrigation; rice, vegetables 2023/24 Tadla large-scale irrigation; sugar beet, cereals 2023/24 Doukkala mixed irrigated and rainfed systems (most rainfed parcels) 2023/24 and 2024/25 El Haouz groundwater irrigation; olives, citrus 2023/24 and 2024/25 Souss advanced drip systems; export crops 2024/25

The figures below show the raw survey, before script 01 cleans it. That is why the counts are slightly higher than the 8,781 labelled parcels (e.g. 1,216 rainfed raw vs 1,196 after cleaning; the cleaned parcels are mapped in Figure 1.3). "Statte" is a small survey zone in the 2024/25 season.

Figure 1.1. Surveyed parcels by irrigation method (raw survey). Figure 1.2. Irrigated and rainfed parcels per survey zone (raw survey). Rainfed parcels are almost all in Doukkala, with a few in Souss.

docs.title: 3.2 Other inputs
docs.text: Data Used for ESA WorldCover 2021 (10 m) label check: share of each parcel mapped as cropland (script 01) Sentinel-2 L2A harmonised + Cloud Score+ monthly imagery of every model (script 03, cloud mask cs_cdf ≥ 0.60) Sentinel-1 GRD monthly VV/VH in the tile store, ascending and descending kept apart; not used by the models for now (D14) FAO GAUL 2015 (level 0) country outline on the maps (data/admin_boundaries/)

docs.title: 4. Script 01 — prepare_labels
docs.text:
Purpose: turn the raw survey into one clean file of labelled cropland parcels. Every later step starts from this file.

flowchart LR A["Survey shapefile"] --> B["Clean geometry<br/>drop empty · repair invalid<br/>drop exact duplicates"] B --> C["Normalise irrigation text<br/>(lower case, trimmed)"] C --> D{"Irrigation<br/>method?"} D -->|"drip · flood · sprinkler<br/>basin · pivot"| E["label 1<br/>irrigated"] D -->|"rainfed"| F["label 2<br/>rainfed"] D -->|"missing"| X["dropped"] E --> G{"Land use is<br/>cropland?"} F --> G G -->|"Seasonal Crop · Trees<br/>Trees + Seasonal"| H["Add attributes<br/>area_ha · ag_season<br/>nn_dist_m · WorldCover share"] G -->|"bare soil · weeds · water"| X H --> I["parcels_labelled.geojson<br/>summary.csv · figures"]

Steps

  1. Read the survey shapefile.
  2. Clean the geometry: drop parcels without geometry, repair invalid polygons, drop exact duplicates.
  3. Label it: any irrigation method (drip, flood, sprinkler, basin, pivot) = 1 irrigated; "rainfed" = 2 rainfed. Spelling variants are normalised.
  4. Keep cropland only: Seasonal Crop, Trees, Trees + Seasonal.
  5. Add these attributes:
  6. area_ha: area in UTM 29N.
  7. ag_season: agricultural year of the survey date (1 Sep – 31 Aug, e.g. 2023/24). This decides which imagery a parcel gets.
  8. nn_dist_m: distance to the nearest other parcel.
  9. wc_cropland_frac, wc_major: optional WorldCover check (CHECK_WORLDCOVER).
  10. Save the parcels, a summary table and four figures.

Result

Agricultural year Irrigated Rainfed Total 2023/24 6,189 (11,034 ha) 698 (836 ha) 6,887 2024/25 1,396 (2,020 ha) 498 (1,286 ha) 1,894 All 7,585 1,196 8,781

Median parcel size: 0.83 ha (10th–90th percentile: 0.30–3.5 ha). Rainfed parcels are 14% of the total, and nearly all of them (1,122 of 1,196) are in Doukkala. The classes are unbalanced, and the class is partly tied to the region, which is why section 5 matters.

Figure 1.3. Spatial distribution of the 8,781 labelled cropland parcels. Rainfed parcels are concentrated in Doukkala on the Atlantic coast. Figure 1.4. Class balance (left; 86.4% irrigated, 13.6% rainfed) and parcel-size distribution per class (right, logarithmic axis). Figure 1.5. Labelled parcels by survey month (December 2023 – January 2025). The survey date determines the agricultural year, and thus the imagery, assigned to each parcel.

Outputs (outputs/morocco/dataset/01_labels/): - parcels_labelled.geojson - summary.csv - parcels_map.png - class_balance_and_size.png - survey_timing.png

docs.title: 5. Script 02 — make_spatial_folds
docs.text: Purpose: split the parcels into 5 folds so a model can be trained on some areas and tested on other areas. This is the dataset's train / validation / test split.

docs.title: 5.1 Why not a random split
docs.text: Surveyed parcels are typically a few hundred metres apart, and neighbouring parcels usually share a class. Under a random 5-fold split, 72% of test parcels have a training parcel within 250 m and 98% within 1 km. Accuracy then reflects the recognition of nearby parcels rather than the ability to map new areas, a bias documented by Roberts et al. (2017), Ploton et al. (2020) and Kattenborn et al. (2022).

docs.title: 5.2 Choosing the block size
docs.text:
The range of spatial dependence is estimated from the proportion of parcel pairs that share a class as a function of their distance. This proportion is compared with the random-placement level, i.e. the probability that two randomly drawn parcels share a class, 0.86² + 0.14² ≈ 76%. Beyond the distance at which the curve reaches this level, proximity carries no information about the class.

Distance between parcels 0.2 km 1 km 5 km 10 km 15 km 20 km 30 km 50 km Same class (%) 96.1 95.2 92.0 91.0 86.7 81.4 79.7 73.7 Figure 1.6. Proportion of parcel pairs sharing a class as a function of distance. The proportion approaches the random-placement level (76%, dashed) at about 20–30 km, which motivates the 20 km block size (dotted).

Candidate block sizes, each with 5 greedy-balanced folds:

Split Rainfed in smallest fold Rainfed share per fold Test parcels with a training parcel ≤ 250 m ≤ 1 km random 239 20–20% 79.4% 98.4% 2 km blocks 239 20–20% 12.8% 65.6% 5 km 239 20–20% 6.3% 31.7% 10 km 239 20–20% 3.2% 18.0% 20 km 238 20–20% 2.0% 10.2% 25 km 239 20–20% 1.8% 9.1% 30 km 142 12–34% 0.6% 4.6% 50 km 202 17–24% 1.2% 5.9%

20 km is the chosen size: - It is near the distance where class similarity approaches the random-placement level. - It cuts leakage to 2% at 250 m. - It still gives five folds with equal class shares.

From 30 km upwards there are too few blocks with rainfed parcels to balance the folds: one fold would hold 12% of the rainfed parcels and another 34%.

Resulting folds (whole blocks per fold):

Fold Irrigated Rainfed Blocks 0 1,528 239 12 1 1,528 239 13 2 1,473 241 42 3 1,528 238 11 4 1,528 239 13

Leakage, all folds averaged:

Training parcel within … 100 m 250 m 500 m 1 km 5 km random split 24.1% 71.7% 90.1% 97.7% 99.7% 20 km spatial split 0.4% 1.8% 3.8% 8.1% 38.0% Figure 1.7. Fold assignment of the parcels (left) and class counts per fold (right). Each fold contains about 1,530 irrigated and 240 rainfed parcels. Figure 1.8. The 20 km blocks and their folds, with enlargements of Doukkala (A) and Tadla (B). Whole blocks are assigned to a single fold. Figure 1.9.
