docs.title: RQ1 · Frozen encoders: embeddings and classifiers
docs.text:
This page documents the frozen-encoder evaluation of Phase 2 (RQ1), which tests whether frozen embeddings of geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) discriminate irrigated from rainfed cropland parcels in Morocco better than a conventional Sentinel-2 feature baseline under an identical spatial validation design. Every input uses Sentinel-2 only (D14).

It reads only the ML-ready dataset produced in ml_dataset_prep/. The rules of the comparison are summarised in the evaluation protocol; reported results are produced as experiments, which run these scripts with the settings of a config file.

Contents

  1. Overview
  2. Research questions and design
  3. Inputs compared
  4. Script 01 — inspect the dataset
  5. Scripts 02a–02d — foundation-model embeddings
  6. Script 03 — train and evaluate
  7. Script 04 — compare inputs
  8. Output layout
  9. Running, settings and run time
  10. Choices to report and open points
  11. References

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
The workflow below leads from the ML-ready dataset of Phase 1 to the final comparison: the five inputs (feature baseline and four frozen foundation models), the classifiers and their tuning grids, the spatial validation and the paired comparison.

flowchart TD FA["<b>Parcel features</b><br/>median of inner pixels"] C8["<b>Chips p8</b><br/>64 × 64 px, 8-px patches"] C16["<b>Chips p16</b><br/>64 × 64 px, 16-px patches"] FO["<b>Spatial folds</b><br/>20 km blocks"] FA --> B0["<b>S2 baseline</b><br/>180 features"] C8 --> B1["<b>Clay v1.5</b><br/>12 × 1024"] C16 --> B2["<b>Prithvi-EO-2.0</b><br/>12 × 1024"] C16 --> B3["<b>TerraMind</b><br/>12 × 768"] C16 --> B4["<b>AgriFM</b><br/>1 × D"] B1 --> POOL["<b>Frozen encoder → parcel embedding</b><br/>patch-share-weighted mean over the parcel<br/>months side by side → standardise → PCA 128<br/>(fitted on the training folds only)"] B2 --> POOL B3 --> POOL B4 --> POOL B0 --> HUB["<b>03 / 03c · train and evaluate</b><br/>LogReg (linear probe) · RF · SVM (E02)<br/>MLP (E03) · L-TAE + MLP (E04)"] POOL --> HUB HUB --> CV["<b>Spatial CV, 5 rounds</b> (PASTIS scheme)<br/>3 folds train · next fold validation · 1 fold test"] FO -. "folds" .-> CV CV --> OOF["<b>Out-of-fold predictions</b><br/>every parcel predicted once, by a model<br/>that never saw its 20 km block<br/>per region (Morocco, Utah)"] OOF --> M["<b>Metrics per run</b><br/>macro-F1 (headline) · per-class F1 · balanced accuracy<br/>PR-AUC · Brier · ECE · 95% block-bootstrap CI"] M --> CMP["<b>04 · compare models</b><br/>same parcels, same bootstrap samples<br/>Δ macro-F1 vs baseline · Holm-adjusted p"] CMP --> ANS(["Does a foundation model beat<br/>the Sentinel-2 baseline?"])

Per-model bands, patches and temporal handling: Foundation models.

Classifier grids: evaluation protocol §4. Optional sensitivity runs: Sentinel-1 added to the baseline and to TerraMind (Morocco), embeddings averaged over the months instead of PCA.

Step Script GPU What it does 1 01_inspect_dataset.py no checks the dataset before any model is trained 2 02a_embed_clay.py … 02d_embed_agrifm.py recommended frozen GeoFM embeddings per parcel 3 03_train_evaluate.py no trains and evaluates the classifiers for one input (run once per input) 4 04_compare_models.py no compares all inputs on the same parcels

docs.title: 2. Research questions and design
docs.text:
1. Main: does a frozen GeoFM embedding classify irrigated vs rainfed parcels better than Sentinel-1/2 parcel features, when tested on areas the model has never seen?
  2. Which GeoFM works best, and does the classifier on top matter?
  3. How much does random cross-validation overstate accuracy compared with spatial cross-validation?
  4. Which months (and, for the baseline, which variables) carry the signal?

The design keeps everything equal except the input:

flowchart LR SAME["<b>Kept identical for every input</b><br/>same parcels (intersection of all runs)<br/>same pixels (one tile store)<br/>same spatial folds (20 km blocks)<br/>same 4 classifiers and grids<br/>same metrics and bootstrap samples"] --> D["<b>Only the input differs</b><br/>S1/S2 features vs<br/>Clay · Prithvi · TerraMind · AgriFM"] D --> C["<b>Paired difference</b><br/>in macro-F1 with<br/>95% block-bootstrap CI"]

The foundation models are used frozen, as fixed feature extractors, following the linear-probing protocol. No fine-tuning is performed at this stage; the evaluation therefore measures the information contained in the pretrained representations, at low computational cost and under identical conditions for all inputs.

docs.title: 3. Inputs compared
docs.text: The five inputs (Sentinel-2 baseline and four frozen GeoFMs, all Sentinel-2 only), their bands, patch sizes and temporal handling, and the optional Sentinel-1 ablation are specified in Foundation models · Configuration.

docs.title: 4. Script 01 — inspect_dataset
docs.text:
Purpose: find problems in the data before they show up as strange model results. It reads the dataset only and changes nothing.

flowchart LR IN["<b>Dataset files</b><br/>parcels · tiles · overlaps<br/>parcel features · chips · views_info"] --> S["<b>Seven checks</b><br/>1 · inventory per class, season, fold<br/>2 · label QA: overlaps, tiny parcels<br/>3 · observations per month (S2, S1)<br/>4 · patch purity, aligned vs centred<br/>5 · seasonal profiles per class<br/>6 · example chips, 12 months<br/>7 · agreement with the old NDVI table"] S --> OUT["outputs/morocco/study/<br/>01_inspection/"]

What to look for: - Inventory: all 8,781 parcels should reach view A and both chip folders. Missing parcels point to tiles that failed to download. - Observations: winter months (Dec–Feb) have the fewest clear Sentinel-2 views. If a month is empty for most parcels, its features carry little information. - Purity: the aligned chips should have a clearly higher median purity than the centred chips, especially for 16-px patches and small parcels. - Profiles: rainfed parcels should peak in winter (around February) and be bare from May. Irrigated parcels should stay green, or green up again, in summer. This is the signal every model should find. - Legacy agreement: high per-month correlation with the old Earth Engine NDVI confirms the new compositing. The old table used 30-day periods rather than calendar months, so the numbers will not be identical.

Outputs: - inventory.csv - label_qa.csv - observations_per_month.csv / .png - purity_summary.csv, purity.png - seasonal_profiles.png - examples_irrigated.png, examples_rainfed.png - legacy_agreement.csv

The resulting figures are shown in Dataset preparation §7.6.

For a closer look in QGIS, tools/a3_export_chips_geotiff.py writes single chips as georeferenced GeoTIFFs to 01_inspection/chips_geotiff/.

docs.title: 5. Scripts 02a–02d — foundation-model embeddings
docs.text:
All four scripts follow the same pattern. Only the model, its bands and its normalisation change.

flowchart TD A["Chip of one parcel<br/>12 months × 15 bands × 64 × 64 px<br/>+ parcel mask"] --> B["Select the bands the model<br/>was pretrained on"] B --> C["Normalise per band: the model's pretraining<br/>mean / std (AgriFM: the region's chip statistics)<br/>NODATA (cloud) → 0 = band mean"] C --> D["Frozen encoder<br/>(no gradient, eval mode)"] D --> E["Patch tokens on their grid<br/>8 × 8 (Clay), 4 × 4 (Prithvi, TerraMind), 2 × 2 (AgriFM)"] A -->|"mask"| W["Patch weight = share of the<br/>patch's pixels inside the parcel"] E --> F["Weighted mean of the patches<br/>covering the parcel"] W --> F F --> G["One vector per month<br/>(AgriFM: one per year)"] G --> H["valid flag = month had<br/>any clear pixel"] G --> O["<model>_agyear_tiles.npz<br/>embeddings [N, steps, D] float16"] H --> O

Pooling. Each patch token is weighted by the share of its pixels inside the parcel. Patches without any parcel pixel get weight 0. The parcel embedding is the weighted mean, so it describes the parcel and not the whole 640 m chip. The patch-aligned chips (dataset §7.3) put most of the weight on one patch centred on the parcel.

Cloudy pixels. NODATA pixels are set to 0 after normalisation, which equals the band mean. A month with no clear pixel at all is flagged valid = False, and script 03 fills it with the training median.

Resume. Embeddings are saved in batches (_parts_<model>_agyear_tiles/) and merged at the end. A stopped run continues from the last batch.

docs.title: 5.1 Scripts per model
docs.text:
Script Model Output 02a_embed_clay.py Clay v1.5 [N, 12, 1024] 02b_embed_prithvi.py Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M-TL [N, 12, 1024] 02c_embed_terramind.py TerraMind-1.0-base [N, 12, 768] 02d_embed_agrifm.py AgriFM [N, 1, 1024]

AgriFM uses the patch size of its pretrained Sentinel-2 patch embedding (4 × 4 px, output stride 32 px), and the script stops unless every encoder weight is loaded from AgriFM.pth; embeddings produced before 6 Nov 2026 came from an untrained encoder (D12).

Model-specific bands, normalisation, auxiliary inputs (date, location, wavelengths) and known limitations are described in Foundation models · Model notes. AgriFM is normalised with the statistics of the region's own chips (D15).

Region. Each script has REGION and VIEWS_NAME at the top; the environment variables EMBED_REGION and EMBED_VIEWS set them without editing the script (Slurm jobs):

python models_run/02a_embed_clay.py                                              # Morocco, views/
EMBED_REGION=utah EMBED_VIEWS=views_2023-24 python models_run/02a_embed_clay.py  # Utah 2023/24

docs.title: 5.2 How each model handles the 12 months
docs.text:
The four models treat time differently. Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind return one embedding per month (12 per parcel), and this study decides how the months are combined (PCA in E02 / E03, L-TAE in E04). AgriFM merges the months inside the network and returns one embedding for the whole year.

Model Months per forward pass Passes per parcel Time steps out per pass Per parcel Months merged inside the model? Clay v1.5 1 12 1 12 × 1,024 no (single-date model) TerraMind 1 12 1 12 × 768 no (single-date model) Prithvi-EO-2.0 4 (FRAMES_PER_PASS = 4, as in its pretraining) 3 4 12 × 1,024 no: months only share context AgriFM 12 (the whole year) 1 1 1 × 1,024 yes: averaged down to one time step flowchart LR subgraph SD["Clay · TerraMind (single date)"] direction TB S1["month 1"] --> SE1["encoder"] --> SO1["embedding 1"] S2["…"] --> SE2["…"] --> SO2["…"] S12["month 12"] --> SE12["encoder"] --> SO12["embedding 12"] end subgraph PR["Prithvi (4 months per pass)"] direction TB P1["Sep–Dec"] --> PE1["encoder"] --> PO1["4 embeddings<br/>Sep · Oct · Nov · Dec"] P2["Jan–Apr"] --> PE2["encoder"] --> PO2["4 embeddings"] P3["May–Aug"] --> PE3["encoder"] --> PO3["4 embeddings"] end subgraph AG["AgriFM (whole year)"] direction TB A1["12 months"] --> AE["encoder:<br/>12 → 3 → 2 → 1 time steps"] --> AO["1 embedding<br/>for the year"] end

Clay and TerraMind are single-date models: each monthly chip is encoded on its own, so every month gets its own embedding and the months never see each other.

Prithvi-EO-2.0 is multi-temporal, but it does not merge the months. It was pretrained on 4 dates per sample, so the script gives it 4 consecutive months per pass: Sep–Dec, Jan–Apr and May–Aug in Morocco (Oct–Jan, Feb–May, Jun–Sep in Utah). Its tokens span 1 month × 16 × 16 px (temporal patch size 1) and no layer reduces the time axis, so 4 months in give 4 sets of tokens out: for a 64 px chip, 4 months × a 4 × 4 patch grid ([B, T, n, n, D] with T = 4 in 02b_embed_prithvi.py). The only effect of passing 4 months together is attention between them: each month's embedding is computed with the other three as context. Three passes × 4 months = 12 embeddings. They could be averaged to one per pass, but they are kept monthly so that the months are combined in the same way as for Clay and TerraMind.

AgriFM is built like a video model (modified Video Swin Transformer; Li et al. 2025) and compresses time inside the network, as it compresses space. In the encoder code (external/AgriFM/AgriFM/models/video_swin_transformer.py):

  1. The pretrained patch embedding covers 4 months × 4 × 4 px (D12), so 12 months become 3 time steps.
  2. With mean_frame_down = True, each downsampling stage also averages neighbouring time steps (padding an odd count): 3 → 2 → 1.
  3. The output (feature_fusion = "cat") folds any remaining time steps into the channels; with one step left this gives 1,024 channels.

The script receives a feature map of 1,024 channels on a 2 × 2 grid (320 m cells for a 64 px chip), pools the cells covering the parcel and stores it as [N, 1, 1024] with the single step "year".

Consequences for the experiments

Clay · Prithvi · TerraMind AgriFM Who combines the months this study (PCA or L-TAE) the pretrained network Input to PCA (E02 / E03) 12 × D = 9,216–12,288 values → PCA 128 1,024 values → PCA 128 (same input size for the head) L-TAE (E04) yes not applicable: no sequence of months Which months matter measurable (permutation importance in E02, attention weights in E04) not measurable: no per-month embeddings valid flag per month (clear pixels in that month) one flag: at least one observed month

Limitation to report. AgriFM was pretrained on dense time series (5-day steps; its configuration uses 32 frames). Here it receives 12 monthly composites, so each of its time tokens spans 4 months instead of about 20 days. The weights load and the input shape is valid, but the model's fine temporal resolution is not used; this is reported next to the Prithvi limitation (pretrained on 30 m HLS, applied to 10 m Sentinel-2).

docs.text:
outputs/<REGION>/study/02_embeddings/<model>_agyear_tiles.npz          Morocco (views/)
outputs/<REGION>/study/02_embeddings/<model>_agyear_tiles_2023-24.npz  Utah (views_2023-24/)
    parcel_id [N]   label [N]   ag_season [N]
    steps [T]                    month names (Sep … Aug), or ["year"] for AgriFM
    embeddings [N, T, D]         float16
    valid [N, T]                 False = month without any clear pixel

docs.title: 6. Script 03 — train_evaluate
docs.text: Purpose: one script for every input, so all inputs are evaluated in exactly the same way. Set INPUT at the top and run it once per input.

docs.title: 6.1 From input to feature matrix
docs.text:
flowchart TD subgraph BASE["INPUT = s1s2 (baseline)"] A1["parcel_features_inner.csv"] --> A2["Drop bookkeeping and count columns<br/>keep one S1 orbit, renamed VV / VH"] A2 --> A3["Fill fully cloudy months by<br/>linear interpolation in time<br/>(per parcel, own values only)"] A3 --> A4["180 features<br/>15 variables × 12 months (Sentinel-2)"] end subgraph EMB["INPUT = GeoFM"] B1["<model>_agyear_tiles.npz"] --> B2{"FEATURE_MODE"} B2 -->|"concat (default)"| B3["all months side by side<br/>e.g. 12 × 1024 = 12,288"] B2 -->|"mean"| B4["average over months"] end A4 --> J["Join with folds (parcels_folds.geojson)<br/>keep parcels present in both"] B3 --> J B4 --> J J --> X["X, y, fold, block_id"]

Preprocessing inside every model pipeline. It is fitted on the training folds only, so no information leaks from the test fold: - Baseline: median imputation of any remaining gap. - Embeddings: median imputation of empty months, then standardisation. In concat mode, PCA to 128 components follows.

docs.title: 6.2 Classifiers and hyperparameter grids
docs.text:
Name Classifier Principle Grid (chosen on the validation fold) Fixed settings logreg Logistic regression one linear decision boundary; on frozen embeddings the standard linear probe (Alain & Bengio, 2016), which measures the information contained in the features C ∈ L2 penalty, lbfgs, max_iter = 5000, class_weight = "balanced", standardised inputs rf Random forest (Breiman, 2001) vote of many decision trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample and random feature subsets; the usual classifier in irrigation mapping max_features ∈ {√p, 0.3}; min_samples_leaf ∈ {1, 5}; class_weight ∈ {none, balanced_subsample} 500 trees, no depth limit, seed 42 svm RBF support vector machine maximum-margin boundary, made non-linear by the RBF kernel; used for irrigation mapping with Sentinel-1/2 (Gao et al., 2018; Elwan et al., 2022) C ∈ {1, 10}; γ ∈ {scale, 0.01} class_weight = "balanced", standardised inputs; no probability calibration (the decision score is used for PR-AUC)

Histogram gradient boosting was a fourth classifier in E01 and is dropped from E02 on (D6). The settings selected in each round are reported per experiment (E01).

The selection score is macro-F1, the mean of the irrigated F1 and rainfed F1. It treats the 14% rainfed class as equally important.

docs.title: 6.3 Spatial cross-validation: train / validation / test
docs.text:
Each round uses the 5 spatial folds in the same way as the PASTIS benchmark (Garnot & Landrieu 2021): 3 folds train, the next fold is the validation fold, and one fold is the test fold. Rotating through 5 rounds tests every fold once.

Round Train Validation Test 1 folds 2, 3, 4 fold 1 fold 0 2 folds 3, 4, 0 fold 2 fold 1 3 folds 4, 0, 1 fold 3 fold 2 4 folds 0, 1, 2 fold 4 fold 3 5 folds 1, 2, 3 fold 0 fold 4 flowchart TD START["5 spatial folds<br/>(20 km blocks)"] --> R{"Round k = 1 … 5"} R --> TE["Test = fold k<br/>held out completely"] R --> VA["Validation = next fold<br/>chooses the hyperparameters"] R --> TR["Train = the other 3 folds"] TR --> G["Train every setting of the grid"] G --> VA2["Score each setting on the validation fold (macro-F1)"] VA --> VA2 VA2 --> BEST["Best setting, trained on the 3 training folds"] BEST --> PRED["Predict test fold k<br/>(class + rainfed score)"] TE --> PRED PRED --> OOF["After 5 rounds: every parcel predicted once,<br/>by a model that never saw its block"] OOF --> MET["Metrics + 95% block-bootstrap CI"]

The validation fold is used only to choose the classifier's hyperparameters; the test fold is never used for any choice. The same scheme is used for every input, so the classifiers and a later neural-network baseline are trained, tuned and tested identically. VALIDATION = "nested" in 03_train_evaluate.py gives the alternative design (tuning by spatial CV on the 4 training folds, refit on all 4), for a sensitivity check; its runs get the suffix _nested.

Every parcel is predicted once, by a model that saw neither its block in training nor any information from it during tuning. That makes the score an estimate of how well the model maps new areas.

docs.title: 6.4 Metrics and uncertainty
docs.text:
Metric Why Macro-F1 (headline) balances both classes; insensitive to the 86 / 14 split F1, precision, recall per class rainfed recall shows how many rainfed parcels are found Balanced accuracy mean recall of both classes Overall accuracy for comparison with the literature; the trivial "all irrigated" model already gets 86% PR-AUC (rainfed) threshold-free ranking quality for the minority class Brier score, expected calibration error quality of the predicted probabilities

95% confidence intervals: block bootstrap. Parcels in one 20 km block are correlated, so blocks, not parcels, are the independent units. Each of the 1,000 draws resamples whole blocks with replacement and recomputes every metric. The 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles give the interval.

flowchart LR A["Out-of-fold predictions<br/>with block_id"] --> B["Draw 91 blocks<br/>with replacement"] B --> C["Recompute metrics on<br/>the parcels of those blocks"] C --> D{"1,000 draws?"} D -->|no| B D -->|yes| E["2.5% / 97.5% quantiles<br/>= 95% CI"]

docs.title: 6.5 Further analyses in the same run
docs.text:
1. Classifier comparison: paired macro-F1 differences between the 3 classifiers on the same parcels, with block-bootstrap CIs.
  2. Spatial vs random CV: the same hyperparameters re-evaluated with the stratified random_fold. The gap shows how much random validation overstates accuracy.
  3. Grouped permutation importance: uses the random forest of each outer fold, on its test fold. For the baseline it is computed by variable (NDVI, VH, …) and by month; for embeddings, by month.
  4. Seasonal profiles (baseline): class medians per variable and month.
  5. Final models: refit on all parcels (final_model_<name>.joblib), for mapping later.

Steps 2, 3 and 5 are skipped in label-efficiency runs (§6.6), which only need the out-of-fold predictions.

Outputs (experiments/<EXPERIMENT>/results/<REGION>/<RUN_NAME>/ in experiment mode; outputs/<REGION>/study/03_models/<RUN_NAME>/ for development runs with EXPERIMENT = None): - metrics_summary.csv, metrics_with_ci.csv, metrics_per_fold.csv - paired_model_differences.csv - cv_random_vs_spatial.csv / .png - oof_predictions.csv - selected_hyperparameters.csv, inner_tuning_scores.csv - importance.csv / .png - confusion_matrices.png - seasonal_profiles.png, gap_filling.csv (baseline only) - final_model_*.joblib - run_config.json, run.log

Run names: - Baseline: s1s2-<variables>_agyear_tiles-<inner|all>[-<orbit>], e.g. s1s2-s2_agyear_tiles-inner (Sentinel-2 only, no orbit) or s1s2-all_agyear_tiles-inner-asc. - GeoFMs: <model>_agyear_tiles[_2023-24]_<concat|mean>, e.g. clay_agyear_tiles_concat (Morocco), clay_agyear_tiles_2023-24_concat (Utah). - Label-efficiency runs end in _f<percent>_d<draw>, e.g. clay_agyear_tiles_concat_f010_d1.

docs.title: 6.6 Regions and label efficiency (scripts 03, 03b, 03c)
docs.text:
Setting Meaning Set by REGION, VIEWS_NAME study area and its views folder (Morocco views, Utah views_2023-24); folds, features and embeddings are read from outputs/<REGION>/ EXPERIMENT_REGION (run_experiment.py, Slurm) TRAIN_FRACTION, FRACTION_DRAW share of the training blocks of each round (1.0 = all; 0.10 / 0.25 / 0.50) and the draw (1–3) EXPERIMENT_FRACTION, EXPERIMENT_DRAW N_SEEDS (03b, 03c) trainings per round; the out-of-fold probability is their mean EXPERIMENT_N_SEEDS (1 in label-efficiency runs) QUICK_TEST fast check of the whole chain EXPERIMENT_QUICK_TEST

The block draw is one shared function (models_run/experiment_utils.py, draw_training_blocks()):

  1. Take the training blocks of the round, counting only parcels of the views' agricultural years (Utah's fold file also holds 2021).
  2. Split them into blocks with rainfed parcels and irrigated-only blocks and put each list in a random order (seed from region, round and draw only).
  3. A fraction takes the first blocks of each list (the same share of each, at least one block each). The draws are therefore nested: the 10% blocks are part of the 25% blocks, which are part of the 50% blocks, so a learning curve shows the effect of adding blocks, not of drawing different ones.
  4. The ordering is accepted only if its first 10% already hold at least 20 rainfed parcels (otherwise the next sub-seed); every fraction then keeps enough rainfed parcels (checked: at least 22 in Morocco, 26 in Utah, over all rounds and draws).
  5. Draw k selects the same blocks in scripts 03, 03b and 03c and for every input: the learning curves of all experiments are paired. The validation and test folds stay complete.

The blocks kept in every round are written to run_config.json (block_draws) and the run log; script 04 reports the mean number of training parcels per fraction.

Quick checks never mix with results. With QUICK_TEST (or QUICK = True in run_experiment.py / submit_slurm.py) the scripts write to experiments/<E>/results_quick/ and no report is written, so a later real run is never skipped as "already done". The runners also remove every EXPERIMENT_* variable left in the shell and set each run's variables explicitly.

docs.title: 6.7 Script 03c — train_ltae (neural heads: E03, E04)
docs.text:
Same parcels, folds, PASTIS rotation and output files as script 03 (oof_predictions.csv with model = mlp or ltae), so script 04 compares it directly with the classical classifiers.

HEAD Input Model Experiment mlp the E02 input: 12 months concatenated, training-median fill, standardised, PCA 128 (baseline: the 180 standardised features) MLP 128 → 256 → 128 → 2, batch normalisation, ReLU, dropout 0.2 E03 ltae the 12 months as a sequence, per-channel standardisation; months without a clear pixel masked in the attention L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020): channels → d_model 256 + sinusoidal encoding of the mid-month day, 16 heads with one learned master query each (d_k 8), output MLP 256-128, linear layer → 2 E04

Training: AdamW (learning rate 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4), batch 128, class-weighted cross-entropy, up to 100 epochs, early stopping on the validation fold's macro-F1 (patience 15), best epoch kept; 3 seeds per round. AgriFM (one vector per year) is only used with HEAD = "mlp". Extra outputs: metrics_per_seed.csv, training_history.csv and, for L-TAE, attention_by_month.csv (attention per month and class on the test folds).

docs.title: 6.8 Script 03b — train_psetae (E05)
docs.text: PSE-TAE (Garnot et al. 2020) trained from scratch on the pixel sets (view B): 10 Sentinel-2 bands × 12 months, 64 pixels sampled per parcel, the same PASTIS rotation and early stopping. Each run is one config file in experiments/E05_psetae_scratch/configs/ (morocco_s2, utah_s2; morocco_s2s1 is the Sentinel-1 ablation). N_SEEDS = 3 trainings per round, averaged; metrics_per_seed.csv holds the spread. Label efficiency as in §6.6.

docs.title: 7. Script 04 — compare_models
docs.text:
Purpose: answer the main research question by comparing every input with the baseline, on the same parcels.

flowchart TD A["oof_predictions.csv<br/>of each run in RUNS"] --> B["Keep parcels predicted in ALL runs"] B --> C["One shared set of 1,000<br/>block-bootstrap samples"] C --> D["Per run × classifier:<br/>macro-F1, rainfed F1,<br/>balanced and overall accuracy, 95% CI"] C --> E["Per GeoFM run × classifier:<br/>Δ macro-F1 vs baseline (same classifier)<br/>95% CI + bootstrap p-value"] E --> F["Holm adjustment over<br/>all comparisons"] D --> OUT["metrics_all_runs.csv<br/>comparison_macro_f1.png"] F --> OUT2["differences_vs_baseline.csv<br/>differs = CI excludes 0 AND Holm p < 0.05"] C --> LC["Label-efficiency runs:<br/>macro-F1 per training fraction<br/>(mean over draws, same samples)"] LC --> OUT3["learning_curve.csv / .png"]
  • Paired: the same bootstrap blocks are used for every run, so each difference is measured on identical resamples (Foody 2009).
  • Multiple comparisons: the experiment's own input × head comparisons with its baseline form one Holm family (runs borrowed from other experiments are not part of it).
  • Same input, earlier experiments' heads (differences_vs_earlier_experiments.csv, own Holm family): every run of this experiment against the runs of the same input in EXTRA_RUNS, e.g. E03 Clay + MLP vs E02 Clay + LogReg / RF / SVM, E04 Clay + L-TAE vs E03 Clay + MLP. This answers Q2 (head) and Q3 (temporal aggregation) with paired tests.
  • Interpretation: an input is better than the baseline only if the 95% interval of Δ macro-F1 lies entirely above 0 and the Holm-adjusted p-value is below 0.05 (column differs; ci_excludes_0 keeps the interval test alone). Before 13 Nov 2026 differs used the interval only; the report pages always applied both conditions.
  • One region at a time (REGION): results are read from experiments/<E>/results/<REGION>/ and written to its comparison/ folder.
  • Runs of other experiments: EXTRA_RUNS lists "<experiment>/<run>" or "<experiment>/*" (all main runs of that experiment in the same region), e.g. E04 compares with "E03_frozen_pca_mlp/*" and "E02_frozen_pca/*". That experiment must have finished first.
  • Baseline: the experiment's own Sentinel-2 baseline run (E03: the baseline with the MLP head; E04: with L-TAE); E05 has none and uses the E02 baseline.
  • Label efficiency: for every run and head, macro-F1 and rainfed F1 at each training fraction, the mean over the draws with a block-bootstrap CI on the same parcels and samples, and the mean training parcels per round (learning_curve.csv, learning_curve.png). Neural label-efficiency runs use one seed per draw; their 100% point is the mean over the main run's 3 seeds scored one by one (oof_per_seed.csv), so every point is single-seed.
  • Missing runs fail loudly: a borrowed experiment without finished runs, or no baseline, stops the script.

In development mode (EXPERIMENT = None) BASELINE_RUN is the Sentinel-2 baseline s1s2-s2_agyear_tiles-inner; for a run with Sentinel-1 it must match the orbit that was actually used (views_info.json), for example s1s2-all_agyear_tiles-inner-asc.

docs.title: 7.1 Script 05 — breakdown_oof (results by region, season and purity)
docs.text:
Purpose: test whether the pooled metrics reflect the irrigation signal or the region. Rainfed parcels are concentrated in Doukkala (94%), and Gharb, Tadla and El Haouz contain almost only irrigated parcels, so a classifier can score well by recognising the region (shortcut learning). The 16-px chips also mix each parcel with its neighbours (median purity 0.30). The script reads the out-of-fold predictions of one experiment; no model is trained. It runs per region (REGION) on every head (LogReg, RF, SVM, MLP, L-TAE, PSE-TAE): the focus zone is Doukkala in Morocco and, in Utah, the zone with most rainfed parcels (found automatically; the Bear River basin holds 58% of them); irrigated-only zones are listed for Morocco and found automatically for Utah (≥ 100 parcels, < 2% rainfed).

Output (experiments/<E>/results/<REGION>/breakdown/) Content focus_zone.csv macro-F1 in the focus zone (Morocco: Doukkala, the only zone with both classes) with 95% block-bootstrap CI and the paired difference to the baseline (E01: doukkala.csv) irrigated_only_zones.csv share of irrigated parcels predicted rainfed in the irrigated-only zones (Morocco: Gharb, Tadla, El Haouz), with CI by_zone_season.csv rainfed recall and precision, false-rainfed rate and macro-F1 per zone and agricultural year by_purity.csv, by_area.csv macro-F1 per 16-px patch-purity bin and per parcel-area bin breakdown.png focus-zone macro-F1 and false-rainfed rate per input

First application (E01, nested CV, 8,775 parcels; AgriFM excluded): in Doukkala, no frozen GeoFM exceeds the baseline (baseline SVM 0.896 [0.818–0.952]; the GeoFM random forests are 0.03–0.07 lower, with intervals that exclude 0). In the irrigated-only zones every input labels at most 2% of the irrigated parcels as rainfed, so these zones contribute little to the differences between inputs. The GeoFM advantage in the hardest fold comes from Souss (69 rainfed parcels): rainfed recall 0.75–0.84 for Clay and Prithvi (SVM) against 0.26 for the baseline. GeoFM macro-F1 increases with patch purity more steeply than that of the baseline. The analysis is repeated on E02.

docs.title: 9. Running, settings and run time
docs.text:
conda activate condaml
python models_run/01_inspect_dataset.py
python models_run/02a_embed_clay.py          # GPU recommended; resumable
python models_run/02b_embed_prithvi.py
python models_run/02c_embed_terramind.py
python models_run/02d_embed_agrifm.py
# an experiment, every region and label-efficiency run (set EXPERIMENT at the top of run_experiment.py):
python experiments/run_experiment.py
# the same on the cluster, one Slurm job per run (on the server; DRY_RUN = True first):
python experiments/submit_slurm.py
# or one run by hand, for development (EXPERIMENT = None in the script, results in outputs/<REGION>/study/):
python models_run/03_train_evaluate.py
EXPERIMENT_REGION=utah EXPERIMENT_INPUT=clay python models_run/03c_train_ltae.py
python models_run/04_compare_models.py

QUICK_TEST = True in a script, or QUICK = True in run_experiment.py / submit_slurm.py, gives a fast check (script 03: 100 trees, 100 bootstrap draws, one setting per classifier; 03b / 03c: 3 epochs).

Order on the cluster: E02 first (E03–E05 compare with its runs), then E03, then E04 (compares with E03), and E05 at any time after E02. Each submit_slurm.py call submits the experiment's training jobs and one compare job per region that waits for them; the report is written on the Mac after copying results/ back (run_experiment.py with ONLY_STEPS = ["report"]).

Script Main settings 01 EXAMPLE_PATCH = 16, N_EXAMPLES = 3, SEED = 42 02a–02d CHIP_SOURCE = "tiles", CHIP_PATCH_PX (8 Clay, 16 others), BATCH_PARCELS, EMBED_BATCH, DEVICE. docs.title: Phase 2 · Model evaluation
docs.text:
Phase 2 addresses Objective 1, the comparison of foundation models and adaptation strategies in Morocco, through two research questions. Both are evaluated on spatially independent areas under one evaluation protocol.

RQ Question Approach Status Page RQ1 What accuracy does each foundation model achieve, compared with a conventional Sentinel-based classifier? frozen encoders → parcel embeddings → classifiers, vs a Sentinel-2 feature baseline ⏳ E01 done; E02–E05 planned (each with label efficiency) (experiment plan) RQ1 · Frozen encoders RQ2 To what extent does parameter-efficient fine-tuning improve on a frozen encoder? segmentation head on frozen and LoRA-adapted encoders; neural baselines 📝 planned RQ2 · Fine-tuning

The remainder of this page summarises the RQ1 workflow, which forms the reference for all later comparisons.

Unit of analysis. Each parcel carries one label recorded in the field survey. Models predict this label from satellite time series alone and are evaluated exclusively on parcels located in areas excluded from training.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text: flowchart TD     subgraph P1["Phase 1 · Dataset"]         GT["<b>Ground data</b><br/>field-surveyed parcels (~10,000)<br/>Dec 2023 – Jan 2025"]         CL["<b>Data cleaning and labels</b><br/>cropland only · irrigated / rainfed<br/>agricultural year → 8,781 parcels"]         SF["<b>Spatial folds</b><br/>20 km blocks → 5 balanced folds"]         TS["<b>Tile store</b> (Google Earth Engine)<br/>Sentinel-2 L2A + Cloud Score+ · Sentinel-1<br/>128 px tiles · 12 months × 19 bands"]         FE["<b>Parcel features</b><br/>monthly medians of S2 bands,<br/>indices and S1 backscatter"]         CH["<b>Chips p8 / p16</b><br/>64 × 64 px around each parcel,<br/>aligned to the model patches"]         GT --> CL --> SF --> TS         TS --> FE         TS --> CH     end      subgraph P2["Phase 2 · Model evaluation"]         BL["<b>S2 baseline</b><br/>180 features per parcel"]         FM["<b>Foundation models (frozen)</b><br/>Clay · Prithvi-EO-2.0 · TerraMind · AgriFM<br/>→ one embedding per parcel"]         CF["<b>Heads</b><br/>LogReg · RF · SVM · MLP · L-TAE<br/>3 train / 1 validation / 1 test folds"]         CM["<b>Comparison</b><br/>same parcels · paired differences<br/>block-bootstrap 95% CI"]         BL --> CF         FM --> CF         CF --> CM     end      FE --> BL     CH --> FM     SF -. "folds" .-> CF     CM --> R(["Does a foundation model beat<br/>the Sentinel-2 baseline?"])

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Labels. The Moroccan field survey (Ouassanouan et al., 2026) records crop type and irrigation system for each parcel. Cropland parcels are labelled irrigated (flood, sprinkler, drip, pivot and related systems) or rainfed. Rainfed parcels constitute 14% of the sample; macro-averaged metrics are therefore used so that both classes carry equal weight.

2. Spatial folds. Spatial autocorrelation between neighbouring parcels inflates accuracy when training and test parcels are adjacent (Roberts et al., 2017). The study area is therefore partitioned into 20 km blocks, and whole blocks are assigned to five folds. Every model is evaluated on blocks that were not used in training.

3. Common image store. For the agricultural year of each parcel (September–August), Sentinel-2 observations (cloud-masked with Cloud Score+) and Sentinel-1 backscatter are aggregated into 12 monthly composites and stored as non-overlapping 1.28 km tiles. The baseline and all foundation models read the same pixels, so that differences in performance are attributable to the representation rather than to the input data.

4. Parcel representations.

  • Feature baseline: for each of the 12 months, the median of the parcel's inner pixels for the Sentinel-2 bands, three spectral indices, yielding 180 features (Sentinel-2 only, D14). Months without clear observations are temporally interpolated.
  • Foundation-model embedding: a 64 × 64 px window (640 m) around the parcel is passed through the frozen encoder. The resulting patch embeddings are averaged with weights equal to the fraction of each patch inside the parcel. Clay, Prithvi-EO-2.0 and TerraMind are applied month by month; AgriFM processes the full year in one pass (Foundation models).

5. Temporal aggregation. A foundation model yields up to 12 × 1,024 values per parcel. Two aggregation schemes are evaluated:

  • PCA pipeline (E02, E03): monthly embeddings are concatenated and reduced to 128 principal components, fitted on the training folds only.
  • L-TAE pipeline (E04): a lightweight temporal attention encoder learns the relative importance of the months, following the PANGAEA benchmark protocol.
PCA pipeline: what it does

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) compresses many correlated numbers into a few new ones that keep most of the differences between parcels.

flowchart LR M["12 monthly embeddings<br/>12 × 1,024 numbers"] --> C["<b>concatenate</b><br/>one row of 12,288 numbers"] C --> S["<b>standardise</b><br/>each number: mean 0, SD 1"] S --> P["<b>PCA</b><br/>keep the 128 directions<br/>with the largest spread"] P --> O["128 numbers per parcel<br/>→ classifier"]
  • What a component is: the first component is the direction in which parcels differ most, the second the next largest spread at right angles to the first, and so on. Each component is a weighted mix of all 12,288 numbers, so it has no simple meaning such as "July NDVI".
  • Why compress: 12,288 numbers against roughly 1,200–5,000 training parcels per round invites overfitting, and neighbouring months and embedding dimensions largely repeat each other. 128 components remove most of this redundancy and give every model an input of the same size.
  • No leakage: in every round, PCA is fitted on the training parcels only and then applied to the validation and test parcels.
  • What PCA does not do: it is unsupervised (it never sees the labels) and treats the months only as positions in a long vector. It cannot learn that, say, July matters more than March.
L-TAE pipeline: what it does

The lightweight temporal attention encoder (L-TAE; Garnot & Landrieu 2020, paper · summary) keeps the 12 months as a sequence and learns, together with the classifier, how much weight each month gets. PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024, paper · summary) uses the same module to combine the dates of single-date GeoFMs; this study follows that protocol.

flowchart LR M["12 monthly embeddings<br/>12 × 1,024"] --> L["<b>project</b><br/>each month → 256 numbers<br/>+ date code (mid-month day)"] L --> A["<b>attention</b><br/>16 heads, each with a learned query:<br/>score every month → softmax<br/>→ month weights (sum = 1)"] A --> W["<b>weighted sum</b><br/>of the months, per head<br/>→ 256 numbers for the year"] W --> H["MLP 256 → 128 → 2<br/>irrigated / rainfed"]
  • Attention: each head scores the 12 months, and softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to 1. A month with weight 0.20 counts more than one with 0.05. The 16 heads can each focus on different months.
  • Date code: a sine/cosine code of the mid-month day is added to each month, so the model knows which month it is looking at (attention by itself ignores order).
  • Missing months: months without a clear Sentinel-2 pixel get weight 0.
  • Trained with the labels: unlike PCA, the weights are learned to separate irrigated from rainfed parcels, and they can differ from parcel to parcel. The average weights per month are reported as a figure in E04.
  • Applies to Clay, Prithvi, TerraMind and the S2 baseline (15 variables × 12 months). It does not apply to AgriFM, which gives one vector for the whole year.

6. Classifiers. Three classical classifiers (logistic regression, random forest and a support vector machine) are trained on every representation with identical hyperparameter grids (D6). Logistic regression on frozen embeddings corresponds to the standard linear probe and measures the information already present in the pretrained representation. Two neural heads are added: an MLP on the PCA input (E03) and the L-TAE with its own MLP (E04). PSE-TAE (E05) is a complete model trained from scratch on the pixels, the neural baseline.

Model Type Input Experiment Runs per round Logistic regression linear (linear probe) PCA 128 (baseline: 180 features) E02 1 Random forest 500 decision trees same E02 1 SVM (RBF kernel) non-linear, margin-based same E02 1 MLP small neural network same E03 3 seeds L-TAE + MLP temporal attention + neural network 12 monthly vectors (no PCA) E04 3 seeds PSE-TAE full model, no pretraining 64 raw pixels per parcel × 12 months E05 3 seeds Logistic regression (linear probe)

Draws one straight boundary (a hyperplane) through the input space: every input number gets a weight, the weighted sum is turned into a probability of "rainfed" with the logistic function, and ≥ 0.5 means rainfed.

  • Why it is used: on frozen embeddings it is the standard linear probe. If a straight boundary already separates the classes, the information is in the embedding itself, not in a clever classifier.
  • Settings: inputs standardised; class weights balanced (rainfed errors count more); grid over the regularisation strength C ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10}. Small C = simpler boundary.
  • Limitation: it cannot model curved boundaries or interactions between inputs.
Random forest

500 decision trees, each grown on a random sample of parcels; at every split a tree looks at a random subset of the inputs and asks one yes/no question about one of them ("is input 37 > 0.4?"). The trees vote, and the share of votes is the probability.

  • Why it is used: the classic classifier of irrigation and crop mapping, and the baseline classifier of the comparison script.
  • Settings: grid over max_features ∈ {√n, 30% of the inputs}, min_samples_leaf ∈ {1, 5} and class_weight ∈ {none, balanced per tree}; fixed seed.
  • Strength and weakness: very good when each input means something on its own (NDVI in August, SWIR in December), so it is the best classifier for the S2 features in Utah. On PCA components, which are mixes of thousands of embedding numbers, one-input-at-a-time splits work poorly: it is the weakest classifier on every GeoFM (E02).
Support vector machine (SVM, RBF kernel)

Finds the boundary with the widest margin between the classes. The RBF kernel measures how similar two parcels are (close in input space = similar), which lets the boundary curve around groups of parcels.

  • Why it is used: a strong non-linear classifier for dense features, used in earlier irrigation-mapping studies with Sentinel-1/2 (Gao et al. 2018; Elwan et al. 2022).
  • Settings: inputs standardised; class weights balanced; grid over C ∈ {1, 10} (how strongly training errors are penalised) and gamma ∈ {scale, 0.01} (how local the similarity is). It gives a decision score, not a calibrated probability.
  • Result: the best classical classifier for every GeoFM, in both regions (E02).
MLP head (E03)

A small neural network on the same PCA input: 128 → 256 → 128 → 2, each hidden layer with batch normalisation, ReLU and dropout 0.2.

  • Why it is used: most GeoFM benchmarks report a linear probe or an MLP head. E03 tests whether a trained, non-linear head gets more out of the embeddings than the classical classifiers.
  • Training: AdamW (learning rate 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4), batch 128, class-weighted cross-entropy, up to 100 epochs, early stopping on the validation fold's macro-F1 (patience 15). Settings are fixed, not tuned.
  • Result: equal to SVM for every input (within ±0.01), clearly better than LogReg and RF on most GeoFMs.
L-TAE + MLP head (E04)

The 12 monthly vectors are not concatenated and compressed with PCA. Instead, a temporal attention encoder learns how much weight each month gets, and its output goes to an MLP (256 → 128 → 2). How it works: see L-TAE pipeline: what it does under step 5. Paper: Garnot & Landrieu (2020), Lightweight temporal self-attention for classifying satellite images time series · summary.

  • Training: the same optimiser, loss, early stopping and 3 seeds as the MLP head; attention and head are trained together.
  • Result: equal to PCA + MLP for every input (within ±0.01). Not used for AgriFM, which has no monthly sequence.
PSE-TAE: pixel-set encoder + temporal attention, trained from scratch (E05)

PSE-TAE (Garnot, Landrieu, Giordano & Chehata 2020, CVPR: Satellite image time series classification with pixel-set encoders and temporal self-attention · code) was designed for exactly this task: classifying agricultural parcels from a satellite time series. It uses no foundation model and no pretraining. It learns everything from our labelled parcels. flowchart TD P["<b>Parcel</b><br/>all inner pixels × 10 S2 bands × 12 months"] --> S["<b>random set of 64 pixels</b><br/>no image grid, no order<br/>(small parcels: all their pixels)"] S --> PSE["<b>1 · Pixel-Set Encoder</b>, per month<br/>each pixel: 10 bands → MLP → 64 numbers<br/>pool over the pixels: mean + SD → 128<br/>→ MLP → 128 numbers per month"] PSE --> TAE["<b>2 · Temporal Attention Encoder</b><br/>12 months + date code<br/>4 attention heads weight the months<br/>→ MLP 512 → 128 → 128: one vector per parcel"] TAE --> DEC["<b>3 · Decoder</b><br/>MLP 128 → 64 → 32 → 2<br/>irrigated / rainfed"]

1. Pixel-Set Encoder (PSE). Parcels have different shapes and sizes, so PSE-TAE treats a parcel as an unordered set of pixels instead of an image. For each month, every one of 64 randomly chosen pixels goes through the same small network (10 band values → 32 → 64 numbers). The 64 results are then pooled in two ways: the mean (what the parcel looks like on average) and the standard deviation (how uniform it is: a patchy field differs from a homogeneous one). A plain parcel average, as in the S2 baseline, loses this second part. Another small network turns the pooled 128 numbers into one 128-number vector per month.

2. Temporal Attention Encoder (TAE). The 12 monthly vectors get a date code (sine/cosine of the mid-month day). Four attention heads score the months and take a weighted sum, so the model learns which parts of the year separate irrigated from rainfed parcels. Unlike L-TAE (E04), the TAE computes its query from the parcel's own sequence, with fewer, larger heads (4 × 32): L-TAE is its lighter successor by the same authors.

3. Decoder. A small network (128 → 64 → 32 → 2) gives the probability of each class.

Setting Value Input inner pixels of the parcel (edge pixels within 10 m left out; parcels with fewer than 4 inner pixels keep all), 10 Sentinel-2 bands × 12 months, standardised with training statistics Pixels per parcel 64, drawn anew every epoch (acts as data augmentation); at prediction, the mean of 5 random draws Layer sizes paper defaults: MLP1 32-64, mean + SD pooling, MLP2 128, 4 heads with d_k 32, MLP3 512-128-128, decoder 64-32-2 Not used the paper's extra parcel-shape features (area, perimeter): the model sees only the pixels Training Adam (learning rate 1e-3, weight decay 1e-4), batch 128, class-weighted cross-entropy, up to 100 epochs, early stopping on validation macro-F1 (patience 15) Seeds 3 per round; the out-of-fold prediction is the mean probability
  • Why it is the right baseline: it learns from the raw pixels and from their spread inside the parcel, with its own temporal attention. If a frozen GeoFM cannot beat it, pretraining adds nothing over a good supervised model.
  • Result (E05): Morocco 0.911, the highest macro-F1 of RQ1, a tie with the best S2 and GeoFM runs. Utah 0.755, equal to the S2 random forest but significantly below Clay (−0.03 to −0.04). It finds the most rainfed parcels of all models, but in Utah it also over-predicts them. E05 report.

7. Evaluation. Five rotations are performed: three folds for training, one for hyperparameter selection and one for testing. Each parcel thus receives exactly one out-of-fold prediction from a model that was not trained on its block.

8. Comparison. All inputs are evaluated on the same parcels. Uncertainty is estimated with a block bootstrap (1,000 resamples of 20 km blocks), using identical resamples for every input so that differences are paired. A foundation model is considered superior only if the 95% confidence interval of the difference in macro-F1 excludes zero after Holm correction for multiple comparisons.

docs.title: Scope of inference
docs.text:
• The results quantify performance on unseen areas within the surveyed Moroccan regions.
  • They do not yet establish performance in other years or in other countries; these are addressed by RQ3 and RQ4.
  • Region and survey year are partly confounded (El Gharb and Tadla surveyed only in 2023/24, Souss only in 2024/25); differences between regions may therefore partly reflect differences between years.

docs.title: Phase 3 · Temporal transferability and a second region
docs.text:
Starter page

Planned for February – March 2027. This page will be extended into an overview and component pages when the work begins.

Objective 2: evaluate the temporal transferability of the models of Phase 2 and whether their results hold in a second, independent region (Utah).

RQ Question Planned test RQ3 (temporal) How temporally consistent is the best model across years? Utah: train on WRLU 2024, test on WRLU 2021 on the folds held out in training (same fields, paired); Morocco: year-to-year consistency of the annual maps RQ4 (second region) Do the results of Morocco hold in a second, independent region? the full Phase 2 comparison repeated in Utah with its own labels and spatial folds (D13); no Morocco → Utah transfer

docs.title: Decided
docs.text:
• Second region and temporal test: Utah (D13); dataset: Utah training data. The temporal test holds out space as well, because the WRLU labels barely change between years.
  • Metrics: macro-F1 per region as in Phase 2; temporal: the drop from WRLU 2024 (score A) to WRLU 2021 (score B) on the same held-out fields.

docs.title: Phase 4 · Multi-model fusion
docs.text:
Starter page

Optional extension, planned for December 2026 – January 2027 if time allows.

Research question RQ5: does fusing the embeddings of several foundation models improve on the best single model?

docs.title: Candidate strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Description Early fusion concatenation of the parcel embeddings of several models before the classifier Late fusion combination of the class probabilities of the single-model classifiers (averaging or stacking) Learned fusion a small network that weights the models' embeddings, trained under the same protocol

All strategies are compared with the best single model of Phase 2 on the same parcels, folds and bootstrap samples (evaluation protocol). The complementarity of the models (e.g. TerraMind with Sentinel-1, AgriFM with its temporal design) motivates the comparison.

docs.title: Phase 5 · Annual irrigated-cropland maps
docs.text:
Starter page

Planned for March 2027. This page will be extended when the mapping work begins.

Aim: produce annual 10 m maps of irrigated and rainfed cropland for Morocco (2021–2025) and for the transfer region, using the best mapping model of Phases 2–4, and assess them against independent data.

docs.text: Step Description Imagery monthly Sentinel-1/2 composites per agricultural year, with the Phase 1 tile pipeline (component 1c) Cropland mask restriction of the maps to cropland (WorldCereal, GLAD cropland or ESA WorldCover; see Data sources) Inference the pixel-level mapping model of RQ2, applied tile by tile Accuracy assessment independent reference points (GMIA-NEXT) and held-out parcels; area estimates with confidence intervals Comparison national statistics (FAO AQUASTAT) and existing products (LGRIP30, GMIE, WorldCereal)

docs.text:
• annual irrigated-cropland maps, Morocco, 2021–2025, 10 m;

docs.title: Heads and mapping: what GeoFM crop studies use
docs.text:
Literature search of 6 Nov 2026: which head is put on a GeoFM for crop classification, which neural baselines are used, and what wall-to-wall mapping requires. Result: decision D11.

Head Used for Papers Classical ML on frozen embeddings (LogReg, RF, GBDT, SVM, kNN) per-pixel / per-parcel classification Presto (Tseng et al. 2023); AlphaEarth irrigated vs rainfed (Yang et al. 2026); AlphaEarth cropland maps (Mughees et al. 2026); Galileo / CropFM + RF (Nedungadi et al. 2026) Small neural head (linear, MLP) per-pixel classification, fine-tuning TESSERA, 2-layer MLP per pixel (Feng et al. 2025); Presto / AlphaEarth + RF or MLP (Tong & Wang 2025); WorldCereal, fine-tuned Presto (Butsko et al. 2025) Segmentation decoder (UPerNet, UNet) wall-to-wall maps from patch-based models PANGAEA (Marsocci et al. 2024); Prithvi-EO-2.0 (Szwarcman et al. 2024) Neural baseline (from scratch) Input Gives maps Note TempCNN (Pelletier et al. 2019) pixel time series yes, per pixel 1D-CNN > RF for irrigated mapping (Bazzi et al. 2019); TempCNN-type models transfer better across regions than GeoFM embeddings (Tong & Wang 2025) L-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2020) pixel or parcel time series yes same module as the E04 pipeline U-TAE (Garnot & Landrieu 2021) image tiles yes, 10 m PASTIS baseline; counterpart of GeoFM + UPerNet PSE-TAE (Garnot et al. 2020) parcel pixel sets no (needs polygons) parcel-level only LSTM, Transformer (BreizhCrops, Rußwurm et al. 2020) pixel time series yes similar to TempCNN in benchmarks

Main points - Several 2025–26 studies find the head choice matters little on frozen embeddings (LogReg within 0.3 pp of a boosted ensemble, Mughees et al. 2026), but E01 shows RF is weaker on dense PCA embeddings, so the linear probe is the fairer headline for GeoFMs. - GeoFM embeddings degrade under large geographic shifts (cross-continent) more than simple temporal CNNs (Tong & Wang 2025): relevant for RQ4. - Fine-tuning helps in operational crop mapping (WorldCereal) but can collapse pretrained features without care (Nedungadi et al. 2026): relevant for RQ2.

docs.title: IrrMap · Mandal et al. (2025)
docs.text:
Citation

Mandal et al. (2025). IrrMap: a large-scale comprehensive dataset for irrigation method mapping. KDD 2025. arXiv:2505.08273 · data: Hugging Face

In one line: a large US dataset of image patches labelled with the irrigation method (flood, sprinkler, drip), built from state agricultural databases.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Labels from state datasets: Arizona (verified irrigated lands), Utah (Water-Related Land Use), Washington (WSDA agricultural land use), Colorado (CDSS).
  • Imagery: single Sentinel-2 scenes (cloud cover ≤ 5%) and Landsat, 11 Sentinel-2 bands, reprojected to EPSG:4326 and cut into 224 × 224 px patches on a fixed grid.
  • Classes: 0 none, 1 flood, 2 sprinkler, 3 drip; plus crop group and a cloud mask. No rainfed class.
  • Split: random 80 / 20 per state and year; U-Net models.

docs.title: Our check of their code and splits (Nov 2026)
docs.text:
• Every acquisition date is a separate sample, so the same place appears many times. Almost every test patch location also appears in training on another date (Washington 2018: 31,056 of 31,064; all states: 423,226 of 423,268). The test set is also used for evaluation after every epoch. Their scores are therefore not spatially independent.
  • Minor code issues (missing argparse import, undefined src_path, a constant land-type band).

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• Not usable as our dataset (no rainfed class), but its label sources are: eastern Washington (WSDA) and Utah (WRLU) contain both irrigated and dryland fields — candidate transfer regions (data sources, decision D10).
  • A concrete example of why spatial folds are needed (protocol §2).

docs.title: GMIA-NEXT · Kebede et al. (2026)
docs.text:
Citation

Kebede, E. A., et al. [and Davis, K. F.] (2026). GMIA-NEXT: next-generation global map of irrigated areas. Research Square (preprint, Data Note). doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10085674/v1 · PDF · maps: Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.17627111 · reference points: Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.20732681 · code: GitHub

In one line: a 30 m global map of irrigated cropland for the 2023/24 growing season, produced with random forests from Landsat and environmental predictors, together with an openly released global set of irrigated and non-irrigated reference points.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Task: binary classification (irrigated / non-irrigated) of every 30 m pixel inside a cropland mask (maximum GLAD cropland extent 2020–2024, to include fallow years).
  • Season: the major irrigation season of each agro-ecological zone (AEZ), from the FAO irrigated crop calendar and the GGCMI Phase III calendars.
  • Predictors (21): seasonal maximum, minimum and mean of EVI, GI, NDVI and NDWI from Landsat 8/9 (Collection 2 Level-2, QA cloud mask); elevation and slope (SRTM); MODIS evapotranspiration, potential evapotranspiration and land surface temperature; SMAP soil moisture; CHIRTS temperature; ERA5-Land vapour pressure deficit; distance to rivers (HydroRIVERS) and to irrigation canals.
  • Reference points: 24,777 newly curated points (8,672 irrigated, 16,105 non-irrigated), sampled at random within cropland stratified by AEZ and labelled by image interpretation (dry-season greenness relative to neighbouring fields, seasonal NDVI, proximity to water, centre-pivot geometry); supplemented by national and regional datasets (LANID, USGS Upper Colorado, LUCAS, MapBiomas, GMIE centre pivots, studies in Zambia, Nigeria and India). In total 230,683 irrigated and 153,194 non-irrigated points; labels from other years were harmonised to 2023/24 with NDVI.
  • Models: random forest per AEZ tile (5 × 2 tiles per continental AEZ, pooled with neighbours where samples are few) or per continent (South America, Africa, Oceania); fixed 50% and tile-optimised probability thresholds; 3 × 3 majority filter.
  • Validation: 60/20/20 split into training, evaluation and test points, with points grouped into 45 m clusters; comparison with MIRCA-OS, AEI and regional products (ECIRA, LANID, CIrrMap250, GMIE, CLUM and others).

docs.title: Key results
docs.text:
Region Accuracy (%) Precision (%) Recall (%) Global 80.5 ± 2.1 72.5 ± 3.2 74.9 ± 3.3 Africa 78.7 ± 6.0 54.9 ± 7.6 74.1 ± 8.4 Europe 89.8 ± 0.2 94.2 ± 0.2 83.4 ± 0.4 North America 92.7 ± 4.5 82.2 ± 1.0 97.0 ± 1.2
  • Low precision in Africa and South America: non-irrigated cropland is often mapped as irrigated.
  • At 5 arc-minutes the map correlates with MIRCA-OS, AEI and Meier et al. (r = 0.74–0.76) and generally shows more irrigated area. Morocco is not discussed; in North Africa only Egypt is compared (with AIM).

docs.title: Data records
docs.text: Record Content Maps (17627111) irrigation probability (0–100%) and binary maps (fixed and dynamic threshold), 30 m, WGS84, one GeoTIFF per continent; 15.4 GB; CC BY 4.0 Reference points (20732681) GMIA-NEXT_GTPs_2024_v0_1 shapefile with the label (irrigated: 1 / 0) and the source of each point; CC BY 4.0 Code Earth Engine scripts (AEZ-tile models) and Python (continental models)

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• Independent test points for the transfer test (RQ4) and for the accuracy assessment of the annual maps (Phase 5); never used for training. Tunisia has 54 points (44 irrigated, 10 rainfed) (D10); tools/a1_gmia_next_points.py checks the points of a country and compares the Moroccan points with the survey parcels.
  • Comparison product for the maps of Phase 5, alongside LGRIP30, GMIE and WorldCereal.
  • Season definition: irrigation is defined for one growing season, consistent with the agricultural-year design of this research (dataset §6.2).
  • Benchmark level: about 80% accuracy globally and 79% in Africa at 30 m with hand-crafted features; a useful reference for the accuracy that this research reaches at 10 m.

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text:
• Resolution and sensor: 30 m Landsat; the authors note spectral mixing for smallholder fields and point to Sentinel or Planet data for such landscapes. This research uses 10 m Sentinel-1/2.
  • Labels by image interpretation, not field visits, for the curated points; harmonisation of other years with an NDVI tolerance adds label noise.
  • "Non-irrigated" is not strictly "rainfed cropland": the label depends on the cropland mask; the check with ESA WorldCover in tools/a1_gmia_next_points.py shows whether a point lies on cropland.
  • Validation design: 45 m clustering is much weaker than the 20 km spatial blocks used here, so the reported accuracies are probably optimistic for unseen areas.
  • Single major season per AEZ: supplementary irrigation in the wet season may be missed.
  • Preprint (v1, June 2026), not yet peer-reviewed.

docs.title: L-TAE · Garnot & Landrieu (2020)
docs.text:
Citation

Garnot, V. S. F., & Landrieu, L. (2020). Lightweight temporal self-attention for classifying satellite images time series. AALTD workshop, ECML-PKDD 2020. arXiv:2007.00586

In one line: a small temporal-attention module that learns which dates of a time series matter, and collapses the series into one vector.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Starts from the temporal attention encoder (TAE) of PSE-TAE and makes it lighter: each attention head has a single learnt master query instead of a query computed from the sequence; channels are split between heads.
  • A positional encoding of the acquisition date keeps the order of the observations.
  • Evaluated on parcel-level crop-type classification from Sentinel-2 time series.

docs.title: Key results
docs.text: • Matches or beats the heavier attention and recurrent models with far fewer parameters and less compute.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• The temporal model of the L-TAE pipeline: attention over the 12 monthly embeddings of Clay, Prithvi and TerraMind, and over the 12 months of the S1/S2 features, so the baseline gets the same temporal model (E04, protocol §5).
  • Default size from the paper (16 heads, d_k 8, d_model 256, MLP 256–128).
  • PANGAEA uses the same module to aggregate dates for single-date GeoFMs (PANGAEA).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text: • Designed for raw reflectance time series of many dates; here it runs on 12 monthly composites or embeddings.

docs.title: Moroccan crop and irrigation survey · Ouassanouan et al. (2026)
docs.text:
Citation

Ouassanouan, Y., Elfarkh, J., Grich, S., Liblab, A., & Chehbouni, A. (2026). Crop and irrigation types ground-truth dataset for Moroccan agricultural regions. Scientific Data, 13, 746. doi:10.1038/s41597-026-06993-y · data: figshare, doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.28486022.v2

In one line: the first openly available, systematically collected parcel-level ground-truth dataset of crop types and irrigation systems for North Africa, and the source of all labels in this research.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Regions: five major agricultural regions of Morocco with contrasting climates and water sources: El Gharb (humid to sub-humid; rice, vegetables; surface water), Tadla (semi-arid to sub-humid; large-scale irrigation; sugar beet, cereals), Doukkala (Mediterranean, ~400 mm; mixed irrigated and rainfed systems), El Haouz (semi-arid, ~250 mm; olives, citrus; groundwater) and Souss (arid; drip-irrigated export crops).
  • Period: December 2023 – January 2025, i.e. two agricultural seasons.
  • Protocol: a standardised survey form built in QGIS and deployed offline in the QField mobile application, with Sentinel-2 false-colour composites (B11, B8, B2) as background. A team of four (the same persons throughout) digitised each parcel on site; two collectors recorded the parcels on either side of the route.
  • Attributes per parcel: polygon, crop type (45 types), agricultural class (seasonal crops, trees, trees + seasonal crops, weeds, bare soil, water bodies), irrigation system, geotagged photograph; for trees also height, crown diameter and row and tree spacing; contextual notes from farmer interviews where possible.
  • Irrigation systems: rainfed and six irrigated systems: flood (traditional surface), basin (structured flood), drip, sprinkler and centre pivot.

docs.title: Data records
docs.text: Record Content Shapefile about 10,000 parcel polygons with crop type, class and irrigation system Photographs one geotagged photo per parcel Sentinel-2 table mean Sentinel-2 bands (B2–B12) and NDVI per parcel for 2024

docs.title: Quality control
docs.text:
• Daily review of the collected data by the team; debriefing after each mission.
  • Post-processing: automated filtering and manual cleaning, removal of overlaps between polygons of different collectors, harmonisation of misspelled and overlapping class labels (e.g. "fruit trees" and "apple trees" merged into Trees), correction of clearly mislabelled parcels.
  • Consistency check with 2024 NDVI time series per class: bare soil 0.1–0.3 all year; seasonal crops 0.7–0.9 in the growing season and 0.1–0.3 from June to October; trees 0.7–0.8, falling to 0.5–0.6 in summer; weeds 0.2–0.4 in February–April.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• Labels: the irrigation-system attribute defines the binary target. Any irrigated system = irrigated, rainfed = rainfed; only the cropland classes (seasonal crops, trees, trees + seasonal) are kept. After cleaning, 8,781 parcels remain (7,585 irrigated, 1,196 rainfed) (ML-ready dataset §4).
  • Agricultural year: the survey date assigns each parcel to the 2023/24 or 2024/25 season, and the imagery is taken from that season (D2).
  • Spatial validation: parcels were recorded along survey routes, so neighbouring parcels are clustered and usually share a class, which motivates the 20 km block cross-validation (dataset §5).
  • Imagery: the provided 2024 Sentinel-2 averages are not used; monthly composites are computed for each parcel's own agricultural year from Earth Engine (dataset §6).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text:
• Class imbalance and regional concentration: rainfed parcels form 14% of the cleaned cropland sample, and 1,122 of the 1,196 rainfed parcels lie in Doukkala; rainfed accuracy therefore largely reflects one region.
  • Region and season are confounded: El Gharb and Tadla were surveyed only in 2023/24 and Souss only in 2024/25.
  • Route-based sampling: parcels close to the survey routes are over-represented; the sample is not a probability sample of Moroccan cropland, so it cannot be used directly for unbiased area estimation (Phase 5).
  • Single-season labels: irrigation status is observed once and may change between years with water availability.
  • Validation of the labels is qualitative (photographs, NDVI consistency); no independent accuracy figure for the labels is reported. Remaining polygon overlaps were found in this research (six parcels fully covered by others; dataset §6.4).

docs.title: PANGAEA · Marsocci et al. (2024)
docs.text:
Citation

Marsocci, V., et al. (2024). PANGAEA: a global and inclusive benchmark for geospatial foundation models. arXiv. arXiv:2412.04204

In one line: a common benchmark that evaluates many geospatial foundation models in the same way, and finds that they do not consistently beat supervised models trained from scratch.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Many GeoFMs on a range of Earth-observation tasks (segmentation, change detection, regression), including the crop datasets PASTIS and a South Sudan crop-type set.
  • Frozen encoders with the same trainable decoder for every model (UPerNet).
  • Time series with single-date models: each date is encoded separately, then the dates are combined by a linear mapping or an L-TAE (L-TAE).
  • Supervised baselines trained from scratch (UNet, ViT); label-fraction experiments.

docs.title: Key results
docs.text:
• GeoFMs do not consistently outperform the supervised baselines.
  • They help most when labels are few.
  • L-TAE aggregation generally beats the linear mapping for multi-temporal tasks.
  • Adding SAR to optical input did not always help.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• Frozen-encoder evaluation with an identical head for every model as the main comparison (protocol).
  • The L-TAE pipeline next to the PCA pipeline (E04, decision D8).
  • A result where GeoFMs only equal a strong baseline is a plausible outcome, not a failure (E01).
  • For maps: a segmentation head (UPerNet) on the frozen encoder (decision D11).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text: • Pixel-level segmentation benchmarks; this research classifies parcels (one label per field), so the "head" is a classifier on a pooled parcel embedding.

docs.title: PASTIS and U-TAE · Garnot & Landrieu (2021)
docs.text:
Citation

Garnot, V. S. F., & Landrieu, L. (2021). Panoptic segmentation of satellite image time series with convolutional temporal attention networks. ICCV 2021. arXiv:2107.07933

In one line: the reference benchmark for crop mapping from Sentinel-2 time series, with a spatio-temporal model (U-TAE) that segments whole image tiles.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• PASTIS dataset: Sentinel-2 time series of agricultural parcels in France on 128 × 128 px patches, with crop-type labels per pixel and per parcel; the patches are split into 5 folds.
  • Fold rotation: in each round 3 folds train, 1 fold validates, 1 fold tests; all five rotations are reported.
  • U-TAE: a U-Net whose temporal dimension is collapsed by temporal self-attention (L-TAE) at the lowest resolution; the attention masks are reused at higher resolutions. Semantic and panoptic segmentation.

docs.title: Key results
docs.text: • U-TAE set the state of the art for semantic segmentation of crop types on PASTIS; the panoptic head separates individual parcels.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• The PASTIS rotation (3 train / 1 validation / 1 test) for every model (decision D3, protocol §2).
  • Non-overlapping 128 px tiles as the shared image store (dataset pipeline).
  • U-TAE as a neural baseline for wall-to-wall maps (decision D11).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text: • Dense labels in France, many crop classes; this research has sparse parcel labels and two classes (irrigated, rainfed). Our folds are 20 km spatial blocks.

docs.title: Invariant features for crop classification · Tong & Wang (2025)
docs.text:
Citation

Tong, X.-Y., & Wang, S. (2025). Invariant features for global crop type classification. arXiv. arXiv:2509.03497

In one line: GeoFM embeddings work for transfer between nearby countries but break down across continents, where a simple temporal CNN on Sentinel-2 time series transfers better.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Crop-type classification with transfer across countries, continents and hemispheres.
  • Inputs and heads: Presto (128-d) and AlphaEarth (64-d) per-pixel embeddings with a random forest (500 trees) or an 8-layer MLP; harmonic features with RF / MLP; deep models on 5-day median Sentinel-2 series (CropNet with 2D spectral-temporal convolutions, a 1D variant, TempCNN, ResNet-50, EfficientNetV2-S, ConvNeXt-Tiny).
  • Time-series augmentation (time shift, time scale, magnitude warping).

docs.title: Key results
docs.text:
• GeoFM embeddings are competitive when the shift is mild (between countries).
  • They degrade strongly across continents and hemispheres (e.g. USA → Australia: overall accuracy 45% for Presto and 46% for AlphaEarth, against 87% for CropNet).
  • Simple 5-day Sentinel-2 series with CropNet beat harmonic features and GeoFM embeddings in every transfer setting; augmentation adds further gains. The authors conclude that inductive bias matters more than model scale or pretraining.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• A temporal CNN (TempCNN) as neural baseline next to the GeoFMs (decision D11).
  • An expectation for RQ4: transfer to a region with different practices may favour simpler temporal models.

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text: • Crop types, not irrigation; pixel-level; different label sources per country.

docs.title: AlphaEarth for irrigated mapping · Yang et al. (2026)
docs.text:
Citation

Yang, L., Gao, Y., Zhao, X., Liang, N., Ma, R., Xi, S., Zhang, X., & Wang, R. (2026). Evaluating the performance of AlphaEarth Foundation embeddings for irrigated cropland mapping across regions and years. Remote Sensing, 18(7), 1065. doi:10.3390/rs18071065

In one line: the closest study to this research — foundation-model embeddings for irrigated vs non-irrigated cropland, compared with Sentinel features and tested across years and regions.

docs.title: What they did
docs.text:
• Regions: Guanzhong Plain, China (main) and Kansas, USA (independent site); years 2022 and 2024, cross-year test on 2023.
  • Inputs: AlphaEarth embeddings vs Sentinel-1/2 features.
  • Classifiers on the embeddings: K-means, decision tree, random forest, gradient boosting (GBDT), linear SVM, RBF SVM, MLP.
  • Feature separability by Jeffries–Matusita distance.

docs.title: Key results
docs.text:
• Embeddings separate the classes better than Sentinel features (best embedding dimension JM 1.58 vs NDWI 0.72).
  • Overall accuracy about 0.95 in the Guanzhong Plain and 0.93 in Kansas; under GBDT, embeddings 0.95 vs Sentinel features 0.84. The paper's abstract, text and tables name different best classifiers (RF, GBDT, DT / RBF-SVM), so the "best head" is not clear-cut.
  • Unsupervised K-means already reaches 0.85 / 0.81.
  • Across years (train 2022, apply 2023 and 2024): stable, OA 0.87–0.88.
  • Across regions (train China, apply Kansas, no retraining): collapses to OA about 0.2–0.47, mostly missed irrigated fields — attributed to different irrigation regimes, phenology and management.

docs.title: What this research takes from it
docs.text:
• Several classifier heads on frozen embeddings, as in our parcel benchmark (E01).
  • A warning for RQ4: temporal transfer can be stable while spatial transfer fails; the transfer region must be close in irrigation practice (decision D10).

docs.title: Differences and limitations
docs.text:
• Two temperate regions and two to three years only; the contribution of each AlphaEarth input source cannot be separated.
  • Pixel-level task; this research classifies parcels and compares four open GeoFMs against a Sentinel baseline.

docs.text:

docs.title: Weeks 2026-W43–44 · first RQ1 result
docs.text: In one line: the frozen foundation models reach the accuracy of the Sentinel-1/2 baseline but do not beat it on average (macro-F1 ≈ 0.91); in the hardest region Clay and Prithvi hold up better than the baseline.

docs.title: 1. Done this week
docs.text:
• First complete RQ1 experiment on the final dataset (shared 128 px tile store, patch-aligned chips, 8,775 parcels, 5 spatial folds): baseline + 4 GeoFMs × 4 classifiers → E01 report.
  • Validation design fixed: PASTIS rotation (3 folds train, next fold validation, 1 fold test) for every model, classical and neural → decision D3. E01 used the earlier nested design; E02 repeats it with the final design.
  • Reproducible experiments: every run now comes from a config file in experiments/ and writes its report; any result can be rerun with one command.
  • Documentation: introduction, overview, evaluation protocol, decisions, results.
  • Literature: PANGAEA (how GeoFM benchmarks handle time series), PASTIS (fold rotation), IrrMap (US irrigation data) → literature notes.
  • Transfer data check (US): of the downloaded state datasets, eastern Washington (WSDA) and Utah (WRLU) contain both irrigated and dryland fields; the USGS and Colorado data are irrigated-only → decision D10.

docs.title: 2. Results (E01)
docs.text:
Input LogReg RF HGB SVM S1/S2 baseline 0.887 0.892 0.899 0.906 Clay v1.5 0.887 0.878 0.895 0.910 Prithvi-EO-2.0 0.880 0.853 0.881 0.905 TerraMind 0.896 0.856 0.878 0.905 AgriFM 0.865 0.839 0.868 0.866

Macro-F1, out-of-fold, same 8,775 parcels.

  • No GeoFM is significantly better than the baseline with any classifier. Clay + SVM (0.910) and the baseline
  • SVM (0.906) are level.
  • Linear probe: TerraMind and Clay equal the baseline, so the frozen embeddings already hold the irrigated / rainfed signal.
  • Random forest suits embeddings least; AgriFM is behind (its input scaling is still to be checked).
  • Hardest region (fold 0, rainfed fields in Doukkala and Souss): baseline 0.80; Prithvi 0.87 and Clay 0.86 (SVM).

docs.title: 3. To discuss / decide
docs.text:
1. Headline classifier. Keep RF (as in the proposal) plus the linear probe as headline, and report HGB / SVM as robustness checks? SVM is the best classifier for every input.
  2. Temporal aggregation. Add the L-TAE pipeline (E03, as in PANGAEA) next to the PCA pipeline, before starting LoRA fine-tuning?
  3. Transfer region (RQ4). Tunisia has 10 rainfed validation points; eastern Washington / Utah would give thousands and several years. Decide after RQ1–RQ2?

docs.title: 4. Next week
docs.text:
• Run E02 (PASTIS validation): the main RQ1 result.
  • Check AgriFM's input normalisation; re-embed if needed.
  • Write models_run/03c_train_ltae.py and run the L-TAE experiment (E04, numbered E03 at the time).
  • Results per region and per season from the out-of-fold predictions.

docs.title: Weeks 2026-W45–46 · RQ1 complete in two regions
docs.text: In one line: frozen GeoFMs do not beat models trained only on our labels in Morocco (a tie at macro-F1 ≈ 0.91), but Clay is ahead by a small, significant margin in Utah (0.79 vs 0.76). Neither the classifier head nor the temporal aggregation changes this.

docs.title: 1. Done this week
docs.text:
• Utah added as a second, independent study area (WRLU 2024, agricultural year 2023/24; 2021 kept for a temporal test): the same pipeline as Morocco, with labels, spatial folds, tile store and model inputs → Utah training data, decision D13.
  • Sentinel-2 only for every input (foundation models and baselines), so that all inputs use the same optical data and both regions are treated alike → D14.
  • Embeddings of all four GeoFMs for both regions (Utah on the HPC cluster).
  • RQ1 experiment plan: four experiments, each changing one thing. Each runs in both regions, with label efficiency (10/25/50% of the training blocks × 3 draws) inside every experiment → experiment plan.
  • E02–E05 run on the cluster (Slurm, about 300 GPU/CPU jobs in total), copied back with checksums. Every experiment has a report with tables, figures, how-to-read notes and an interpretation:
    • E02 · PCA + LogReg / RF / SVM
    • E03 · PCA + MLP head
    • E04 · L-TAE temporal attention + MLP
    • E05 · PSE-TAE trained from scratch (neural baseline)

docs.title: 2. Results
docs.text:
Best macro-F1 of each input over all heads of E02–E05 (out-of-fold, 5 spatial folds, same parcels per region):

Input Morocco Utah 2023/24 S2 baseline (180 features) 0.908 (MLP) 0.764 (RF) PSE-TAE from scratch (S2 pixels) 0.911 0.755 Clay v1.5 0.906 (L-TAE) 0.791 (SVM) Prithvi-EO-2.0 0.899 (SVM) 0.782 (SVM, L-TAE) TerraMind 0.899 (SVM) 0.785 (MLP) AgriFM 0.857 (MLP) 0.747 (MLP)

  • Morocco: a tie. PSE-TAE, S2 + MLP and Clay + L-TAE are all within ±0.01, and no difference is significant.
  • Utah: Clay is ahead. Clay + SVM beats PSE-TAE by +0.036 [+0.015, +0.056]. The gain is largest in Bear River, the main rainfed zone (+0.05 to +0.09).
  • The head matters only until it is non-linear. SVM, MLP and L-TAE give the same result for every input (within ±0.01). RF is weak on embeddings.
  • Temporal attention (L-TAE) adds nothing over concatenating the 12 months and reducing them with PCA.
  • Label efficiency: no advantage for the GeoFMs in Morocco. In Utah, Clay with 25% of the training blocks equals the S2 baseline with all blocks.
  • Correction of an early finding: E02 suggested that the GeoFMs work better in Souss. E03 showed that this was an effect of the classical heads: with an MLP, the S2 features find 84% of the rainfed parcels there.
  • AgriFM is the weakest input: it gives one embedding for the whole year, so the seasonal profile is lost.

docs.title: 4. Next week
docs.text:
• RQ1 summary: best-vs-best comparison in the report generator (reproducible, Holm-corrected); update the progress page, research plan and Phase 2 overview.
  • Simple fine-tuning of Clay and Prithvi (RQ2): the encoder is trained together with the head, with the same folds, parcels and evaluation as RQ1, so the results compare directly with E02–E05; mapping head (D11); compute estimate.
  • LoRA fine-tuning of the same models: only small low-rank adapters are trained and the encoder weights stay frozen. Compare it with full fine-tuning and the frozen encoders (accuracy, training time, memory).
